items.title: Zelensky criticises 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
items.content:
# Zelensky criticises 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview

Watch: Zelensky questions "strange" Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview

- Published

**Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives.**

In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin.

"Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.

"He's an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.

Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the United States.

Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.

The latest round of peace talks, mediated in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.

He said talks were expected to resume in December.

On Thursday, Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".

But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.

And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.

The Kremlin appears to be resisting.

- Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
  - Published7 days ago
- Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend
  - Published5 days ago

Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.

Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.

So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".

"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.

The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.

In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.

The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.

Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.

Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.

But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Americans were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.

"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them more… It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.

"The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."

He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink – and its military version, Starshield – were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.

Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.

So whose decision was that?

"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."

## Tough winter

Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.

On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.

Zelensky defended the move, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".

He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without co-ordinating with its partners.

He declined to be more specific.

But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.

Recent attacks on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.

Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.

They have also plunged much of the city into darkness.

"\[Russia\] wants us to run away, of course," Zelensky said.

"People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."

items.title: Nvidia hits pause on chip shipments to Southeast Asia
items.content:
Nvidia is under pressure to do things differently, and a new WSJ report shows how far that’s going.

According to the Journal, Nvidia has told manufacturing partners, including Dell and Super Micro, to hit pause on server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia for an unspecified period as it assesses whether its regional partners are meeting U.S. export requirements.

As for why those countries, Chinese companies have been tapping Nvidia chips remotely from data centers there, a loophole the US Commerce Department closed — reportedly grudgingly — earlier this month. The Journal notes that the think tank Institute for Progress estimates remote data centers like these supply about 24% of China’s AI computing power.

items.title: Is Alice Huang a spy or not?
items.content:
The central, still-unproven claim in the Nvidia scandal is that Alice Huang, a former executive at the data-center company Megaspeed, is a Chinese spy. She had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who abruptly resigned on Nov. 12 after acknowledging it and was just as abruptly reinstated on Monday of this week.

What’s publicly known is murkier than the headlines suggest. U.S. intelligence has reportedly tracked Alice Huang’s contact with an officer of China’s spy agency, but officials haven’t offered public evidence that she was commissioned to target Nvidia’s chief. In the past week, after President Trump successfully pushed to bring Jensen Huang back, the administration has played down the allegations it once circulated internally. Whether that reflects new intelligence or political pressure is the big question.

Undisputed reporting shows the claim emerged from the White House itself. It first appeared in a highly classified memo written in March under the oversight of Secretary of State Marco Rubio and circulated to White House officials ahead of Trump’s trip to China in May. The memo formed the partial basis for the New York Times’ initial reporting on the scandal, published Oct. 29 and its existence was first reported on Nov. 8.

The memo did not definitively say, according to the Wall Street Journal, that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. CNN, by contrast, has reported that the memo concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset.

What’s better established is that Alice Huang was in touch with Chinese intelligence. The Ministry of State Security (MSS) is Beijing’s civilian spy agency, responsible for both foreign intelligence and domestic counterintelligence. Last weekend, the Times, citing people with knowledge of U.S. intelligence reports, reported that Huang was in contact with an MSS officer from the spring of 2025 until this fall, a period that overlaps her relationship with Jensen Huang. (The Chinese government has called the spy claims a “smear,” and Megaspeed says Huang left the company in August 2025 and that its business is legitimate.)

Top Trump officials have nonetheless all but discredited the espionage claims, along with the suggestion that Nvidia fell prey to spying or foreign influence.

Attorney General Todd Blanche, who was Trump’s personal defense lawyer before taking over the Justice Department, told journalists on Tuesday: “I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.” On the same day, Trump said a pardon was an option for Jensen Huang but that he did not think one would be needed. Senior intelligence officials reportedly told Congress that the government apparently has no actual evidence that the MSS directed Alice Huang to pursue an affair with Jensen Huang.

None of those statements necessarily exonerates Alice Huang as an intelligence agent. Instead, they support the alternate theory that the Chinese government didn’t tell her to begin the affair and that Jensen Huang broke no law by having it. Not being directed to have an affair isn’t the same as not being a spy, though.

From a certain angle, the circumstantial evidence surrounding Alice Huang looks quite suspicious. She was a top executive at a company investigated for illicitly channeling Nvidia chips to China, and her husband, Kang Wei, is said to have even closer ties to the MSS, with some sources saying he worked for the agency.

The timing of the government’s reversal is at the heart of the matter. Trump has said he lobbied the board “directly and indirectly” to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, so it wouldn’t be surprising if officials who serve at his pleasure were recasting the case in terms that satisfy his agenda. That wouldn’t necessarily make their assessments wrong. But unless new intelligence has actually resolved the question, and none has been publicly identified as yet, that backdrop is critical to keep in mind. CBS has also reported that Rubio, whose office oversaw the original memo, has privately voiced concerns about aspects of Jensen Huang’s return.

Doubts persist elsewhere, too. Earlier this month, CNN reported that the intelligence community was still working to understand Alice Huang’s relationship with Jensen Huang and that the intelligence collected on her to date does not prove she was acting as a spy for Beijing. After a briefing by top intelligence officials earlier this month, Rep. Jim Himes (D-Conn.), the incoming chair of the House Intelligence Committee, said he was unsure whether she was a spy or a “useful idiot.” And this week, the Wall Street Journal pointed out that under Chinese leader Xi Jinping, top corporate executives routinely maintain ties to the country’s intelligence service without being formally deputized as assets.

The crush of conflicting claims, most from anonymous government sources, obviously leaves large questions unanswered as to what actually transpired. Some of those questions that naturally spring to mind:

- Alice Huang is said to have been under U.S. surveillance for over a year. If the government suspected her of espionage, why wasn’t Jensen Huang warned earlier (and privately, so as not to cause the stock-market-destabilizing maelstrom that followed the more recent disclosure)? One explanation that has been given is that alerting the Nvidia chief might have tipped off Huang that her cover had been blown.
- If Alice Huang was a spy, what information did she pass to the Chinese government, and what influence did she actually have?
- Most critically, how did the allegation reach the public at all? The likeliest answer is a leak. A source told CNN that Rubio briefed Trump on the intelligence in May, yet Trump has since said he only recently learned of the concerns, and in October he presented Jensen Huang with the National Medal of Science. Officials who felt they could not get through to the president may have turned to reporters instead, which would explain how the contents of a memo whose existence has never been disputed found their way into print. What remains unclear is who leaked it, and whether they anticipated the fallout.

There are answers to all of these questions, of course, but when the public will get them is anybody’s guess. Jensen Huang is due to appear before the Senate Banking Committee next week, and by the look from the statements of some of its members, he’s likely in for a rough ride. Unfortunately, congressional hearings, particularly public ones, rarely unearth secrets that haven’t already been disclosed.

items.title: X finally gets parental controls after 20 years
items.content:
After 20 years of existence, X, the social network formerly known as Twitter, has finally added parental controls for teenagers, giving parents and guardians a way to manage what their kids see and interact with on the platform. But unlike most platforms’ implementation of such controls, X is putting its own spin on the system by giving teens a say in the matter.

The company said accounts belonging to 13-to-17-year-olds will be set to “protected mode” by default, meaning they won’t be able to see sensitive content, and won’t be served targeted ads. However, X is allowing teenagers to retain a measure of control over their accounts, letting them see what restrictions were made to their accounts. Parents and guardians will also not be able to read their teens’ private messages, see search or viewing history, or post as their teen.

The controls let parents see how much time their teen spends on X per week, set daily limits, require their approval for new followers, limit feed recommendations and videos to already followed accounts, filter specific words, turn off sensitive media, specify who can send their teen DMs, and see who they are messaging.

The controls arrive months after X came under fire for a lack of controls preventing the platform’s AI chatbot from being used to generate sexualized images of children and women. The social network has also long been rife with child sexual abuse material, misinformation, AI bots, and openly lets users post porn.

X has generally not been a platform aimed at teenagers, but that doesn’t mean they don’t use the platform. A 2024 study found that nearly a third of Gen Alpha kids have an X account. The platform itself requires users to be at least 13 years old, though that’s not a high bar given the kind of content on the platform.

“Parents want practical tools, and teens deserve room to grow. With Parental Controls on X, families can set the guardrails that fit their home, while teens keep ownership of their accounts and can see every change. Striking that balance is vital and what we set out to build.” Michael O’Herlihy, head of safety at X, wrote in a blog post.

items.title: A month with the iPhone Duo has changed how I use my phone
items.content:
For years, the definition of a premium smartphone depended on its cameras, processors, and how light it felt when you stowed it in your pocket. The iPhone Duo challenges that concept by asking consumers to pay more for a fundamentally different smartphone experience, even if it means sacrificing what they’ve long thought of as high-end features.

In a little under a month of using the Duo, I’ve found that the trade-offs I was initially concerned about matter far less to me than I had expected. What’s been more interesting is how the Duo’s foldable form factor has changed my everyday habits, including how I interact with apps, which apps I use, and how I organize and personalize the phone itself.

I also easily forgot a number of my initial concerns about switching to the Duo. The apps, for the most part, are now optimized for the Duo; I’ve reacquainted myself with Touch ID; and I don’t miss the Pro Max camera on most days.

That’s not to say the Duo doesn’t have its shortcomings. I still miss that telephoto lens sometimes, and I’m still longing for Face ID — though not as much since Apple shipped a face unlock feature in the latest update. But after a month of using the Duo, I’ve found these compromises have had less of an impact on my day-to-day experience compared with the benefits that the new form factor brings.

## Multitasking feels more natural

I was surprised by how much I’ve grown to appreciate the Duo’s multitasking capabilities. Initially, I didn’t think I’d regularly use it to view two apps side by side, given the still fairly limited screen space even while the phone is unfolded, especially compared with an iPad. But I’ve found myself snapping apps to both halves of the screen more often than I had imagined.

For starters, Apple has made this side-by-side mode incredibly intuitive and easy to use — you simply drag the app over to the left or right side of the screen and drop it into the target box that appears.

I have regularly taken advantage of this feature to do all sorts of things.

**Image Credits:**Apple

I really enjoy keeping X open as I read through the news, which allows me to switch back and forth between the article I’m reading and real-time reactions to it. Sometimes I’ll keep email or Slack open on the side while I’m working on something else so I don’t miss an important message or notification.

And much like the overstimulated members of Gen Z (which I am not), I sometimes like scrolling social media while engaging with some other media off to the side.

Case in point: I passively watched Netflix’s “Love is Blind” reunion while reading the gossipy tweets and Reddit posts about the main characters on the other side of the screen. This sort of TV watching behavior used to be called second-screen viewing, but now it’s morphing into something new. Everything is happening on one screen, so should we call it “Duo screen viewing,” perhaps? It makes me long for even more interactive TV experiences where commentary and content are combined.

## It really is like having two phones

I’ve noticed another shift in my behavior since adopting the Duo as my main device. When I’m out and about, the Duo feels more like an (arguably heavier) iPhone mini. For those who still miss smaller iPhones, the Duo is the next best thing. Despite its weight, the phone *feels* small. You can cover it with one hand; you can type with a thumb; you can reach the top and bottom easily; and you can even fit it into your front and back pockets. The Pro Max now feels unbelievably strange in my hand — how was I ever comfortable wrangling this giant rectangle?

The Duo’s small screen works well when you’re on the go, especially for short interactions like responding to a quick text or pulling up directions to a destination. It’s not as great for mindless scrolling, which I appreciate, as it forces me to engage with the real world instead of killing every moment of boredom or unease by opening up apps.

**Image Credits:**NurPhoto / Contributor (opens in a new window) / Getty Images

But when you’re home or somewhere with time to kill, you can unfold the screen and enjoy your apps super-sized. It’s the best of both worlds.

I find that I instinctively unfold the phone when I’m preparing to watch videos, because the larger screen is best for that. It’s also unfolded if I’m shopping, as it’s more convenient for looking at products, zooming in to examine the details, or complete checkout forms.

Generally, I also unfold the Duo when I’m actively using apps. This setup has also allowed me to rethink my Home Screen layout: With the Duo closed, I prefer to see just widgets on the small screen with key information like weather, time, battery life, and so on. Meanwhile, the only app icons on the Home Screen are those in the dock.

## The Duo apps are ready now

In the weeks since its launch, most of the apps that weren’t yet optimized for the Duo have been upgraded to support its foldable form factor. In mid-November, Apple said there were over 200,000 Duo-ready apps, and in my experience, that certainly feels true. A majority of my so-called “daily drivers” — with the glaring exception of key Google apps like Gmail and Drive — have dropped the black band on the side of the screen that was frustrating early testers of the phone.

Most apps now take advantage of the available space, whether that’s on the Duo’s small front screen or the wider, unfolded one.

I’ve also found it interesting to see the different interpretations developers have had for how to best optimize their app for Duo.

Some have used the form factor as a way to bring in some sort of novelty: there’s a note-taking app that opens and closes like a notebook, with pages you can write on with the Apple Pencil; a retro Walkman-like music player; a tiny typewriter; a gaming handheld; a game where you close the phone to make grilled cheese.

**Image Credits:**Tiny Computers

As much as I love the whimsy of this group of apps, I appreciate how my everyday apps feel better to use on the unfolded screen. Spotify, at last, feels less cluttered when it has more screen real estate. A number of note-taking, list-making, and calendar apps also feel somehow more usable when spread out.

The Netflix app is actually fantastic with its support for multiple viewing modes, which include playing video on the closed outer display, the “laptop” orientation with its big player controls, and the “tent” mode.

**Image Credits:**Apple

Other developers have similarly reimagined how their app would work if it had originally been designed for the Duo’s small and larger screens.

One good example of this is Sofa, a handy utility for organizing the books, movies, TV shows, podcasts, albums, and games you want to check out. When the Duo is closed, its navigation is tucked off to the right side in a vertical bar, while the main screen focuses on the items you’ve saved. But when the Duo is unfolded, the number of items displayed on the screen also expands into a two-column layout, with more of your items featured on the screen and your lists on the left side. It doesn’t feel like two different apps, but like you’ve opened up the app itself and given it more space to spread out.

**Image Credits:**Sofa (screenshot from their Threads post) (opens in a new window)

In terms of your daily social media scroll, apps like TikTok and Instagram have been updated to be perfectly usable on the Duo, whether the phone is open or closed. When closed, TikTok now stretches the video to cover the screen, instead of showing the ugly black bar. Scrolling short-form videos on the Duo, while unfolded like a slightly smaller iPad mini, has become my preferred way to watch.

**Image Credits:**TikTok screenshot from folded Duo

## I’m reading more books

Here’s another surprise: I’ve spent less time with my Kindle, and am instead reading books on my Duo. Unfolded, the Duo is a decent enough replacement for an e-book reader, albeit it can be a bit more stimulating as it’s not an e-ink device. However, the matte inner screen isn’t quite as bright and distracting as your typical glossy OLED display. There’s less glare and softer reflections, but there’s also something about the display that just feels calmer than a smartphone, allowing you to more fully engage with a book’s text.

Unfolded and held vertically, reading on the Duo feels a lot like reading on the standard Kindle, at least in terms of hand-feel. And putting your phone into the “Do Not Disturb” focus mode can help you not be distracted by incoming notifications and messages while you read.

**Image Credits:**Actually Read (opens in a new window)

You can also unfold the device while keeping it in landscape orientation, with the screens bent slightly inward like a real book. For even more fun, you can turn on Kindle’s page-turn animation, which makes it seem as if you’re turning the page in a physical book. And I love how you can “performatively read” using an app like Book2Life or Actually Read — they display the book’s cover on the Duo’s outer screen as you read the text on the inner screen.

E-book readers will likely find they can carry one less device when they’re out and about, because the Duo can stand in for whatever Kindle or other reader you typically keep in your purse or bag. You can save the Kindle for other times, whether that’s at home, on long travel days, or when you don’t want to worry about sand getting into your $2,000 phone.

## **I don’t need a PopSocket**

On the big-screened iPhone 17 Pro Max I used to carry, I tended to keep a PopSocket of some sort on the back because the phone was both heavy and large, which made it hard to hold for longer periods of time. The Duo is similarly heavy, but its shape makes it far easier to hold in one hand without the extra help.

Folded, you can do the usual one-handed hold where the bottom edge of the phone rests on your pinky, your other three fingers cradle the back, and your thumb is free to navigate the screen.

Unfolded, the Duo’s like using a small Kindle or iPad mini, where two hands are required. You also don’t need a PopSocket for balancing the phone on the side, because it can be propped up like a tent or opened like a tiny laptop. Or, if you prefer, Apple and others offer Duo cases with a built-in stand. (Apple’s case comes in navy and taupe, though, so if you’re not boring, you’ll probably want to shop from third-party vendors).

**Image Credits:**PopSockets (opens in a new window)

If you think you still might need a PopSocket at times, or you just aren’t ready to give it up, the brand now makes a slimmer version: its Low-Pro Grip. There are other competitors, like the OhSnap grips, which aren’t a bad alternative either.

## It’s inspiring personalization

There’s something about the Duo that seems to have kicked off a new iPhone personalization trend, at least judging by what I’ve been seeing on social media.

Unlike a regular iPhone, where every phone case is simply a shell that offers a degree of protection based on the materials used, the Duo case lineup provides far more variety.

You can buy cases with and without built-in screen protectors, and some use adhesive to better stick to the outer screen, while others don’t. Some cases let you customize the band around the outer screen with a different color than the case that protects the rest of the phone.

Then you have cases that cover the hinge, while others leave it exposed. There are cases that offer holes where you can attach straps, wristlets, and charms. Some of those have attachment points at the bottom and others on the side.

Essentially, there are a lot of options for customizing how you want to carry the Duo and how you want to express your own style.

I’m also now starting to see whimsical cases that come with attached pens. (Thank goodness — most of the pen cases so far have been kind of plain!)

**Image Credits:**Kai Studio (opens in a new window)

I also believe there’s something about the Duo that particularly appeals to women. Maybe because it’s small, or maybe it’s because you can attach a strap to its side and carry it like a little purse. Or maybe because, like a purse, you can deck it out with chains and charms — a choice that’s grown increasingly popular as young people have embraced whimsical, retro tech as a way to express their individuality and sense of fashion.

The Duo easily lends itself to this trend, perhaps even more than a regular iPhone. It becomes an accessory you want on display, not one buried in a bag.

**Image Credits:**Cases.com (opens in a new window)

Before switching to the Duo, I spent a lot of time thinking about what I’d be giving up by moving away from the Pro Max.

I’m surprised to find that, a month later, I only think about what I’d have to give up if I switched back to a traditional iPhone. It’s not just the extra space of the unfolded screen I’d miss — it’s all the little habits I’ve developed around having different screen sizes for different purposes.

The Duo makes me pause and think about how I want to use an app. That small moment of deliberation, before I even open the phone, has helped me break some of my more mindless smartphone habits, particularly around social media.

That’s not a benefit I could have anticipated if I’d judged the device by its specifications alone.

items.title: ‘I’m no longer a UAE official’: UN hopeful Lana Nusseibeh tries to shake off Sudan record
items.content:
Lana Nusseibeh is in Britain this week, attempting to present herself as a potential future UN secretary general, and shift the focus from her past as a United Arab Emirates diplomat who denied the country’s role in arming a militia accused of war crimes and genocide in Sudan’s four-year civil war.

It is a high-risk strategy that involves meeting ministers, MPs, academics and holding a public event with the UN Association.

Labelled by many British NGOs and others as an apologist for war crimes, Nusseibeh is presenting herself as a skilled diplomat with the network to put the UN back at the centre of mediation, development and human rights.

“These are very geopolitical times,” she said in an interview. “You need a geopolitical secretary general, because the fact is these geopolitical ruptures are not going away. These fissures in the international system are not going to dissolve any time soon.”

Nusseibeh had a setback last Friday, when three permanent members of the UN security council, China, France and the UK, all voted to “discourage” her candidature. The UN’s electoral system requires that she secure nine positive votes from the 15-strong security council, and no discouragement from the permanent five (P5) before being recommended to the UN general assembly.

She has the backing of the US and Russia, and thinks her cause is not lost. “Sometimes, the use of the veto is tactical. Sometimes, it’s a holding position, sometimes it’s a leveraging position. There are a number of different theories”.

The centre of the resistance to Nusseibeh’s candidacy is probably London, and specifically the Foreign Office, the penholder on Sudan at the UN, and this may explain the UK political blitz.

When questioned about her role in Sudan, she asked that her candidacy be seen in the round, highlighting her role in forcing humanitarian aid into Gaza, her support for Afghan women and promoting interfaith tolerance.

“Like every candidate, I come from somewhere, but the independence of the incoming secretary general is the key to their credibility.

“I’ve taken a leave of absence from my role in \[the\] UAE government in order to independently campaign for this role. But I think that if I was secretary general, Sudan would be the litmus test of success for any incoming secretary because it’s such a horrific humanitarian crisis.”

The war in Sudan, which erupted in April 2023 after a power struggle between the military and the Rapid Support Forces, has displaced more than 14 million people and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. Multiple regional powers, including the UAE, have backed different local proxies since the beginning of the conflict in an attempt to win influence and strategic resources.

The UAE has long been accused of supporting the RSF in Sudan, a charge repeatedly denied by Nusseibeh, who has publicly disputed the findings of UN investigators.

A UN panel of experts suggested last month that the UAE had supplied crucial support to the RSF.

Asked if she regretted dissembling during her time as a diplomat, by denying the UAE had armed the RSF, or her personal role in challenging the UN reports critical of the UAE, Nusseibeh said she regretted that “the Sudanese civil war had continued for so long”.

Nusseibeh added: “But I don’t think saying that is enough for the Sudanese people and the people in the surrounding countries where they’ve also felt the impact of this war, or for the victims of sexual violence and in this conflict, the atrocities committed in El Fasher without accountability, and the use of chemical weapons against the civilian population; all of these are a litany of suffering that has been inflicted on the Sudanese people.”

Asked if the UAE had been supplying weapons to the RSF in a breach of a UN embargo, she replied: “I’m aware of the allegations. I haven’t read the last UN panel of experts report, but I’m not going to comment as I’m no longer a UAE official. In this campaign, I am a secretary general candidate.

“As secretary general, I would fully back the findings of all UN panel of experts reports and I’m aware that I think several countries have been mentioned in various reports.”She later added: “I would call out countries that are supplying arms to any of the parties, including those in the RSF … this needs a process that requires accountability for atrocities that have been committed. That it needs to be a process primarily led by the Sudanese people.”

Nusseibeh said she was willing to take risks to mediate and to put UN values, expertise and its development toolkit at the centre of disputes. Her analysis of contemporary diplomacy was that the world had descended into a default setting of non-cooperation, and the UN needed to restate the case for collaboration between nations as being in the self-interest of everyone.

The UN had been missing from too many conflicts, she argued, and she would set up a mediation board to try to use the full UN toolkit, ranging from confidence-building measures to development to secure peace. “What’s missing is this idea of a secretary general that is a strategist and a mediator-in-chief that is looking at the sort of the blips on the dashboard of conflict and saying, ‘How do we deploy to have maximum impact for most effective use of resource and cost?’ Because resources are not going up, they’re going down. I mean, we’re looking at, since 2010, 40% increase in military spending. So we’re using a lot of hard power as countries and systems to deter, but it’s not actually working.”

That would require some prioritisation at the UN – it has 4,000 different open mandates.

Her intelligence and skills as a diplomat are not in question. However, her track record over Sudan is.

One critic said: “It is a very smart strategic play by the UAE that seeks autocratic capture, and then the asset-stripping of the UN and its standards. The UAE would end the UN’s role on climate. It would be a catastrophe.”

The next security council vote is on Monday. By then some of the backmarkers may have dropped out of the race. The diplomats of the P5 may also be clearer on the flexibility of their mandates, in which case the papal conclave may finally produce white smoke.

items.title: 手表和眼镜，如何成为AI智能体的「随身感官」？
items.content:
去年，Humane关闭了AI Pin的消费者云服务。这款别在衣服上的AI设备一度被寄予厚望，用户只需开口，就能完成许多原本需要掏出手机才能做的事。AI Pin最终没能进入主流市场，却给后来者留下了一道产品定义题，手机已经有了成熟的计算、通信和应用生态，用户为什么还需要一件戴在身上的AI设备？

11月25日，在深圳举行的第七届紫光展锐智能穿戴沙龙上，紫光展锐智能穿戴产品线总经理李彬重新提起了AI Pin。在他看来，交互延迟、发热和应用生态都影响了体验，更根本的问题出在定位上。一件体积和电池都更小的设备，试图接过一部手机的任务，最容易丢掉的恰好是它贴身佩戴的优势。

李彬给出了另一种分工。手机继续承担复杂计算、数据和任务管理，手表持续感知人的身体状态，眼镜从第一视角观察环境。当AI需要理解一个人此刻身在何处、正在做什么，手腕和眼前这两个位置，能提供手机放在口袋里时很难获得的信息。

这给了手表和眼镜成为智能体入口的理由，也改变了芯片厂商要解的题。要让这套随身感官工作一整天，工程师先得算清楚，用户还没有发出指令时，设备已经花了多少电。

**从记录数据到主动服务，穿戴设备要读懂用户的处境**

过去几年，智能手表的升级很直观。屏幕越做越大，心率、血氧、体温等传感器陆续加了进来，续航从一天延长到一周甚至更久。用户抬腕可以看消息、接电话，运动结束后还能看到配速、心率和消耗的热量。

李彬认为，随着硬件不断升级，单靠参数迭代给用户带来的体验提升已经越来越有限。

如今的手表已经能在后台持续记录，也能在心率达到预设阈值时发出提醒。到了智能体时代，设备需要进一步判断，同一个信号在这个人此时此地的处境里意味着什么。

以跑步为例。如果用户正在按训练计划加速，心率上升本来就在预期之中。如果已经进入恢复阶段，配速降了下来，心率却迟迟没有回落，这时候提醒用户调整节奏才更有价值。两种情况下，传感器测到的心率可能相同。要决定该不该开口，手表还得知道用户原本打算怎么跑，以及过去几分钟里发生了什么。

眼镜把这种变化从感知身体延伸到了感知环境。

比如到了车站，手机里有车票和行程，眼镜看到的是用户面前的指示牌。如果两台设备能够协作，AI就有机会在用户走错方向时给出提示。对赶车的人来说，省掉的是停下来、找车票、查检票口、再抬头辨认方向的几个动作。其中一些信息原本就存储在手机里，只是手机缺少一个视角，判断人此刻正走向哪里。

李彬把未来的可穿戴形容为一套随身的感官，也希望它是带着一套跟着你走的记忆。

感官让AI获得当下的身体和环境信息，记忆让它把眼前的变化与训练目标、出行计划和个人习惯联系起来。由此，手表和眼镜有机会把服务往前移一步，在用户主动打开应用、描述问题之前，就完成一部分判断。

难点也来自这一步。用户主动拍一张指示牌问路，按下快门的动作已经告诉设备，哪一帧值得处理。

要让眼镜主动提供帮助，连什么时候值得看清楚，都要由设备自己判断。采样太少，可能错过指示牌。每帧都看、每帧都算，摄像头、存储和处理器就得一直消耗镜腿里那块电池的电量。

要让这套随身感官工作一整天，穿戴芯片最先碰到的瓶颈是什么？

**穿戴设备要持续感知，为什么续航和存储带宽排在算力前面？**

要把AI放进手表和眼镜，很容易首先思考的是芯片能跑多大的模型。

紫光展锐产品架构部高级总监张慧敏在可穿戴沙龙先问了另外两个问题，一块穿戴设备的电池怎么让AI一整天都在？低功耗系统只有几MB片上内存，怎么让它持续看懂周围的世界？排在第三位的，才是怎么让眼镜算得动。

这个顺序有一个前提，讨论的是全天候感知。拍一次照片、做一次翻译，任务结束后设备就能休眠。要在用户开口前发现值得留意的变化，哪怕一段时间里什么都没发生，负责观察的那部分系统也已经工作了很久。偶尔运行几秒的高性能任务，可以集中调用算力。需要常开的功能，每多用一点功率，都要按佩戴时间算进续航。

因此，张慧敏给基础感知链路定的目标是毫瓦级功耗。展锐的做法是在芯片里划出一个独立供电的常开域，用专用片上存储器SRAM和低功耗NPU处理传感器数据。

以摄像头为例，平时先降低采样规格，用较少的图像信息判断画面里有没有值得关注的变化。需要看清文字、全画质拍摄或者做更复杂的识别时，再打开高性能影像通路。

降低采样规格，也减轻了存储带宽的压力。摄像头一帧接一帧地送来数据，低功耗感知通路里的SRAM只有几MB。容量决定一次能缓存多少数据，带宽决定单位时间能读写多少数据。当分辨率提高、帧率上升，芯片既要为图像处理付出功耗，也要为搬运这些图像付出功耗。即便NPU还有算力，下一帧也得先送到它手里。

佰维存储PDT总经理王慧莲从整机角度补充了一个细节。带显示的眼镜处理摄像头画面时，还可能同时刷新显示、读取模型数据。几项任务并行，争用的是同一套设备里有限的存储资源。对芯片和存储厂商而言，在数据进入主系统之前先做一次筛选，可以同时减少后面的数据搬运和计算。

到了算力这一层，问题就变得具体了，什么任务在哪里算，什么时候值得唤醒更大的系统？

张慧敏介绍，展锐的方案里常开域负责事件检测，命中后再唤醒主域，调用主NPU处理较复杂的模型，或打开全分辨率影像通路。任务完成，主域可以整体断电。这个设计对初步判断的准确性提出了要求。一次误判可能只让用户多看一条提示，也可能让整套高性能系统多醒一次。唤醒得过于频繁，常开域省下的电会很快用回去。

这种分工还可以延伸到穿戴设备、手机和云端，也就是端边云协同。

眼镜先在本地判断看到了什么，手机把画面线索与行程、位置等信息结合起来，计算量更大的任务再考虑交给云端。外部算力可以分担推理，连接网络、上传数据和等待结果也都有成本。用户走到岔路口时需要的提示，留给系统的响应时间，显然与事后整理一段行程记录不同。

展锐在现场展示的Android＋RTOS混动双擎，让计算在穿戴设备上就可以按需调用。用户从Android桌面点开应用，主控SoC把启动请求发给低功耗MCU，同时移交显示和触控的控制权。随后由MCU运行应用、绘制界面、响应触控，退出应用后再回到Android桌面。用户看到的是一次连续操作，后台已经换了一颗芯片干活。

李彬说，“上一届可穿戴沙龙就有客户问，Android、RTOS两套系统能否做到真正的混动。经过一年打磨，这项技术已在客户端量产上市。”

展锐还在可穿戴沙龙上公布了基于Android 16深度定制的Android Lite OS，可以在1 GB内存配置下运行。

据李彬介绍，这套系统已在儿童手表、成人手表和智能眼镜上落地。混动双擎决定哪些任务可以交给低功耗系统，Android Lite OS则让设备在有限内存下保留新版Android的应用兼容性和安全能力。

**展锐发布W927和G1，分别瞄准手表独立联网和眼镜常开感知**

手表从4G升级到5G，套片面积还能做得更小。这是李彬介绍展锐首款5G RedCap SoC W927时，给出的一个具体对照。按他的说法，经过主控封装和配套芯片的小型化设计，W927套片面积小于展锐此前的4G智能手表方案，在儿童手表上可以做到单面布板。

这个指标对儿童手表尤其有意义。孩子离开家长和手机之后，通话、定位信息回传都需要独立连接。但表壳要适合孩子的手腕，主板和电池要共用有限的空间。升级通信制式的同时能把套片做小，终端厂商就有更多余地安排电池和其他器件。

W927采用大小核异构设计，增强小核的感知能力，并通过双系统调配不同负载。雷峰网了解到，W927计划于2027年量产上市。展锐还将为终端客户提供软硬件设计方案、双系统功耗调优和外设适配支持。最终能有多少面积留给电池、独立联网时能使用多久，还要看整机厂商的设计。

面向智能眼镜的G1视听一体智能眼镜旗舰平台，则把原本可由主控SoC和外部MCU分担的工作集成到一颗芯片上。前面提到两颗芯片如何面对不同的应用，G1进一步把眼镜所需的两类任务放进同一颗芯片：小系统承担常驻感知，大系统按需处理影像、音视频、显示和较复杂的端侧推理。

这种集成一方面能减轻布板压力，另一方面也给眼镜厂商留下了产品选择。音频、拍摄眼镜可以优先考虑语音交互和第一视角感知，带显示的眼镜还要为图像输出和显示预留功耗。

按展锐公布的时间表，G1计划于2027年下半年推向市场。

做整机的人还要算另一笔账。谷东智能首席运营官曹炳辰提到，有些带显示的眼镜会从镜片前侧漏光，旁人能看见佩戴者眼前的亮光。外界光线照到镜片上产生的彩虹纹，又会影响佩戴者看外面的世界。他希望在保证光学效果的前提下，尽量做到无感。

这个细节和芯片功耗谈的是同一件事。要让眼镜有机会感知一整天，先得让人愿意戴它一整天。

智能体正在改变可穿戴产品的设计起点。过去，运动记录、独立通话、第一视角拍摄，各自就能支撑一类产品。往后，手表记录的身体变化、眼镜看到的环境，都可能成为智能体发起下一次服务的依据。哪些信息值得持续获取，哪些判断应该留在本地，哪些任务适合与手机协作，将直接影响下一代手表和眼镜的形态。

产业链面对的挑战和机会也随之扩大。对芯片和存储厂商，难题是在有限的电量和空间里处理更多信息，机会是从架构设计阶段就参与定义终端能力。对整机、模型和应用厂商，机会是把过去需要用户打开应用才能获得的服务，带到运动、出行等具体时刻。

更难的考验随之而来：哪些事重要到值得设备留意一整天，又能在真正发生时，让用户觉得这件设备值得一直戴着？雷峰网

items.title: MU, SNDK, SKHY Jump As Nvidia Tests Kioxia Memory Fix — Analyst Presses Memory Giants For ‘Massive’ Buybacks - Yahoo Finance
items.content:
# MU, SNDK, SKHY Jump As Nvidia Tests Kioxia Memory Fix — Analyst Presses Memory Giants For ‘Massive’ Buybacks

- The Nvidia Way author Tae Kim urged memory chipmakers to back their long-term forecasts with "massive stock buybacks."
- Micron can begin using its $35.16 billion buyback authorization on Dec. 9 under its U.S. CHIPS Act funding agreements.
- SanDisk spent $5 billion on buybacks in its latest quarter. SK hynix plans to buy back and retire at least 60 trillion won worth of shares.

Shares of Micron (MU), SanDisk (SNDK) and SK hynix (SKHY) jumped overnight heading into Thursday after Kioxia said its flash drives could help Nvidia's AI chips access a database of up to 2 trillion vectors. For 'The Nvidia Way' author Tae Kim, the question is how much confidence memory chipmakers have in their own long-term forecasts. He urged them to show it with "massive stock buybacks."

SNDK led the gains overnight, rising 4%, followed by SKHY up nearly 3%, MU up over 2%, and NVDA up over 1%.

In Tokyo, Kioxia Holdings shares climbed nearly 15% to 7,895 yen on Thursday. A day earlier, the company said its operating unit would pay it 2.21 trillion yen on Friday. The cash stays within the Kioxia group. Shareholders will receive a separate payout on Dec. 8, when Kioxia pays its first interim dividend.

## **Nvidia Tests A Way Past GPU Memory Limits**

Nvidia's (NVDA) GB200 NVL72 rack pairs 72 GPUs with 13.4 terabytes of high-bandwidth memory (HBM). When an AI database exceeds capacity, the system may have to process it in batches and repeatedly move data between storage and memory. Nvidia's SCADA software lets the GPUs retrieve small blocks of data directly from solid-state drives.

For the test, Kioxia equipped one rack with 144 XD8 drives, adding about 1.1 petabytes of raw flash storage, which is 80 times the capacity of the rack's high-bandwidth memory. Kioxia estimates that the setup could support a database of up to 2 trillion 512-byte vectors, the numerical representations AI systems use to find related information. The companies are still evaluating how efficiently the rack can process data at that scale.

"The intelligence of AI agents will increasingly depend on the knowledge they can access, not just the compute power they consume," said Jason Hardy, Nvidia's vice president of storage tech.

Kioxia also reported results for its next-gen GP2 drive. In a separate test, it handled more than 18 million random reads per second using 512-byte blocks, nearly twice its predecessor's rate. Kioxia expects to send evaluation samples to select customers by the end of 2027.

items.title: 机器人量产背后，物理AI开始算新账：研发底座何必各自建？
items.content:
**2026年，人形机器人加速走出实验室。**

但是让机器人在真实世界产生价值，依然复杂而成本高昂。

从数据采集、物理仿真到模型训练、真机验证，机器人每掌握一项新技能，背后都可能是一整套研发流程的反复运转。

更复杂的是，这些能力分散在不同的专业厂商手中。产业分工越来越细，如何将分散的技术能力组织起来，反而成了一道新的难题。

**当机器人开始规模化交付，产业需要解决的不只是如何造出更多机器人，还有如何让更多企业以更低的成本训练机器人。**

这也让物理AI产业出现了一个新的机会：谁有能力将分散的研发资源组织成可复用的基础设施，谁就有机会成为产业链上的重要组织者。

九章云极正尝试从算力供应商向物理AI开发平台延伸，通过物理AI工厂、生态联盟和标准化接口，参与这场产业分工的重构。

****01****

#### ****机器人越造越多，研发底座开始走向共建****

《2026年人形机器人产业发展报告》显示，今年上半年，中国人形机器人出货量已超过4万台。

机器人走出实验室后，需要掌握更多技能，适应不同的工作环境。每进入一个新的应用场景，机器人企业都可能需要开发新的技能，研发任务也随之增加。

这背后是一条需要不断重复的研发链。

举个简单的例子，智能机器人完成一个抓取动作，要经过数据采集、仿真、训练和真机验证。物理AI的特殊之处就在于，仿真中成功的抓取，可能会因为现实中的光照、物体材质或位置变化而失败。

一旦抓取失败，相关数据还得回流训练，推动下一轮调整。这样的试错可能反复发生，那随之而来的是持续增长的数据处理、仿真和训练需求。

对物理AI研发企业来说，研发成本不仅来自算力和设备，还来自不同系统之间的集成与适配。

数据采集、仿真、训练和验证可以交给不同的专业厂商，但分工之后如何让不同环节顺利衔接，又成了新的难题。

模型训练完成后，需要适配不同的仿真环境。真机测试产生的失败数据，还需要经过处理才能进入下一轮训练。不同厂商的数据格式、开发工具和运行环境存在差异，研发团队仍要花费大量精力完成系统对接。

这也是物理AI产业分工不断细化后面临的新矛盾，**各个环节的专业化程度越来越高，跨环节协同的复杂度也在增加。**

如果每家物理AI研发企业都要自行整合算力、仿真和验证工具，重复建设的问题并没有真正解决，只是从硬件设施转向了软件适配和系统集成。

随着越来越多企业参与物理AI研发，一套能够共享基础资源、连接不同工具和研发流程的底座，开始具有经济上的吸引力。

这种基础设施共建的趋势，已经在全球多个市场出现。

在日本，由索尼、软银、NEC、本田等44家企业及机构参与投资的Noetra，规划建设140兆瓦AI工厂，为物理AI基础模型研发提供算力支持。

德国通过Robotics Institute Germany（德国机器人研究院）推动高校和科研机构共享实验室、研究数据及软件工具；韩国则通过Physical AI Global Alliance（物理AI全球联盟），组织整机制造、AI技术及应用企业开展合作。

三国路径虽然不同，但都反映了很接近的产业趋势。随着物理AI的研发投入与技术复杂度不断提高，企业开始通过共建基础设施、共享研发资源来分担成本，实现专业化分工。

中国也在建设具身智能数据平台、训练场和公共测试设施，但资源分散、接口标准不统一、不同机器人平台的数据兼容等问题依然存在。

随着物理AI产业分工逐渐细化，单个企业拥有的数据、算力和研发工具，已经难以满足跨领域协作的需求。**产业需要一套共用的研发底座，让不同企业能够在共享基础设施的同时，发挥各自的专业优势。**

谁能推动这套体系的建设，谁就有机会成为物理AI产业分工中的重要组织者。

九章云极正尝试从这一环节切入。作为独立第三方AI基础设施服务商，九章云极提出建设物理AI工厂，以算力调度和研发工具为基础，通过生态合作连接数据、仿真、模型训练和真机验证等专业能力。

但把研发资源连接起来只是第一步。共用底座能否真正创造价值，最终还要看它能否让每一次训练和验证变得更高效、更便宜。

****02****

#### ****物理AI工厂，要让每一次试错都更便宜****

共用研发底座的价值，核心不在共享本身，而在提高整条研发链的运行效率。

物理AI研发需要反复经历仿真、训练和真机验证。一轮训练结束后，如果模型在真实环境中未能完成任务，就需要将失败数据重新投入下一轮训练。

在这个过程中，算力资源能否及时分配、不同研发环节能否顺利衔接、已有的数据和模型能否重复利用，都会影响每一轮试错的时间和成本。

因此，衡量物理AI研发效率，除了计算资源消耗，还需要看这些投入最终带来了多少经过验证的有效成果。

在11月25日举行的“算力唤醒真实世界”2026物理AI行业峰会暨九章云极智算生态大会（下称大会）上，九章云极AI首席科学家缪旭提出了物理AI工厂（Physical AI Factory）的建设思路，试图通过算力调度和研发工具的工程化，将数据、仿真、训练与真实反馈组织成持续迭代的研发体系。

要让这套体系高效运转，首先需要解决的是不同研发任务之间的算力资源错配问题。

与大语言模型训练相对集中的计算负载不同，物理AI的研发同时涉及物理引擎计算、图形渲染、模型训练和实时推理，不同任务对CPU、GPU及部署环境的要求存在差异。

例如，大规模仿真可能需要大量CPU和图形GPU资源，强化学习又需要计算资源在仿真与模型训练之间高效衔接。若缺乏统一调度，就可能出现部分计算设备排队、另一部分设备闲置的情况。

这类需求推动物理AI基础设施从单一算力供给走向异构计算资源的统一管理。

九章云极提出的混合算力编排（Hybrid Compute Orchestration），正是希望根据研发任务的负载变化动态分配计算资源，并支持模型与运行轨迹在不同计算环境之间传输。

与此同时，物理AI的训练与部署还横跨云、边、端不同环境。云端承担基础模型训练、大规模并行仿真和分布式强化学习；边缘侧处理低延迟推理、区域数据和局部仿真；设备端则负责传感器融合、实时控制和物理执行。

如何让不同计算环境之间的任务、模型和数据有效衔接，也是九章云极提出云边端协同混合计算架构的原因。

缪旭将这一思路概括为：“**把对的算力，在对的时间，放到对的任务上。**”

但算力调度解决的主要是资源利用问题，物理AI研发的另一部分成本，来自大量重复性的工程操作。

以强化学习为例，如果每轮训练都需要人工配置环境、启动仿真任务、迁移数据，再对训练结果进行评测，即使底层算力充足，研发效率依然可能受到任务衔接和人工操作的制约。

因此，物理AI研发平台还需要将仿真、训练和评测等环节组织为可以自动执行的工作流程，同时让模型、仿真场景、合成数据、失败案例及评测报告成为可复用的研发资产。

九章云极的物理AI工厂，也将多阶段任务编排与研发成果复用纳入工具体系，希望减少研发人员在重复配置和跨系统操作上的时间消耗。

算力调度与工具链优化最终需要回答同一个问题：花同样的成本，究竟能完成多少次有效训练和验证？

九章云极为此提出了Factory Efficiency这一衡量口径：

**Factory Efficiency = 验证通过的有效物理经验 ÷ 总计算与运行成本**

Factory Efficiency将研发成本与经过验证的有效成果联系起来，为衡量物理AI工厂的研发效率提供了一个新思路。

从算力利用率到有效试错成本，物理AI基础设施的价值正在从资源供给延伸至研发效率。

算力调度和研发工具解决了底座问题，底座之上还有一层分工，仿真、算法、真机验证等专业能力分散在不同厂商手中。

如何让这些企业的技术能力真正接入同一套体系，并形成可持续的协作关系，则是平台建设的下一道门槛。

****03****

#### ****两层API背后，物理AI的开发平台生意****

要让不同厂商的专业能力在同一套研发体系中协同，首先需要解决两个问题。

不同定位的企业如何分工，不同环节的技术和工具又如何衔接。

一次完整的强化学习任务，可能同时用到GPU算力、仿真引擎、训练框架和模型评测，而这些能力来自不同厂商，软件环境、数据格式和调用方式各不相同。

物理AI研发平台不能只把算力和工具集中起来，还要让这些分散的能力变成可以按需调用的服务。

九章云极选择的路径，是以自身积累的异构算力调度、模型开发和强化学习训练能力作为底座，通过生态合作引入其他专业厂商的技术能力。

在大会上，九章云极发布物理AI生态联盟计划，联合仿真、算法、本体及应用场景等领域的企业，共同参与物理AI研发体系建设。

九章云极董事长方磊表示，**九章云极希望以算力底座为基础，与生态伙伴共建产业生态，推动不同厂商的接口兼容、标准协商和研发成果共享。**

在这套架构中，物理AI工厂被划分为数据工厂、模型工厂、仿真验证工厂、真实世界验证工厂及运营部署平台，分别承担数据处理、模型训练、仿真评测、真机验证及后续部署运营等任务。

不过，**联盟解决的是谁来提供专业能力的问题，真正让这些能力协同运转，还需要统一的技术接口。**

不同厂商即使加入同一个联盟，如果仍然需要针对每个客户分别开发接口、适配运行环境，产业协作的成本就没有得到根本改善。

中国电子技术标准化研究院副院长范科峰则指出，随着物理AI走向规模化部署，数据接口、通信协议及安全边界等标准化问题将愈发突出。

针对不同厂商研发工具的接入与调用问题，九章云极提出了两层API体系。

其中，Physical AI Infra API面向基础设施资源，提供标准化的资源调用接口；Physical AI Dev API面向开发任务，让开发者通过接口调用仿真、训练等专业工具。

对于物理AI研发企业而言，如果这些能力能够通过统一接口调用，开发者就不必分别对接算力、仿真和训练服务商，而可以围绕具体研发任务组合所需资源。对于仿真、算法等技术供应商，接入统一平台则有机会减少针对不同客户的重复适配，并触达更多开发者。

更重要的是，当研发任务可以通过统一接口发起，平台就有机会进一步记录算力使用量、工具调用次数等信息，并在此基础上建立计量和收费机制。

**这意味着平台的商业价值可能不再局限于出租计算资源，而是进一步延伸至研发服务的组织、计量与商业分配。**

九章云极试图通过物理AI工厂、生态联盟和两层API，完成从算力供应商向研发协作平台的延伸。前者提供基础设施与工程化工具，后者则尝试把不同企业的专业能力连接起来，形成可持续的服务体系。

随着更多技术供应商与开发者参与，物理AI基础设施的竞争也将进一步延伸至开发工具、接口标准和开发者生态。

****04****

#### ****物理AI，正在寻找自己的CUDA****

物理AI的研发环节越分越细，连接这些环节的角色也就越重要。

未来物理AI产业的竞争，除了看模型、本体和算力产品，还要看谁能把研发资源组织得更便宜，让更多开发者和供应商愿意留在同一套体系里。

在计算产业，英伟达CUDA已经证明了开发者生态的长期价值。

CUDA的竞争力并非来自单一编程接口，而是在近二十年的发展中，逐渐积累起计算库、编译器、开发工具和庞大的开发者群体。

英伟达GPU的市场规模吸引开发者使用CUDA，不断完善的软件生态又反过来推动GPU销售，最终形成了硬件性能之外的竞争壁垒。

德国国家科学与工程院正式院士Peter Sachsenmeier在大会现场

**物理AI也可能经历类似的生态竞争，只是其技术体系更加复杂。**

不同机器人在本体结构、传感器配置、控制方式和应用环境上存在差异，模型、仿真工具和数据标准也尚未统一。单一企业很难覆盖所有技术路线，更难独立承担整条研发链的建设成本。

**产业越是高度分散，能够连接不同技术路线、降低协作成本的平台，就越有机会体现自身价值。**

从这一角度看，九章云极布局物理AI的战略价值**不在于把算力服务延伸到机器人研发这个动作本身，而在于改变自身在产业链中的位置。**

过去，AI基础设施服务商的竞争主要围绕算力资源、价格和交付能力展开。但随着物理AI研发任务越来越复杂，客户需要的不再只是计算资源，还包括能够持续完成仿真、训练、验证和迭代的研发环境。

九章云极选择以物理AI工厂承接共性研发需求，通过生态联盟连接专业技术供应商，再以两层API推动研发资源和工具的标准化调用。

这套布局也体现了九章云极对自身产业位置的判断：**以共用研发底座支撑不同技术路线的发展，将机器人本体、模型和仿真等专业领域留给生态伙伴，通过产业分工形成互补。**

在方磊看来，物理AI距离稳定的真实世界交互仍有很长的路要走，仿真到真机的迁移、长程任务和研发成本都是尚未解决的难题。

“**行业不缺乏主角，但永远缺少愿意站在底层、为整个产业提供支撑的企业。九章云极希望成为其中一员。**”方磊说。

对于独立第三方AI基础设施服务商而言，这也是一种值得关注的战略选择。不必以某一种机器人形态或模型架构为前提，而是尝试在不同技术路线之间建立连接。

对于物理AI研发企业，平台可以降低重复建设和跨系统适配成本。对于仿真、算法等专业厂商，平台有机会提供更多客户入口，让技术能力以标准化服务的方式参与产业分工。

更长远来看，当越来越多的研发任务通过统一平台完成，开发者积累的代码、工具配置、训练流程和研发经验，也有机会沉淀为可复用的生态资产。这些积累不仅有助于提升平台自身的服务能力，也可能进一步降低整个产业的研发门槛。

当然，CUDA生态的形成经历了长期的技术投入和开发者积累。物理AI能否形成类似的开发平台，以及最终由谁主导，仍然取决于真实的技术兼容性、开发效率和产业应用规模。

但九章云极的布局值得关注之处在于，它已经开始从算力供给的竞争，转向研发效率和生态组织能力的竞争。

**当越来越多的企业开始制造机器人，九章云极选择思考的，是如何让整个产业以更低的成本训练机器人。**

从提供算力，到组织研发资源，再到尝试建立跨企业协作的开发平台，这种角色转变的价值，可能比单纯扩大算力规模更值得关注。

物理AI产业走向成熟，除了更多聪明的机器人，还需要一套能够支撑机器人持续学习、低成本迭代的研发体系。

而谁能率先将分散的产业能力组织起来，谁就更有机会在物理AI的下一阶段竞争中占据关键位置。

items.title: At least 31 killed as fuel tanker crash ignites large fire on Cairo highway
items.content:
A crash involving a fuel tanker ignited a huge fire on a highway surrounding Cairo on Wednesday, killing at least 31 people, Egyptian authorities said.

The blaze on the ring road, a key artery that encircles the Egyptian capital, also injured at least 21 people and left more than two dozen cars and motorcycles charred, according to the latest figures released by the health ministry.

The stretch of the highway where the crash occurred was in Waraq, a densely populated neighbourhood in Giza, part of the Greater Cairo area, the ministry said.

At the scene, rescue workers were pulling people out of burning cars. An Associated Press video showed firefighters working to put out the fire spreading among the cars. Hundreds of people gathered near the scene in the Warraq district of Imbaba, a Cairo suburb.

The Egyptian president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, expressed his condolences to the victims in a statement. The public prosecutor’s office said DNA investigations were under way to identify the victims.

The health minister, Khaled Abdel Ghaffar, said the injured were taken to nearby hospitals and that he would head to the scene. He said the death toll was preliminary, raising concerns it could rise further.

Deadly traffic incidents claim thousands of lives every year in Egypt, which has a poor transportation safety record. Speeding, bad roads and poor enforcement of traffic laws are the main reasons behind most of the crashes.

In January, 21 people were killed and 16 were injured in a multicar pileup on a road near the southern province of Beni Suef.

items.title: Evaluating Recent Model Releases on GDPx
items.content:
Earlier this month we released GDPx, a benchmark designed to measure the domains most valuable for frontier intelligence. Most agentic benchmarks only measure a single domain like coding or legal. The few that try to be comprehensive, like GDPVal or Agent’s Last Exam, make the mistake of selecting domains based on percentage of GDP or the O\*NET taxonomy.

AI’s impact is nowhere near evenly distributed across the economy today, and we expect this trend to intensify in the future. Many tasks already can’t justify paying for Fable 5.2, much less Fable 7. Thus, **if your goal is to track the progress of frontier models, you should focus on the domains where they will be most impactful.**

It’s for this reason that GDPx intentionally forgoes industries like government and real estate, and instead covers the following domains:

- Chip design
- Cybersecurity
- Biology
- Finance
- Legal
- Quant trading
- Recursive self-improvement (RSI)
- Hardware design
- Materials science
- Alignment
- Software engineering

Our methodology is also unique. To ensure all our tasks are truly representative of their respective domains, we partnered with 14 specialized data partners to make 206 tasks.

**The single most notable thing about GDPx, however, is its difficulty.** Whereas other benchmarks will often debut with the top model scoring over 50%, Opus 5.5—the highest-scoring model on release day—scored just 12% on GDPx. This massive headroom is what allows GDPx to discriminate between future model releases, unlike saturated benchmarks such as Terminal Bench 4.0.

Speaking of new model releases, it’s been a very busy month indeed.

**SemiAnalysis is hiring for GDPx! If you’re interested in helping cement GDPx v2 as the world’s best benchmark, reach out to gdpx@semianalysis.com.**

# A flurry of new model releases

Since launching GDPx on November 1st, both Anthropic and OpenAI have released new frontier models. Google made a dramatic resurgence with the Gemini 4 series, and we’ve seen notable releases from Alibaba and Moonshot as well. The GDPx leaderboard now looks like this:

**It’s worth emphasizing that certain models like Fable 5.2 and GPT-6.2 Astra have sandbagged overall scores due to their safety classifiers.** If we exclude cyber, biology, and alignment, the three domains where safety classifiers sometimes kick in, and switch to partial grading to get more signal from the extremely difficult legal and finance domains (which default to binary grading), we get the following leaderboard instead.

We think you can argue either of these is the “correct” GDPx leaderboard. On one hand, safety classifiers truly limit the usefulness of models in domains like cyber and bio. On the other hand, if the goal is to measure a model’s intelligence, penalizing it for refusing to attempt a task due to safety concerns feels quite unfair. As an aside, we did find that 6.2 Astra’s classifiers are weaker than 6 Astra’s, but the model itself will refuse to do tasks that 6 Astra’s classifiers previously blocked.

Either way, **OpenAI is the current king of GDPx**. Going off the main leaderboard, which covers all domains, 6.2 Astra ranks first with a score of 19.3%. Fable 5.2 ranks second at 16.4%, and the best non-OpenAI/Anthropic model, Gemini 4 Carbon, ranks fifth at 10.9%. Carbon just barely edges out the highly lauded Gemini 4 Neon, which ranks sixth with a score of 10.1%.

The cost-performance Pareto frontier is also entirely dominated by OpenAI. DeepSeek v4.1 Flash just barely sneaks in at the very low end.

Although the Twitter hive mind has recently been dumping on 6.2 Astra and praising Gemini 4 Neon, we believe GDPx accurately captures the true relative ranking of model capabilities in frontier domains. This will become clearer as we break down overall scores by domain in later sections, but **Astra and Fable remain decisively above all other models in terms of raw intelligence**. It’s just that most Twitter influencers simply aren’t working on hard enough problems today to truly push frontier models to their limits, which is why we believe Twitter vibes are more a reflection of how pleasant models are to work with, rather than raw model IQ. We agree that OpenAI’s newest round of models is extremely unpleasant to work with, much like that 1 autistic coworker who is just so cracked everyone deals with their bullshit. We attribute this to OpenAI RLing the model extremely hard and very far while having poor SFT data.

# Gemini 4 Neon

Gemini 4 Neon is the model of the moment, with some declaring it the single best model in the world.

Earlier this year, we published a newsletter predicting the demise of Gemini/DeepMind. Clearly we were wrong. Compared to their competitors offerings at the time, Gemini 4 Neon is much better than Gemini 3.8 Flash was, and model progress at DeepMind has inflected up over the past few months. Neon is the best at Bio, but likely because OpenAI and Anthropic have more refusals.

With that being said, **the GDPx results show Gemini is still decisively behind both Anthropic and OpenAI across virtually all frontier domains**.

6.2 Astra significantly outperforms Gemini 4 Neon at RSI, materials science, and hardware design, while Fable 5.2 dominates in chip design, software engineering, and quant trading. Neon is the top-scoring model in biology, but this is likely due to more lenient safety classifiers (though we did find Neon to have stricter safety classifiers in cyber than other Google models).

We believe Gemini 4 Neon’s overwhelmingly positive reception is largely due to model behavior and not intelligence. Put simply, Neon is a pleasant model to talk to. Its liberal use of exclamation marks and cheerfulness reminds us of GPT 4o, which was a similarly adored model.

**In terms of the overall AI race, we believe Anthropic and OpenAI are still clearly in a tier of their own.** Google is a distant third, but also deserves its own tier. Meta, SpaceX, Moonshot, Alibaba, etc. are all fighting for 4th.

Lastly, as we previously explained to Tokenomics Model subscribers, **it’s worth noting that Neon is unnecessarily expensive to run because Google’s prompt caching lags behind its competitors.** Running Neon on GDPx cost us $15,286. Had Neon matched Opus 5.5’s cache hit rate, that bill would have been $12,536, about 18% less. At 6.2 Astra’s cache hit rate, it would have been $10,403, about 32% less. We compare theoretical cache hit rates here, meaning the share of cacheable input tokens that were actually served from cache, since that isolates the quality of each provider’s caching stack from how a particular workload is structured.

To its credit, Google shipped a caching update just today (another 4.5% increase to Neon’s cache hit rate, which would cut this bill by roughly 17-18%), so some of this gap may already be closing. Improving an inference serving stack is also something models are rapidly becoming superhuman at, so we expect this gap to continue closing in the near future.

# GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol

GPT-6.2 Astra and 6.2 Sol both do extremely well on GDPx, scoring 19.3% and 11.5%, respectively. Interestingly, this goes against most people’s subjective impressions of the models. Public reception to 6.2 Astra on X was embarrassingly bad, with one influencer calling it the “worst model OpenAI has ever released.”

However, 6.2 Astra also represents a significant drop in base model log-perplexity, which OpenAI recently disclosed as one of the best proxies for measuring models pretraining intelligence, and therefore sample efficiency. How do you explain this apparent contradiction?

Taking a closer look at individual GDPx domains reveals the answer. GPT-6.2 Astra excels on tasks that require complex reasoning like chip design, hardware design, materials science, and RSI. It’s also the first model to score higher than 0% on legal, and it is SOTA on finance.

Notably, 6.2 Astra is lackluster at software engineering, which is the domain most people on X evaluate models on. It scores half that of Fable 5.2. Qualitatively, the model is also often too literal when following instructions, fails to infer user intent/make reasonable assumptions, and is just generally annoying to talk to. Most users aren’t working on science problems hard enough for 6.2 Astra to flex its genius, so it’s no wonder why public sentiment was generally poor.

Interestingly, we did observe some examples of 6.2 Astra having a very good understanding of industry norms for particular domains. As an example, it knows that before adding an acquisition to a buyout model, you check whether anything the company has signed since the model was built changes the numbers. On one of our M&A tasks, it searched the data room for every document dated after the model it was given and found a signed letter that changes a payment the company already owes. That was the first correct answer any model has produced on that task.

It’s also worth emphasizing that 6.2 Astra scores extremely high on alignment. It appears that OpenAI’s safety commitments post Hugging Face weren’t just for show, and it’s reassuring to see such rapid progress here.

6.2 Sol is similarly spiky to 6.2 Astra and worse at everything except quant and SWE. **Overall, we believe the current negative sentiment around OpenAI’s models is overblown.** The 6.2 series is clearly extremely smart, and OpenAI completely dominates the cost-performance pareto frontier as well—they just need to do a better job making their models pleasant to work with.

# Fable 5.2

Fable 5.2 is the second-best model on GDPx at 16.4%, behind only 6.2 Astra, and the gap narrows once safety classifiers are taken out (29.9% vs 32.2% with partial grading). It’s also by far the most expensive model to run. **At $88 and 1.23M output tokens per task, Fable 5.2 costs 1.9x as much as 6.2 Astra and uses 3.9x as many output tokens, for a lower score.**

Much of this comes from Fable 5.2’s increased persistence and its proclivity for spawning subagents for testing and review. For now, all GDPx runs are done at the highest possible reasoning level.

Materials science is the starkest example. Fable 5.2 costs 2x as much as 6.2 Astra per task and uses 3.7x as many output tokens, yet scores 19 points lower (21.8% vs 41.3%). Even 6.2 Sol beats it (25.8%) at roughly a tenth of the cost ($8 vs $79 per task).

Finance tells a similar story. With partial grading, Fable 5.2 scores 53.6%, effectively tied with Opus 5.5 (54.6%) and 6.2 Astra (53.5%). But it uses 2.3x as many output tokens as Opus 5.5 and 12x as many as 6.2 Astra, which makes it 6.6x as expensive as 6.2 Astra per task.

Software engineering is where Fable 5.2 shines. At 24.4%, it nearly triples Opus 5.5 (8.9%) and is well ahead of the next best model, 6.2 Sol (15.6%). Even here the extra capability isn’t free: compared with Opus 5.5, its cost per task rises by about the same multiple as its score (2.8x), and it costs 17x as much as 6.2 Sol.

It’s also interesting to note that 6.2 Astra does significantly better than Fable 5.2 at RSI (33.22% vs 24.13%). However, we think this is largely due to Anthropic explicitly nerfing their public models’ AI research abilities.

# Qwen4-Max and Kimi K3.1 Pro

Qwen4-Max is the highest scoring Chinese model on GDPx at 7.44%. It’s a little worse than Claude Sonnet 5.5, though significantly cheaper. Qwen4’s biggest gains vs Qwen3.8 are in software engineering, RSI, cyber, and bio.

Kimi K3.1 Pro performs comparatively worse on GDPx than other benchmarks like the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, but this is largely because K3.1 Pro is benchmaxxed on Terminal Bench 4.1 (which is 10% of the AA index). K3.1 is unironically the number one model on Terminal Bench, when in reality, the model clearly still lags Fable 5.2, Gemini 4 Neon, 6.2 Astra, etc on agentic coding.

We believe GDPx provides the most accurate relative ranking of model quality and continue to be pleasantly surprised how well the benchmark matches our subjective opinions.

We’d also like to thank Modal for being our inference provider for Kimi K3.1 Pro.

# Custom cyber post-trains

As part of this update, we also evaluated a number of custom cyber models. It’s clear that domain specific models are becoming significantly more relevant as Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google continue to crackdown on their safety classifiers. Speaking from firsthand experience, it is extremely non-trivial to get unmitigated cyber/bio access from any of these providers. We believe this is a good thing for the safety of the world, but it also means that from here on out, the majority of users will be better off using models from different providers for these select domains.

Furthermore, Anthropic is also explicitly nerfing capabilities like RSI, and there are other domains like materials science where having proprietary data can enable non-frontier labs to train state of the art models. **We plan to continue evaluating many more domain-specific models on GDPx in the future.**

We tested 3 custom models on GDPx cyber

- A cyber post-train of DeepSeek v4.1 Flash from Hinoki called HO1
- Abliterated versions of Kimi K3.1 Pro and DeepSeek v4.1 Flash from Boundless

Surprisingly, the 2 abliteratred models performed slightly worse than their vanilla open source counterparts, while Hinoki HO1 performed marginally better.

We think this is largely because the vanilla OSS models never refused any of our cyber tasks to begin with and we’re still in the early days of training domain specific models. It will be interesting to see whether custom models can demonstrate stronger GDPx performance in the near future with additional post-training.

items.title: IPO之后，Anthropic公司员工身家暴涨
items.content:
公司上市后，Anthropic总裁丹妮拉·阿莫代伊（左）与首席执行官达里奥·阿莫代伊（右）的个人净资产跃升至200亿美元。图片来源：Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Anthropic的5300名员工以他们几天前做梦也难以想象的财富身家开启了新的一周。

该公司的IPO使员工集体财富直线飙升，非创始人员工的平均身家估计超过4400万美元。据路透社（Reuters）援引私募市场投资公司Hill的报告，其中598名非创始人员工如今名下资产至少达到1亿美元。

这意味着Anthropic内部的亿万富豪人数已超过整个伦敦、巴黎或洛杉矶的亿万富豪人数。据财富迁移公司Henley & Partners统计，仅有旧金山和纽约市的亿万富豪人数多于Anthropic。

上述估算基于Anthropic每股83美元的IPO发行价，随着市场震荡，其股价目前略低于这个水平。上周四收盘，Anthropic股价攀升至97.17美元，使Anthropic员工及七位联合创始人的集体估计财富达到约4330亿美元——据史蒂夫·拉特纳（Steve Rattner）所写的一篇广为流传的分析，这一财富规模超过美国最底层三分之一人口的总财富。

**Anthropic创造的财富凸显了对不平等加剧的担忧**

自2021年创立以来，Anthropic的崛起可谓迅猛。但批评人士警告称，其快速增长所创造的财富引发了关于谁将从AI热潮中受益——以及谁可能被抛在时代身后——的质疑。

前芝加哥市长拉姆·伊曼纽尔（Rahm Emanuel）本月早些时候出席《财富》美国500强创新论坛时表示，税法需要进行修改，避免让如此多的财富集中于少数人之手。

“AI有潜力创造巨大的繁荣。但如果所有财富都流向顶层少数人群，而工薪家庭却难以改善生活，那么这样的经济模式无法带我们走向未来，”他在X上发文写道，“我们在重蹈过去的覆辙。”

反贫困非营利组织乐施会美国分会（Oxfam America）私营部门倡导与运动高级经理哈娜·伊万霍（Hana Ivanhoe）向《财富》表示，Anthropic的IPO生动地说明了AI热潮可能用何种方式加剧当前的经济两级分化。

“Anthropic的IPO所引发的财富集中程度显然令人震惊，它揭示了已经构成我们经济特征的极端不平等，未来，类似的IPO必将进一步加剧这种不平等，”她说。

这些财富飞升之时，也正是舆论对AI迅速发展、以及AI对就业市场——甚至对人类自身——潜在影响的质疑日益增多之际。

“问题不仅在于IPO让少数富人更加富有，更在于他们是以牺牲其他所有人为代价变得更加富有，”伊万霍补充道，“这里既有财富不平等，也有影响的不平等。”

**达里奥·阿莫代伊也曾就AI驱动的财富集中发出警告**

Anthropic首席执行官达里奥·阿莫代伊的净资产随着公司上市飙升至约210亿美元，但他也曾对AI推动财富聚集的后果表示担忧。

“值得担忧的是那种会撕裂社会的财富集中程度，”他在今年1月发布的一封信中写道。

作为回应，阿莫代伊与其他六位创始人承诺将把Anthropic股权的80%捐赠给慈善事业——并呼吁更多人慷慨捐赠。尽管阿莫代伊本人也对AI系统失控、被用于网络攻击和生物恐怖主义或造成严重经济混乱感到担忧，并呼吁AI行业放缓发展步伐，但Anthropic仍然公开上市了，部分原因在于需要更多融资来安全地开发AI。竞争对手OpenAI则将其IPO推迟至2027年。（财富中文网）

译者：珠珠

items.title: SIA Applauds Introduction of Bipartisan Legislation to Extend Semiconductor Investment Credit
items.content:
The Semiconductor Industry Association (SIA) released the following statement from President and CEO Michael Robbins applauding bipartisan legislation [introduced](https://www.cornyn.senate.gov/news/cornyn-kelly-introduce-bill-to-incentivize-domestic-semiconductor-manufacturing-outcompete-china/) by Sens. John Cornyn (R-TX) and Mark Kelly (D-AZ) (S.5809) to extend the hugely successful semiconductor advanced manufacturing investment credit (AMIC) for five years. The credit is currently set to expire at the end of 2026.

“SIA applauds Sens. Cornyn and Kelly for introducing bipartisan legislation to extend the advanced manufacturing investment tax credit, a proven catalyst for strengthening America’s semiconductor manufacturing base. This incentive has helped drive more than $825 billion in historic private-sector investment in domestic chip manufacturing, creating high-skilled jobs, strengthening our national security and supply chain resilience, and advancing U.S. technology leadership amid intense global competition. Extending the credit for five years would provide the long-term policy certainty needed to sustain this momentum, encourage continued investment in U.S. semiconductor manufacturing, and ensure America remains the global leader in semiconductor and super intelligence technologies. In the absence of the credit, the U.S. risks ceding ground to our global competitors in the race to attract critical semiconductor investment. We thank Sens. Cornyn and Kelly for their leadership and urge Congress to make it a priority to advance this important legislation this year before it adjourns.”

Semiconductor manufacturing requires extraordinary capital commitments and long-term planning, with investment decisions made years before facilities become operational. Without an extension, the U.S. will lack a critical tool to incentivize new semiconductor manufacturing investments, jeopardizing the ability of the U.S. to capture the next wave of investment to meet growing demand.

The AMIC has helped catalyze a [historic resurgence](https://www.semiconductors.org/chip-supply-chain-investments/) in U.S. semiconductor manufacturing. Companies across the semiconductor supply ecosystem have announced more than $825 billion in private investments across more than 160 projects in 30 states, which are expected to create and support more than 525,000 American jobs. These investments include new, upgraded, or expanded U.S. manufacturing capacity in leading-edge, memory, and foundational semiconductor production, equipment, and advanced packaging.

items.title: STMicroelectronics Introduces Miniature Time-of-Flight Sensor With 8-Meter Range
items.content:
STMicroelectronics, a global semiconductor leader serving customers across the spectrum of electronics applications, introduces the FlightSense [VL53LB](https://www.st.com/en/imaging-and-photonics-solutions/vl53lbca.html?icmp=tt51883_gl_pron_nov2026), a new direct Time-of-Flight (dToF) sensor designed to help smartphone and consumer electronics manufacturers add longer-range and more power-efficient distance sensing to increasingly compact products. The new sensor addresses a clear market need: extended range capability without compromising battery life, and smaller product size for better design flexibility.

The VL53LB combines direct Time-of-Flight ranging beyond 8 meters, low active-ranging power consumption, and an ultracompact all-in-one architecture. For OEMs, this means more room to add advanced sensing features while keeping printed circuit board (PCB) footprint, integration effort and power budgets under control.

The sensor enables applications such as camera selection assistance, autofocus support, presence sensing, obstacle detection, positioning assistance, and touch-free interaction. Its combination of range, compact size, and low-power operation also makes it suitable for robotics and industrial automation systems.

“Device manufacturers are looking for sensing solutions that add capability without forcing tradeoffs in power consumption, product size, or user experience,” said Alexandre Balmefrezol, Executive Vice President and General Manager of the Imaging Sub-Group at STMicroelectronics. “The VL53LB brings longer-range measurement, low power consumption, and compact integration together in a single module. It demonstrates how ST continues to evolve FlightSense technology while advancing our broader vision of transforming light into trusted data through intelligent optical sensing.”

“The Time-of-Flight sensing market continues to benefit from demand for enhanced camera functions, spatial awareness, and intelligent device interaction”, explains Anas Chalak, Market & Technology Analyst, Imaging at Yole Group. “Annual shipments of ToF-enabled devices are expected to reach more than 665 million units by 2031. As manufacturers expand sensing capabilities while preserving battery life and industrial design flexibility, technologies that combine extended ranging performance, compact integration, and lower power consumption are well positioned to support future growth.” (1)

**Helping OEMs integrate more sensing capabilities in less space**

The VL53LB is the fourth generation of ST’s single-zone FlightSense technology. It delivers ranging capability from less than 5 mm to beyond 8 meters. Compared with previous generations and the competition, the new sensors double the sensing range while reducing active-ranging power consumption by a factor of 2. It also supports an ultralow-power mode that consumes as little as 50 µW while maintaining an exceptionally compact footprint of only 4.0 mm × 1.8 mm × 1.0 mm, 30% smaller than competition and previous generation. On top, the radiated emissions (EMI/EMC) are well controlled with advanced architecture, and VL53LB does not require metal shielding cans above the sensors, unlike competitor ICs.

The all-in-one sensor integrates the CMOS sensor, a 940 nm infrared emitter, and embedded processing within a miniature package, which simplifies design integration and reduces overall system complexity. Support for I3C connectivity further facilitates implementation within the most recent next-generation mobile platforms.

**Designed for camera assistance, presence sensing and next-gen smart devices**

The combination of compact dimensions, wide-ranging capability, and low-power operation enables OEM manufacturers to introduce advanced sensing functions in smartphones and other smart devices without increasing product size or battery requirements.

Applications include:
 Multi-camera selection and autofocus support
 Presence and distance sensing
 Obstacle detection
 Navigation and positioning assistance
 Touch-free interaction
 Robotics and industrial automation systems

Strong ambient-light performance, with more than beyond 1 meter capability under 120kLux, advanced electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) resilience, and ultralow-power operating modes help developers deploy reliable sensing across a broader range of use cases, including battery-powered and always-on devices.

**Building on ST’s FlightSense leadership**

VL53LB builds on ST’s FlightSense portfolio, which has shipped more than 3 billion Time-of-Flight sensors worldwide for smartphone, consumer, industrial, and smart-device applications. The sensor leverages ST’s proprietary single photon avalanche diode (SPAD) technology and is manufactured within ST’s integrated device manufacturer model, with research and development (R&D) teams in Scotland, France, Singapore, and China and front-end wafer manufacturing in 40nm process, located in Crolles, France.

The post [STMicroelectronics Introduces Miniature Time-of-Flight Sensor With 8-Meter Range](https://www.semiconductor-digest.com/stmicroelectronics-introduces-miniature-time-of-flight-sensor-with-8-meter-range/) appeared first on [Semiconductor Digest](https://www.semiconductor-digest.com).

items.title: Seoul Semiconductor Enables Beyond-OLED Picture Quality with LCD
items.content:
[Seoul Semiconductor Co., Ltd.](https://cts.businesswire.com/ct/CT?id=smartlink&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.seoulsemicon.com%2Fen&esheet=54645946&newsitemid=20261125876304&lan=en-US&anchor=Seoul+Semiconductor+Co.%2C+Ltd.&index=1&md5=5b0174a135cd216c4a5eed27cf131bbd), a global opto-semiconductor company, today announced that its ‘WICOP Pixel’—the world’s first package-free technology, developed by its subsidiary [Seoul Viosys](https://cts.businesswire.com/ct/CT?id=smartlink&url=https%3A%2F%2Fseoulviosys.com%2Fen&esheet=54645946&newsitemid=20261125876304&lan=en-US&anchor=Seoul+Viosys&index=2&md5=5a739b8c6f20fef34c838dd8d08a07cc) —arranges RGB chips at an ultra-fine pitch of several tens of micrometers (µm) to render tens of thousands of colors. Replacing conventional white-light LCD backlights, the technology achieves 100% of DCI-P3 color gamut, the international film industry standard for reproducing natural colors, while delivering more than three times the brightness of OLED displays. The company has entered full-scale mass production and begun expanding supply to global TV manufacturers.

Seoul Semiconductor’s display-related revenue in the third quarter rose nearly 20% year-over-year. To meet capacity needs across the global market, the company plans to convert its existing white backlight light-source capacity to WICOP Pixel production rather than make large new investments, while expanding both revenue and profit through a global patent licensing program. In this way, it will support stable production for its customers while generating royalty income, which it plans to invest in expanded research and development in future fields such as biotechnology, 3D printing, AR and AI data communications.

The core of the ‘WICOP Pixel’ RGB backlight technology is that, while using a standard LCD panel, it reproduces natural colors and scenes more faithfully than OLED and heightens immersion even in bright settings such as living rooms and public spaces. This strengthens its appeal for home-theater TVs and raises product value and profitability for TV manufacturers. In addition, it reduces dependence on expensive LCD panels, and to cut costs further, the company is also researching technology to eliminate the color filter, which accounts for about 20% of LCD panel material costs.

The technology also covers 100% of the DCI-P3 color gamut, the international standard for digital cinema, enabling richer, more vivid color than OLED. Its peak brightness of up to 3,000 nits is more than three times that of OLED, delivering sharp images and strong immersion even in bright indoor and outdoor environments. Experts expect this to further strengthen TV’s role as home theaters and to deliver clear images even in bright public spaces. It also offers more than twice the lifespan of OLED.

According to a market research firm Omdia, the shift to RGB backlights—the category that WICOP Pixel technology addresses—is accelerating. Global RGB TV shipments, led by the large-screen premium segment, are expected to reach about 7 million units by 2030, representing more than 10% of global TV market revenue. As the current white-backlight market of about USD 3 billion shifts to RGB, the market is expected to more than double in size with the adoption of Advanced Packaging technology.

**\* DCI-P3 (Digital Cinema Initiatives – P3):** An international color gamut standard used in the digital cinema industry that defines the range of colors a display can reproduce. 100% DCI-P3 coverage means a display can reproduce the standard’s entire color gamut.
**\* BT.2020:** An international standard for ultra-high-definition video established by the International Telecommunication Union (ITU).
**\* WICOP Pixel:** Seoul Viosys’ WICOP is the world’s first opto-semiconductor technology that achieves a robust chip structure without a separate package, allowing it to be used like an ordinary electronic component. The WICOP technology previously applied to blue opto-semiconductors has been extended to all wavelengths, including green, red and UV. WICOP Pixel integrates multiple wavelengths, such as red, green and blue, into a single pixel unit. Each color is controlled independently and combined precisely, reproducing tens of thousands of natural colors efficiently and vividly.

The post [Seoul Semiconductor Enables Beyond-OLED Picture Quality with LCD](https://www.semiconductor-digest.com/seoul-semiconductor-enables-beyond-oled-picture-quality-with-lcd/) appeared first on [Semiconductor Digest](https://www.semiconductor-digest.com).

items.title: Backblaze explains why it's sharing customer information with advertisers
items.content:
Some customers have raised concerns about Backblaze's privacy policy taking effect next month, which says the backup and cloud storage company may sell certain personal information to advertisers.

Backblaze’s [current privacy policy](https://www.backblaze.com/company/policy/privacy-april-2026) says that in addition to the personal information that users may provide, such as their email address when creating an account, it may also “automatically” collect information, such as “your software, the operating system you use when accessing our service, your Internet Protocol address, and the date and time of each request you make to Backblaze.”

The current policy adds: “Under no circumstances do we rent, trade, or share your address or e-mail address with any other company for their marketing purposes without your consent.” It also makes no mention of advertisers.
