items.title: Supermicro SYS-E103-14P-H Review: A Fanless Panther Lake Edge Appliance
items.content:
The Supermicro SYS-E103-14P-H is an interesting little fanless appliance that pairs Intel’s new Panther Lake Core Ultra X7 368H processor with a dense industrial I/O layout. It packs a heterogeneous 16-core CPU, replaceable SODIMM memory and M.2 storage into a finned chassis that Supermicro rates for fanless operation in edge deployments.

Let us get to it.

## Supermicro SYS-E103-14P-H External Overview

Here is the front panel of the E103-14P-H, showing a dense array of industrial I/O. You can see three RJ45 Ethernet jacks labeled LAN1 through LAN3, alongside four white USB 2.0 Type-A ports and two red USB 3.2 Gen2 connectors.

The front panel of the E103-14P-H carries most of the connectivity. This industrial gateway-style layout puts nearly everything you need to cable on one face. The chassis itself measures 185 x 83 x 140mm (7.28″ x 3.27″ x 5.5″) per Supermicro’s datasheet, which makes it a compact box that can sit on a DIN rail or behind an edge display.

The front face is a dense black panel with the two DB9 COM ports on the bottom row. A blue GPIO connector sits at the left edge of this same panel, while RJ45, USB, HDMI, and DC connectors fill out the rest of the layout.

Let us get into some of these a bit closer, starting with power.

The front panel places the power button on the right side adjacent to two indicator lamps. A close-up of the status LEDs reveals two distinct indicators: an amber light marked with a cylinder icon for storage activity, and a green light marked with a bulb icon for system power. These sit just above the main power button on the front bezel.

The network configuration deserves a closer look because it is not uniform. The system has two Intel I226-IT controllers driving the 2.5GbE ports, plus one Intel I219-LM controller for the single 1GbE port. That third port supports Intel vPro management so while there is no IPMI, you get vPro. We captured all three interfaces in Linux: eno1 and eno2 are the I226-IT parts on PCIe root ports, while eno3 is the I219-LM integrated into the PCH.

Two white USB Type-A connectors sit above the LAN ports. These are USB 2.0 interfaces, which Supermicro specifies for low-speed peripherals and industrial accessories that do not require higher bandwidth.

The USB 2.0 ports are useful for low-speed peripherals like dongles and serial adapters without wasting the faster USB 3.2 Gen2 ports on the red connectors. For an edge gateway, that is a sensible split because many industrial accessories do not need more than USB 2.0 bandwidth.

Next to the final Ethernet jack, two red Type-A ports are stacked vertically with SuperSpeed USB markings. These provide USB 3.2 Gen2 connectivity for faster external storage or other high-bandwidth devices.

Moving across the front panel, two HDMI 2.1 ports provide display output from the integrated Intel Arc B390 GPU. The processor supports up to four displays per Intel’s specifications, and Supermicro exposes two of them on this chassis. Next to those are two male DB9 connectors labeled as COM ports supporting RS-232/422/485.

Below the USB and video outputs, a male DB9 connector labeled COM1 is visible. This port supports RS-232/422/485 serial communication, providing legacy industrial interface options alongside modern networking.

This close-up shows the second serial connector, labeled COM2. It is a male DB9 port with nine pins and two threaded standoffs for securing cables.

The blue female DB9 port on this system is an 8-bit GPIO/SMBus interface.

The locking DC input sits at the right end of the front panel. Supermicro rates this system for 12V to 36V wide-range DC input, which is a useful feature for industrial sites with existing DC power distribution rather than standard AC outlets. A locking connector is great, since you do not want someone to pull the power out if this is running automation for systems on an assembly line or running an important digital signage kiosk (as examples.)

The enclosure itself does most of the thermal work here since there are no fans. The top and bottom surfaces carry pronounced cooling fins that increase surface area for passive heat dissipation. This is a common approach in fanless industrial systems, where the chassis metal becomes the heatsink.

The side panel features three antenna knockouts marked ANT. These openings allow wireless module connectors to pass through when an M.2 radio card is installed.

The rear of the unit is comparatively sparse because most I/O moved to the front. Antenna knockouts on the rear and sides support wireless modules, which can be used with the M.2 E-key slot inside that can host a Wi-Fi or other radio card.

There are plenty of knockouts for putting antennas around this chassis.

You can use this box and then have antennas come out of the different sides depending on how you mount it, which we can see being handy in tighter installations.

The underside has much shallower heatsink fins.

Here is the mounting bracket.

With that, let us open the enclosure to examine the mainboard layout and internal components.

# This May Be the Best Artificial Intelligence (AI) Stock to Buy in December (Hint: It’s Not Micron or Oracle)

Snowflake's shares have jumped nicely over the past six months, and they can get a shot in the arm following the upcoming earnings report.

By Harsh Chauhan –

## Key Points

- Software stocks have performed relatively better than hardware stocks over the past six months.
- Snowflake has capitalized on the rally in software stocks, driven by the growing demand for its AI solutions.
- Snowflake's growing customer base and higher spending by existing customers could send the stock higher when it reports its quarterly results next month.

**Micron Technology** and **Oracle** are poised to release their quarterly reports next month, and both artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure companies will be looking for a turnaround in their fortunes following a big slide in their stock prices lately.

However, weak investor sentiment toward AI hardware stocks may make it difficult for these stocks to rally, even if they deliver strong results and guidance. That's why I think **Snowflake** (SNOW +3.20%) could be a safer investment compared to Oracle and Micron in December.

Let's look at the reasons why.

Image source: Snowflake.

## Software stocks have been safer than hardware stocks lately

The **iShares Semiconductor ETF** has lost 28% of its value over the past six months. Investors have been booking profits in semiconductor stocks amid concerns about the state of AI infrastructure spending in a higher-interest rate environment. Software stocks have fared substantially better. The **iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF**, which tracks North American software companies, has fared better with a 1.5% gain over the past six months.

It is easy to see why that's the case. Companies offering AI products and solutions are witnessing solid growth in revenue and earnings, suggesting that enterprises and governments have been adopting the technology to unlock productivity gains. Snowflake has been a beneficiary of the growing AI adoption, and that reflects on its stock market performance.

## SNOW Snowflake

NYSE · As of 1:00 PM ET 11/27/26

Snowflake stock has surged by 57% over the past six months, while the **Nasdaq-100 Technology Sector** index has lost 17% over the same period. The company will release results for the third quarter of fiscal 2027 on Dec. 2, and I won't be surprised to see its shares get a nice shot in the arm.

## Snowflake surged impressively the last time it released results, and that may happen again

Snowflake's fiscal Q2 results, which were released in early September, sent the stock soaring. The company beat Wall Street's expectations and raised its full-year guidance, driven by growing demand for its AI solutions.

Customers can use Snowflake's cloud platform to build AI agents and applications using their proprietary data. The demand for its AI tools is improving at a nice clip, helping Snowflake attract more customers and land bigger contracts with existing customers. The company's customer base increased by 32% year over year in fiscal Q2 to just over 14,500. Meanwhile, its net revenue retention rate of 126% suggests that existing customers gave Snowflake more business.

Snowflake management remarked on the September earnings call that "growth in both migrations and AI use cases" led to the expansion in its net revenue retention rate. Given that Snowflake saw a sharp jump in new customers last quarter, I won't be surprised to see the company win more business from them as they expand adoption of its AI solutions.

For instance, management notes that more than 9,100 customer accounts were using its Snowflake CoCo AI coding agent in fiscal Q2, while 5,800 customer accounts were using the CoWork AI platform. So, there are still many customer accounts to which Snowflake can cross-sell its AI solutions. That's why I think the company can outperform expectations and raise guidance on Dec. 2.

The company anticipates an increase of 37% to 38% in product revenue for fiscal Q3 to $1.59 billion. That would be a slight improvement over Snowflake's 37% product revenue growth in fiscal Q2. Moreover, Snowflake is launching new products at a solid pace this year. It has made more than 330 product capabilities generally available to customers in the first half of fiscal 2027, up 35% from the year-ago period.

The new offerings should increase Snowflake's cross-selling opportunities, eventually boosting its margins and driving stronger earnings growth. Analysts are expecting Snowflake's earnings per share (EPS) to increase by 78% in the current fiscal year to $2.23. The estimates for the next couple of years have been inching higher, as seen in the following chart.

SNOW EPS Estimates for Current Fiscal Year data by YCharts

There is a strong chance Snowflake will deliver stronger-than-expected earnings growth in the future, driven by improving adoption of its AI services. Moreover, Wall Street expects the stock to surge by 62% over the next 12 months, based on its median price target of $440, according to CNN. So, this AI stock can still deliver incredible gains despite rising impressively over the past six months.

As such, buying Snowflake ahead of its upcoming earnings report could be a smart move, as another beat-and-raise quarter could send its shares soaring.

items.title: 算力唤醒真实世界：九章云极发布物理AI工厂与生态开放计划
items.content:
11月25日，以“算力唤醒真实世界”为主题的2026物理AI行业峰会暨九章云极智算生态大会在深圳举行。会议由九章云极DataCanvas主办，深圳市龙华区工业和信息化局支持，清华大学互联网产业研究院为学术指导单位。来自标准机构、高校与科研院所、投资机构，以及机器人本体、世界模型、仿真软件、智算云等领域的上百位嘉宾代表出席。中国电子技术标准化研究院副院长范科峰，深圳市龙华区委常委、常务副区长张智，九章云极DataCanvas董事长方磊分别致辞。

会议聚焦的核心命题是：当机器人、世界模型与仿真软件相继通过技术验证，物理AI如何跨越从实验室到产线的产业化鸿沟。答案集中在两个方向：以工程化能力将算力组织为生产体系的物理AI工厂，以及将产业链专业能力联结为整体协作的物理AI生态。

范科峰指出，物理AI正在加速连接数字世界与物理世界，跨域协同对标准供给提出了迫切要求，数据接口、通信协议、安全边界等标准化问题将愈发突出，坚持标准先行，才能为物理AI的规模化落地提供关键支撑。

中国电子技术标准化研究院副院长范科峰致辞

张智常务在致辞中表示，龙华是大湾区机器人产业核心承载区、全省人工智能产业核心区，有超两万家制造业企业、超600家人工智能及机器人企业，数字经济核心产业增加值占GDP超35%；已率先建成“鸿蒙+昇腾”双生态数字孪生底座、全国首个虚实融合具身智能训练场（EAI Park），形成了从世界模型、基础设施到Sim-to-Real、场景应用的全链条支撑，是物理AI的绝佳转化地和“超级试验场”。欢迎企业借助在龙华成立的物理AI联盟，把项目、技术、人才带到龙华，龙华区将做好保障服务，与企业协同共建物理AI产业生态，跑出新质生产力“加速度”。

深圳市龙华区委常委、常务副区长张智致辞

方磊提到，过去十年AI在学会“说话”，过去三年在学会“思考”，接下来的十年要学习的是“动手”。物理AI与数字AI的差异首先体现在错误的代价上：“Agent错了可以重试，机器人撞了不能重来。”数字AI比拼的是聪明，物理AI比拼的是可靠，而可靠是一项需要基础设施承担的工程能力。

九章云极DataCanvas董事长方磊致辞

**335亿元市场 物理AI进入工程化拐点**

国盛证券具身智能研究院院长张一鸣表示，物理AI的价值焦点将依次转移：早期，高质量人类行为数据的稀缺性凸显；中期，真机后训练与触觉感知成为重要增量；长期，随着模型能力扩散，产业竞争重心有望向优质机械本体转移。而无论哪条技术路线胜出，数据处理、仿真与训练都是绕不开的共同需求——这正是智算服务商的机会所在。

国盛证券具身智能研究院院长张一鸣发表演讲

易观合伙人张澄宇发布《2026年中国（亚洲）物理AI开发基础设施市场专题研究报告》，报告显示，2026年中国物理AI开发基础设施市场规模约335亿元，2030年预计超800亿元，其中数据、仿真与验证环节贡献约58%的新增支出；支撑物理AI的算力容量约178 EFLOPS当量，至2030年复合增速39%。

易观合伙人张澄宇发布《2026年中国（亚洲）物理AI开发基础设施市场专题研究报告》

清华大学经济管理学院教授朱岩从产业经济角度指出，数据、算力、电力、碳排放四个环节正在同步抬升而增速各异，最慢的一环在电力侧；算随电走、荷随源动、算力资产从成本项转为资产项、治理走向跨域协同，是随之发生的四个转变。落到企业决策，算力支出从一次性资本开支转为持续运营开支，投资评估的锚点便从“拥有多少算力”移向“单位算力产出多少有效结果”。

清华大学经济管理学院教授朱岩发表演讲

**推出Physical AI Factory：联合伙伴打造物理AI基础设施与工具栈**

产业化的第一层跨越，发生在基础设施侧。会上，九章云极在既有算力底座之上叠加物理AI工具栈，推出面向物理AI的算力基础设施与工具栈服务体系（Physical AI Factory）。它以异构算力统一调度、弹性训练与推理资源、强化学习运行环境、多阶段任务自动化编排为核心，支撑物理AI在“场景数据—模型训练—仿真验证—合成数据扩展—真实环境反馈”闭环中的持续迭代；其中仿真引擎、合成数据生成、SIL/HIL真机验证等环节，由九章云极联合生态伙伴共同提供。这一思路与多位学者的判断相互印证。德国国家科学与工程院院士Peter Sachsenmeier以工业4.0的演进为线索指出，当智能从屏幕进入产线与设备，制造系统的组织方式、验证机制与人才结构都需要重新安排，物理AI的产业化本质上是生产组织方式的重构。

德国国家科学与工程院院士Peter Sachsenmeier发表演讲

上海交通大学特聘教授熊红凯给出技术侧约束：物理AI的研发链上并行着训练、渲染、物理求解与边缘推理四类负载，基础设施的核心命题是把异构资源组织进同一条链条，以交付稳定性为尺度。

上海交通大学特聘教授熊红凯发表演讲

九章云极DataCanvas AI首席科学家缪旭指出，物理AI的Scaling，在模型之外，同样发生在“数据、仿真、训练和真实反馈”的循环之中；与生态伙伴共同建设的Physical AI Factory，是一座持续生产可验证科学知识与物理智能的工厂。

九章云极DataCanvas AI首席科学家缪旭发表演讲

**发起物理AI产业生态联盟：开放两层API，让能力可调用**

产业化的第二层跨越依托于生态协作。数据、模型、仿真和真机部署环节彼此割裂，任何单一主体都难以独立补齐，这也是物理AI产业生态联盟启动的动因。“极光物理AI产业生态联盟”由九章云极发起，在深圳龙华区成立，学术指导单位为北京大学软件工程国家工程研究中心，理事单位包括亿欧、中国质检院人工智能检测中心等，首批成员企业来自机器人本体、世界模型、仿真平台、科研机构及智算云服务等领域，覆盖从技术研究、工具开发到产业应用的多个环节。同步开放合作计划正式开启，联盟围绕算力共建、标准共建、场景开放、产业研究、交流研讨、人才与开源六大方向组织工作，将分散于产业链各环节的专业能力，转化为可共享的公共能力。

连接之上还需实现可调用。联盟面向行业伙伴开放标准化接口的开放路线图与试点接入机制：面向底层资源调度的Physical AI Infra API，封装异构算力池化、弹性集群编排与存储加速能力；面向开发任务的Physical AI Dev API，覆盖强化学习训练、仿真样本生成与真机策略验证，提供标准化的任务提交与结果回传接口。通过两层接口，底层算力与上层工具链接入统一服务入口，开发者不必自行搭建资源调度体系，可以把重心放在模型、仿真环境与场景策略的研发上。

**多项重要战略合作签约达成：生态协作落到具体场景**

大会现场，多个重磅战略签约将生态协作推进到具体产业场景。深圳市龙华区工业和信息化局、北京清程智汇有限公司、深圳市怡亚通供应链股份有限公司与北京九章云极科技股份有限公司共同签署物理AI工厂项目战略合作协议，四方围绕物理AI工厂开展合作，目标打造物理AI一体化项目：龙华区提供贴近产线的产业场景，清程智汇衔接前沿研究力量，怡亚通连接从部件到整机、从工厂到市场的产业通道，九章云极承担算力与工程化底座。四方各有所长，共同构成一条完整的协作链。

物理AI工厂项目战略合作签约

此外，九章云极还分别与佳都科技集团股份有限公司、北京数字政通科技股份有限公司签署AI算力产业协同战略合作协议：佳都科技深耕城市交通智能化，数字政通长期服务数字政府与城市治理，与九章云极的算力底座相结合，智算能力将沿着这些行业网络，继续向城市场景延伸。

AI算力产业协同战略合作签约

**给产业一把公共的尺子：九章云极核心共建“中国算力采购信心指数”**

会上，中国经济信息社新华指数研究院副院长周宇涵宣布“中国算力采购信心指数”正式启动。我国智能算力规模高速增长，但训练与推理、东西部布局、层级供需三重错配依然存在，算力租赁价格波动加剧，市场需要一个能够回答“下个季度需求是扩张还是收缩”的先行指标。算力采购信心指数正是针对这一信息缺口而生，九章云极作为核心共建单位，参与指数体系搭建。它以景气调查捕捉市场预期，与记录真实成交价格的全球算力价格指数互为补充，正在为算力市场从“野蛮生长”走向“精细化运营”提供一套不可或缺的度量衡，也为市场主体的经营研判、行业的监测治理和算力资产的定价、交易与资产化，提供持续可信的决策支撑。

中国经济信息社新华指数研究院副院长周宇涵宣布“中国算力采购信心指数”正式启动

产业侧实践提供了印证。普渡机器人联合创始人兼CTO郭璁分享了“一脑多形”具身智能的关键技术路线：专用、类人形与人形三种形态将长期共存，统一智能底座是跨形态复用能力的关键。

普渡机器人联合创始人兼CTO郭璁分享

松延动力产品副总裁唐子洋回顾了运动控制技术从 ZMP、MPC 到强化学习的演进，指出结合感知的避障越障与全身实时遥操作，是悬在运控领域头上的“两朵乌云”，而驱散它们靠的是“算力托底”——基于端到端架构训练世界模型，先预测身体状态与摔倒概率再行动，再叠加大数据集预训练与跨本体基座模型。在他看来，运控的上限已不由本体电机与结构单独决定，而由可调用的训练算力和集群调度能力共同定义。

松延动力产品副总裁唐子洋分享

**圆桌论坛的思想碰撞：算力如何承载真实世界**

圆桌论坛由数字生命卡兹克主理人卡兹克主持，九章云极联合创始人兼COO尚明栋与申万宏源证券计算机行业首席分析师黄忠煌、中科慧灵副总裁和书平、深朴智能联合创始人兼技术副总裁李明磊共同参与。尚明栋表示，衡量算力产业不能只看建设规模，更要看资源是否真正被使用、能否服务更多产业主体。九章智算云按实际用量计费的DCU模式，正是为了适配物理AI研发团队在技术路线未定、需求波动阶段的弹性用算需求。

圆桌论坛

从工厂到联盟，从接口到指数，本次大会给出的答案指向同一方向：物理AI的产业化，需要让算力在工厂中被组织、在生态中被调用、在度量中被验证、在场景中被检验。当AI走出数字世界、进入真实的产线与城市，算力的角色也从支撑模型训练的资源，成为承载真实世界运行的基础设施。物理AI的产业化之路，自此进入工程化与生态化并行推进的新阶段。

items.title: Swiss tourist killed and British and Americans injured by elephants in Cameroon
items.content:
A Swiss tourist has been killed and British and American tourists have been injured when a group of hikers encountered a herd of elephants in Cameroon.

The group of six tourists, four British, one Swiss and one American, accompanied by local guides, were hiking near the village of Bakingili in the south of the Mount Cameroon national park on 19 November, on a path used by elephants to access a nearby lake, when they encountered the herd of about 15 animals, according to media reports.

The elephants attacked the group and Alain Throo, a Swiss insurance executive based in London, was reportedly gored and one of the guides tossed into a ditch on top of Throo, while the others hid in trees.

Throo had a black eye and was initially responsive and complaining about an injury to his arm, one of the British female hikers told Cameroonian media, which said they had feared he was bleeding internally.

“He said that the elephant attacked him,” an unidentified Cameroonian man added, according to a video posted by CBS Radio Buea FM. “It smashed him.”

Throo later died of his injuries and his body was carried out of the park by a combined team of park staff and the military to a mortuary in the town of Limbeon 21 November. The American hiker was treated at the same hospital and later discharged, according to local media.

One of the British tourists, who said he had hid in a tree stump for two hours, recalled the moment the elephants attacked their group. “I saw these elephants almost next to me. And I thought, if I go down this path as well, I’m going to get hit. So I just moved to the opposite direction. They ran down the path, I ran and hid in a bush. And I heard some screaming.”

Sean McGovern, the UK chief executive of the insurer Axa XL, where Throo had worked for 13 years, confirmed the death, saying Throo was a “valued member of our team, respected colleague and friend whose contribution, professionalism and warmth touched many people”.

Cameroonian media reported that clashes between elephants and local people had been happening for the past 10 years.

after newsletter promotion

Mount Cameroon is the highest mountain in west and central Africa, at more than 4,000 metres. The African forest elephant was declared critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature in 2021. There are about 195,000 left in the wild, less than 15% of its population 50 years ago, according to the World Wildlife Fund.

Just 5% of forest elephants, which are smaller than their savannah-based counterparts, are found outside central Africa. In Cameroon, there are about 6,000 forest elephants, according to the NGO Global Conservation, which said the species was at risk from poaching syndicates.

A spokesperson for Britain’s Foreign Office said: “We offered assistance after a number of British nationals were injured in Cameroon.”

导语：北京九章云极科技股份有限公司（下称“九章云极”）作为核心共建单位，参与指数体系搭建。

11月25日，在2026物理AI行业峰会暨九章云极智算生态大会上，中国经济信息社新华指数研究院副院长周宇涵宣布“中国算力采购信心指数”正式启动。北京九章云极科技股份有限公司（下称“九章云极”）作为核心共建单位，参与指数体系搭建。

当前，中国算力产业正处于高速增长与结构性调整并行的阶段。我国智能算力规模高速增长，但训练与推理、东西部布局、层级供需三重错配依然存在，算力租赁价格波动加剧。对于算力需求方，采购决策往往依赖于分散的市场信息，难以形成对行业整体景气程度的系统认知；对于算力供给方，产能规划与定价策略同样缺少来自真实交易一线的反馈信号。市场需要一个能够回答“下个季度需求是扩张还是收缩”的先行指标。算力采购信心指数正是针对这一信息缺口而生：它以景气调查捕捉市场预期，与记录真实成交价格的全球算力价格指数互为补充——一个着眼预期，一个着眼交易，共同拼出算力市场的完整图景。此前，九章云极作为核心共建单位参与了全球算力价格指数的编制建设，这套方法论经验也延续到了采购信心指数的共建之中。

该指数借鉴PMI（采购经理指数）的编制逻辑，采用景气扩散方法，通过问卷的方式采集新增订单、价格变化、消耗增减、资源获取周期、闲置与预留等关键信息，通过加权计算形成综合指数及分项指标，反映算力市场的景气程度与变化趋势。指数覆盖算力品类、采购规模、价格预期、交付周期等关键维度，既能呈现整体市场的冷暖变化，也能在分项层面揭示结构性特征。作为指数的核心共建单位，九章云极为指标口径的确定与方法论的验证提供了来自产业实践侧的参考。在样本采集与指数计算环节，中国经济信息社新华指数研究院将独立承担数据处理与发布工作，共建方不参与指数值的计算。中国算力采购信心指数是一个宏观数据和产业风向标，也是贯穿算力产业链上下游的决策依据。对算力需求方而言，指数提供了判断市场供需态势与价格走势的参照系，有助于优化采购节奏与预算配置，降低因信息不对称带来的决策风险。对算力供给方而言，指数反映的景气信号可作为产能规划与产品策略调整的依据，使供给结构更贴近真实市场需求。对行业主管部门与研究机构而言，指数持续积累的数据能够为产业运行监测、政策效果评估提供量化支撑，推动算力资源在区域间、行业间的更优配置。从更长周期看，采购信心指数的预期读数与全球算力价格指数记录的真实成交价格长期互为对照，还将为算力资产的定价与风险管理沉淀数据基础，为算力资产化、证券化等金融创新提供支撑条件。

指数的持续运行，离不开样本池的共建与扩充。启动会现场，九章云极与中国经济信息社共同向算力产业链上下游企业发出邀请，欢迎算力供给方、需求方及第三方服务机构加入样本池，参与数据采集与指标共建。按照计划，指数将逐步形成“月度读数、季度专题、年度白皮书”的产品体系，逐步扩大样本覆盖范围与行业代表性。随着样本量的积累和方法论的迭代，中国算力采购信心指数有望成为常态化观察国内算力产业运行的重要窗口、感知产业周期冷暖的先行信号。它与其记录真实交易的全球算力价格指数一起，正在为算力市场从“野蛮生长”走向“精细化运营”提供一套不可或缺的度量衡，也为市场主体的经营研判、行业的监测治理和算力资产的定价、交易与资产化，提供持续可信的决策支撑。

items.title: 九章云极携手多方战略合作，物理AI工厂生态协作走进真实场景
items.content:
11月25日，在2026物理AI行业峰会暨九章云极智算生态大会上，北京九章云极科技股份有限公司（九章云极DataCanvas，下称“九章云极”）与深圳市龙华区工业和信息化局、北京清程智汇有限公司、深圳市怡亚通供应链股份有限公司签署物理AI工厂项目战略合作协议；另外两场签约中，九章云极分别与佳都科技集团股份有限公司、北京数字政通科技股份有限公司签署AI算力产业协同战略合作协议。

物理AI正处在一个关键节点：机器人、世界模型与仿真软件相继通过技术验证，但跨过从实验室到产线的鸿沟，需要的不仅是算法突破，更是工程化的系统能力。模型在仿真环境里跑得再好，到了真实产线上也可能因为环境噪声、传感器误差和动力学差异而失效。

问题在于，验证必须在真实场景中完成。但真实场景分散在政府、制造企业、科研机构和服务商手中，单一厂商无法同时握有场景、研究能力和算力底座，产业链的协作机制尚未建立。大会现场的系列签约，让物理AI的验证环境有了多方共建的载体。

**共建龙华物理AI工厂项目，搭起“场景—研究—基础设施”协作链**

物理AI工厂项目战略合作协议围绕物理AI工厂开展合作，目标打造物理AI一体化项目。龙华区是深圳制造业最密集的产业腹地之一，电子信息、智能制造和高端装备产业集聚，产线在楼下、工厂在门口，为物理AI提供了贴近真实产线的场景与产业配套。清程智汇衔接前沿研究力量，将具身智能领域的科研积累带入产业现场。怡亚通以供应链服务网络，连接从部件到整机、从工厂到市场的产业通道。九章云极则以智算云与物理AI工具栈，承担算力与工程化底座。四方各有所长，共同构成一条完整的协作链，形成“场景—研究—基础设施”贯通的验证环境。

上述共建项目依托于九章云极面向物理AI领域构建的智算基础设施与工具栈体系。九章云极面向物理AI开放的两层API，为协作提供了技术接口：Physical AI Infra API面向底层资源调度，封装异构算力池化、弹性集群编排与存储加速能力，让多方不必各自搭建复杂的资源调度体系；Physical AI Dev API面向开发任务，覆盖强化学习训练、仿真样本生成与真机策略验证，提供标准化的任务提交与结果回传接口，把物理AI研发中重复性最高的工程化环节抽象成可调用的服务。联盟提供组织形态与产业连接，接口提供可调用性与技术入口，二者共同构成生态的运行基础。对参与共建的各方而言，这意味着可以把重心放在各自的专业领域，而不必重复投入基础设施建设。

**算力协同拓展城市场景，连接产业一线**

与物理AI工厂项目同步推进的，是算力产业协同战略合作。佳都科技深耕城市轨道交通与道路交通智能化，自动售检票、站台门、交通信号控制与交通大脑等系统覆盖多座城市，日均处理大规模客流与运营调度数据；数字政通长期服务数字政府与城市治理，其数字化城市管理平台已覆盖街道与社区的管理流程，支撑城市运行的精细化管理。随着城市智能化程度的提升，交通调度、公共安全、市政管理等系统对实时计算和智能决策的需求持续增长，城市场景的算力需求呈明显波动特征，对弹性供给提出更高要求。与九章云极的算力底座相结合，智算能力将沿着这些已经铺开的行业网络向城市场景延伸，探索AI算力在产业侧的协同应用模式。对物理AI而言，这意味着算力与工具栈能力开始与真实运转的城市基础设施对接；对城市治理与交通运营而言，这意味着算力资源有了新的调用入口，可以在不重建基础设施的前提下，获得弹性、可扩展的智算支持，按实际用量调配资源，提升资源使用效率。

**探索物理AI产业化的协作方向**

系列签约覆盖了物理AI从基础设施到场景应用的不同环节。对产业而言，其价值不只在于合作框架的达成，更在于为物理AI产业化提供了一种多方协作的方向：政府开放场景、研究机构供给方法、供应链企业衔接产业资源、智算服务商交付底座，多方协同推进，物理AI的验证和迭代才具备持续推进的条件。这种协作模式也意味着，物理AI的研发向资源共享的方向探索，降低进入门槛；物理AI的技术路线也有望从封闭迭代，走向开放验证，为从实验室到产线的进程提供更多可能。

未来，各方将围绕上述方向持续深化协同，推动技术成果在真实业务场景中落地。物理AI工厂的共建与算力的产业协同，指向的是同一件事：让物理AI的每一次验证，都有真实的场景、可用的算力和可复用的基础设施支撑。

items.title: Sri Lankan asylum seeker killed himself after being sent by UK to Eswatini
items.content:
The UK sent a Sri Lankan asylum seeker who had been convicted of sexual assault to Eswatini, a southern African country to which he had no connection and where he killed himself.

Kishanth Peramalya was part of a group that set sail from India hoping to reach Canada and claim asylum there. The boat was rescued by the Royal Navy in October 2021 when it got into difficulty and brought to Diego Garcia in the remote British Indian Ocean Territory, which hosts a US-UK military base.

In November 2024, the UK allowed 61 migrants to enter from Diego Garcia after a damning UN report about conditions in the camp. However, the then home secretary, Yvette Cooper, denied Peramalya entry to the UK due to his criminal convictions while he was on Diego Garcia for four counts of sexual assault, one count of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and one count of arson. Cooper’s decision was upheld by UK courts.

Peramalya had been granted protection from being returned to Sri Lanka, having been tortured and sexually abused by Sri Lankan military personnel as a teenager. In late March, the Maldives said it would take him for 30 days, according to the BBC. He was then transferred to Eswatini, a country landlocked by South Africa and Mozambique and formerly known as Swaziland, where he killed himself on 13 September.

A draft deal between the UK and Eswatini governments would have committed Downing Street to cover the costs of Peramalya’s resettlement there for three years, according to the BBC, which said the UK was also finalising arrangements for Peramalya to live in Eswatini permanently.

The Guardian has not seen the draft deal. Thabile Mdluli, a spokesperson for Eswatini’s government, said: “The initial arrangement was temporary in nature and intended to safeguard Mr Peramalya’s safety while the government of the United Kingdom worked towards a long-term solution regarding his circumstances.”

She said that no formal agreement was ever reached over Peramalya’s long-term residency status with the UK and declined to comment further on the specific arrangements of his stay in Eswatini or the circumstances around his death.

Mdluli said: “Eswatini has not received any other similar request from the government of the United Kingdom. The government of the Kingdom of Eswatini remains committed to ensuring that any agreements entered into with external partners safeguard national interest as well as the safety and security of Emaswati \[Swazi people\].”

A UK government spokesperson said: “Keeping the British public safe will always be our first priority, and we will continue to take the decisions necessary to protect the British people. That includes taking steps to ensure high harm foreign criminals cannot enter the UK. We continue to work with the Eswatini authorities in relation to this case.”

Peramalya had post-traumatic stress disorder and attempted suicide multiple times on Diego Garcia, according to a UK high court judgment in February 2025.

Peramalya’s family told the BBC he was initially housed alone in an isolated guesthouse in Eswatini. “My brother did not want to go there at all,” said his sister, speaking from India. “He couldn’t manage being there alone, he was very lonely.”

She said he had called her four times a day and was initially having weekly psychiatric appointments, which were made daily when his mental health deteriorated, as well as having someone brought in to prepare his food.

Peramalya’s relatives said they were not aware of his convictions for sexual offences or any plan to make his transfer to Eswatini permanent.

Eswatini has accepted dozens of third-country deportees from the US since July 2025. In November 2025, its government confirmed it had received $5.1m in exchange for taking up to 160 migrants from the US.

items.title: Blog Review: Nov. 25
items.content:
Cadence’s Igor Krause examines PCIe’s [Streamlined Virtual Channel Extended Capability](https://community.cadence.com/cadence_blogs_8/b/fv/posts/unraveling-streamlined-virtual-channel-extended-capability-svc), which aims to address limitations of the traditional PCIe ordering model in modern multi-host fabrics by introducing a standardized approach for TC-to-VC assignment.

Synopsys’ Greg Sorber chats with Sanjay Gangadhara about [co-packaged optics](https://www.synopsys.com/blogs/chip-design/co-packaged-optics-ai-infrastructure.html), including how it differs from pluggable modules, why the approach is gaining traction now, and what it will take to make it work at scale.

Siemens’ Benoit Honel simulates a 5.22 MW [liquid-cooled AI data center](https://blogs.sw.siemens.com/simcenter/ai-data-center-liquid-cooling-simulation/) pod together with its cooling plant, solar PV system, battery storage, and grid connection to determine how climate impacts cooling performance.

Arm’s Erick Amador explores when [lookup-table GEMM](https://developer.arm.com/community/arm-community-blogs/b/architectures-and-processors-blog/posts/when-do-lookups-beat-multiplies) can outperform traditional multiplication for ultra-low-bit LLMs, and how model shapes, packing, and hardware affect the result.

Keysight’s Katharine Edmonds highlights how connected design data and IP lifecycle management support long-term [automotive semiconductor traceability](https://www.keysight.com/blogs/en/tech/sim-des/will-todays-design-record-explain-tomorrow-s-automotive-chip-failure).

Plus, check out blogs featured in the latest [Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials](https://semiengineering.com/newsletter/manufacturing-packaging-materials-nov-2026/) and [Systems & Design](https://semiengineering.com/newsletter/systems-design-nov-2026/) newsletters:

Amkor Technology’s Gerard John demonstrates why just [meeting a spec](https://semiengineering.com/beyond-pass-fail-characterizing-silicon-margin-with-pvtw/) is no longer sufficient.

Lam Research’s Taeyeon Oh illustrates how to model [process variation](https://semiengineering.com/how-virtual-twins-and-machine-learning-optimize-dram-yield/), detect multiple failure modes, and evaluate DRAM solutions with less wafer experimentation.

Intel Foundry’s Lori Scott explains why [trusted data](https://semiengineering.com/from-metrology-to-autonomy-scaling-yield-quality-and-innovation/) is a critical starting point for intelligent chip manufacturing.

SEMI’s Sungho Yoon zeroes in on the explosion of new and upcoming [production lines](https://semiengineering.com/what-is-driving-silicon-wafer-demand-recovery/) driving silicon wafer demand.

Axiomise’s Fabiana Muto explores how [most re-spins](https://semiengineering.com/hope-is-not-a-strategy-what-first-silicon-success-really-takes/) are caused by logic and functional flaws, not hard-to-predict physical effects.

Keysight’s Chris Maloney explains why a component can meet its individual design targets and still behave differently as part of a complete [optical link](https://semiengineering.com/why-photonic-design-is-becoming-a-system-level-challenge/).

Cadence’s Paul Graykowski looks at the benefits of combining [architectural proof](https://semiengineering.com/designing-a-microarchitecture-from-formal-proof-to-full-system/), software-driven verification, simulation, emulation, and cloud-based compute infrastructure.

ChipAgents’ Emily Yan details how shortening the path from design intent to verified implementation could put [custom silicon](https://semiengineering.com/how-can-ai-build-faster-and-better-silicon-for-physical-ai/) within reach of more teams.

Arteris’ Andy Nightingale demonstrates how to maintain consistent [communication behavior](https://semiengineering.com/a-link-is-not-architecture-why-multi-die-systems-need-more-than-die-to-die-connectivity/), integration, and security across configurations.

Siemens EDA’s Ujjwal Negi and Prashant Dixit show how to validate [UCIe.mem](https://semiengineering.com/verifying-ucie-mem-flexible-verification-for-compute-and-memory-chiplets/) implementations across development stages while reusing a common verification environment.

The post [Blog Review: Nov. 25](https://semiengineering.com/blog-review-nov-25-3/) appeared first on [Semiconductor Engineering](https://semiengineering.com).

items.title: Agentic system personalizes physical controls to help users “DJ their art”
items.content:
In 2017, Apple [removed the home button](https://apnews.com/article/ad9e1a52b5dc4d48bc55256a1124315b) from its iPhones. Users lost a convenient, tangible control — part of a larger shift to digital buttons, knobs, and sliders we also see in cars (like with radio presets and air conditioning) and kitchens (see smart fridges).

We can’t leave physical controls behind entirely, though. They tend to be more convenient and efficient — think of how you can use a physical gaming controller without looking at it — and, at times, more precise, like when you use a dial to get the volume just right. But tangible controls are typically preprogrammed to do a specific thing, minimizing their usefulness.

A new system called “[TangiMap](https://yunyi-zhu.github.io/tangimap/),” co-developed by an MIT graduate student and researcher at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL), helps bring tangible control back to your software. The system personalizes the physical controls on everyday devices by mapping digital widgets onto tangible inputs, turning things like editing photos, animation, performing music, and creating 3D models into more dynamic and tactile experiences. Just as a DJ’s pads switch between triggering cues, loops, and samples, TangiMap gives a device’s controls entirely new roles.

But how, exactly? TangiMap relies on an AI agent, or semi-autonomous programs that “think” and complete well-defined tasks, to find and act on context about the software you’re using, your tendencies, and the device used to control that program. To gather the required context, the agent can draw on sources such as the program’s API (the rules that let programs talk to each other), an MCP server (a standard that connects AI agents to apps), or a screenshot interpreted by a vision-language model. Then, the agent uses a large language model to put all the info it's gathered into a file before mapping specific digital functions to physical controls.

“TangiMap builds on our broader vision of reprogramming common objects to be more dynamic,” says Yunyi Zhu ’20, MEng ’21, a doctoral student in the MIT Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and a CSAIL researcher whose advisor is MIT Associate Professor Stefanie Mueller. “Here, AI agents help us adapt physical controls to whatever we’re working on. We want to bring back physical controls so we can interact with our devices eyes-free, the way you adjust a car’s volume without looking away from the road. Physical controls also let you adjust several settings at once, like tweaking brightness and contrast together when editing an image, which is hard to do on a screen.”

The system helped the researchers turn a standard mixer into a photo-editing controller. That way, they could adjust color in Adobe Lightroom, with a complementary visualization of those controls displayed on their screen. The team did the same with sound-mixing software, so that performers can adjust their music in real-time with their own inputs to knobs and faders.

The researchers also reprogrammed a simpler mixer to work with the 3D modeling program Blender. Their interface included an area where users can type in a prompt, and once the model was generated, users could adjust features like shininess on a mixer using physical controls. Within Adobe’s Character Animator software, TangiMap connected specific expressions and movements to buttons on a control pad so users could animate (or “puppeteer”) a cartoon character live.

Zhu and co-author Chang Xiao, an assistant professor at Boston University, [presented their tool at the ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3830398.3830602) earlier this month.

Zhu and Xiao created a custom user interface (UI) for each application. While that adds another layer of personalization to the creative process, the team is hoping to create a more streamlined system that helps the designer to generate the UI for their device by taking a picture.

The researchers are also considering the physical aspects of user interactions. They want to use more ergonomic devices and also ensure that TangiMap accounts for where users position their hands when doing different tasks. For example, users typically hold a mixer differently when they’re using it to make music than, say, when playing a video game. You may want controls mapped closer or further apart, depending on what you’re doing.

Zhu is hoping to do a user study to get more feedback about TangiMap, and whether this kind of “smart DJing” could indeed improve those experiences. But the dynamic reprogramming she ultimately envisions is even more ambitious.

“The same way our phones and computers generalize to a range of tasks, we want other objects to be more intelligent,” she says. “I would like to build physical items that use an AI agent as a brain to decide what to reprogram into. They could understand what to transform into, given a specific situation.”

A chemical jar, for instance, could tell you if it’s sealed correctly when asked, and when you want to see what it’s typically used for, the container would instead display that information. While that kind of versatility and interactivity is a ways off, more powerful agents and more intricate fabrication pipelines could bring everyday objects to life.

Their work was supported, in part, by Google’s Gemini Academic Program Award.

items.title: ASUS Turbo Radeon AI PRO R9700 Review
items.content:
While much of the attention in the market for AI inference has been focused on servers and datacenter-scale deployments, the heart and soul of the modern AI revolution started with video cards. And that is where it still beats on today, overshadowed by servers but still an important market segment overall.

Within the AMD ecosystem, the company has taken a very visible pivot in how it markets and categorizes its professional video cards. The Radeon Pro lineup, once the backbone of AMD’s workstation graphics efforts, has become the Radeon AI Pro lineup, and the backbone of AMD’s add-in video card/AI accelerator efforts. The flagship for this line, in turn, is the Radeon AI Pro R9700, a 32GB VRAM card that AMD and its partners are positioning as a more budget-friendly alternative to NVIDIA’s RTX PRO Blackwell lineup of workstation cards.

Today we are taking a look at one of those R9700 cards in the form of ASUS’s Turbo Radeon AI Pro R9700. The sub-$2000 card have been heavily optimized for workstation use, balancing graphics needs and display outputs with the ability to fit up to four cards into a single system for larger AI workloads.

## ASUS Turbo Radeon AI PRO R9700 Hardware Overview

As AMD is not selling their own reference design workstation cards for this generation, it falls to AMD’s partners to sell the cards instead. Which is a production strategy that they are well-accustomed to on the consumer side of matters, but is a bit more unusual for a workstation card.

Notably, AMD has been keeping their Radeon Pro partners on a rather short leash with card designs. AMD is curating a very specific image for a very specific market here, not the least of which is the ability to install multiple cards in a single workstation. As a result, though AMD is not selling their reference card their partner cards are all quite similar in their high-level design as dual slot blowers, a form factor you will not readily find outside of workstation video cards these days.

That brings us to ASUS’s Turbo Radeon AI PRO R9700. ASUS has long been a heavyweight in the world of video cards, so it is no surprise to see them jump on board producing a Radeon Pro card.

ASUS’s R9700 card is, in all practical application, exactly what you would expect from a workstation card given the form factor and the AMD’s constraints. This is a dual slot video card that follows the PCIe specifications to a T in terms of width and height, in order to ensure that it (and perhaps a few of its friends) can fit into a workstation chassis.

Under the hood, the card is powered by AMD’s Navi 48 GPU, which is the most powerful RDNA 4 GPU offered in this generation. The GPU offers 64 of AMD’s CUs, which in turn is comprised of a total of 4096 shading units for vector math and 128 AI accelerator cores for matrix operations.

With a peak clock speed of 2.92GHz, this gives the R9700 a peak matrix math throughput of 382.7 TFLOPS with dense FP8 math, or double that with sparsity. One of the key improvements in this generation of RDNA architecture is the addition of FP8 support, which not only further improves the compute throughput of the card, but it better aligns AMD’s hardware with the general trends in the industry towards lower precision weights, and fitting a large number of weights within a given amount of memory.

On that note, as is traditional for a workstation card, AMD and ASUS have packed the R9700 with as much memory as the card can handle. With Navi 48 sporting a 256-bit bus, the card has been equipped with 32GB of GDDR6 memory organized as 16 2Gbit chips in clamshell mode. Above all else, memory support is a key differentiator between AMD’s consumer and professional cards, so 32GB is something you will only find on the Radeon AI Pro cards.

The GDDR6 memory itself is clocked at 20Gbps, allowing for a total of 640GB/second of memory bandwidth for the card. Soft ECC is also available, though only under Linux (and even then, it has to be manually enabled). This allows for an extra degree of reliability for systems and racks based around the card.

Navi 48 itself is somewhere between a mid to high-end GPU as far as die size (357mm2) and transistor counts (53.9B) go, which makes it a bit of an oddity within AMD’s lineup as far as card progression is concerned. AMD did not produce a true high-end GPU this generation, and as a result the R9700 actually has less VRAM than the previous-generation 48GB Radeon Pro W7900. This means that it is a step back in terms of overall memory capacity, but AMD is looking to make up the difference with compute throughput, thanks in large part to the newer chip architecture.

One advantage of being a smaller chip, however, is that it keeps TDPs in check. AMD (and ASUS’s) Total Board Power figure for the card is just 300 Watts, which makes it relatively easy to keep a blower-style card cooled without a blowout on noise. This also means that even 4 cards in a system is not going to result in excessive power requirements, though it will certainly be pushing the limits of a single power supply.

## ASUS Turbo Radeon AI PRO R9700 Build and Design

As far as video card designs go, ASUS’s Turbo Radeon AI Pro R9700 is a very typical dual slot blower design. With a need to ensure that the card can be installed in multiples together, ASUS has kept things tightly tuned to PCIe specifications, with a dual slot card measuring 10.5 inches long and 4.4 inches high.

Interestingly, the blower design here is open-backed, that is, the back side of the card has open vents so that the card can pull in air from both sides of the card.

The fan itself is a pretty typical blower design. According to ASUS they are using dual ball bearings here.

Taking a look at the rear of the card, we can better see the venting cut into the card’s PCB and its shroud. For that matter, we can also see that the card even has a shroud on its back side. As noted earlier, the 32GB of GDDR6 is organized in a clamshell configuration on the R9700, meaning that 8 chips are on the rear of the card and need to be protected and cooled, just as with all of the chips on the front side of the card.

Being that this is a workstation card, ASUS has also put some thought into their power connector placement. The Turbo R9700 uses an ATX 12V-2×6 connector, which has been placed on the rear of the card instead of the top, another workstation-centric design element that makes it easier to install multiple cards in a system. The 12V-2×6 connector is rated for up to 600W, so the 300W TBP R9700 is well within the cable’s limits.

Meanwhile, at the front of the card we find a not too subtle reminder that this is a video card, with 4 display outputs – the maximum number of displays the Navi 48 GPU can drive. ASUS has given their card a triple DisplayPort plus single HDMI port configuration. The DisplayPorts are all DisplayPort 2.1a, while the HDMI port supports HDMI 2.1b. Coupled with DSC, and the card can drive displays at up to 12K in resolution.

Otherwise, besides the display outputs, the rest of the front of the card is almost entirely vent cut-outs. 300W is still a lot of heat to expel from a blower card, so ASUS does not hold back here, and you can clearly see the fins from the heatsink running within the card.

With our hardware tour complete, let us take a look at the performance of the Turbo R9700

items.title: Amazon says hackers' AI agents found and exploited 0-day with little human input
items.content:
Amazon said AI agents recently found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability with no human oversight beyond a simple instruction to get root access on an East Asian university server.

The agents were running on Cairn, an open source AI penetration-testing framework. The hackers, who provided prompts in simplified Chinese and configured the model to the Chinese Standard Time zone, gave the agents a list of IP addresses and the goal: “obtain shell access.” In short order, the agents discovered a zero-day in an open source medical imaging AI application running on one of the target servers. The agents then exploited the vulnerability and gained full control of the system.

“These findings show that agentic offensive operations are already happening, and defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable,” Amazon [said](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/chinese-nexus-actors-cairn-ai-agents-found-a-zero-day-on-their-own/).

[Read full article](https://arstechnica.com/security/2026/11/amazon-says-hackers-ai-agents-found-and-exploited-0-day-with-little-human-input/)

items.title: Why AI Struggles To Reuse Chip Designs
items.content:
**Key Takeaways:**

- AI can accelerate derivative chip design, but those derivatives may not be physically viable or cost-effective.
- AI-assisted reuse depends on the availability of accurate design data, engineering knowledge, and proven methodologies.
- End-to-end automation is limited by gaps in multi-physics simulation, implementation, and verification.

---

Chipmakers are seeing mixed results when they apply AI to derivative and new chip designs, finding that AI-generated solutions can be substantially different and more costly than expected, and that AI-driven designs introduce new manufacturing and verification challenges.

Several key problems have emerged when incorporating AI in chip design. Among them:

- The data needed to ensure that follow-on designs will function as expected may not be complete because some of that data resides in other companies, such as foundries, OSATs, and various equipment and process providers;
- Integrating rapidly evolving AI capabilities into established EDA flows remains challenging, especially where predictability, traceability, and silicon-proven results are required.
- Many organizations have customized tools for their own chips, markets, and expertise, and AI tools have not yet adapted to those changes.

“There’s the engineer in me that says if AI can take us to brave new worlds where humans haven’t yet gone, that’s an exciting thing,” said Nilesh Kamdar, general manager of [Keysight EDA](https://semiengineering.com/entities/keysight-technologies/). “But I’ve seen it run into problems. For example, I had a low-pass filter, which we call a pixelated model, and it looks like a QR code in the middle. There’s a high-frequency part running at about 2 GHz. If I want to change it to 2.5 GHz, a human would look it up in a textbook. There are traditional ways to do it, and they would create something that any other human would recognize. AI looks at this, says, ‘I don’t understand your textbook, so I’m going to just turn on and off any single part of this grid, and I’ll come up with something.’ It does sort of work, but there are constraints. Is this manufacturable? Is this cost-effective? Did I learn anything out of this? Yes, AI solved a problem for me, but as a human, I had intuition about what worked at 2 GHz. Now, if I want to shift to 2.5 GHz, that same intuition will change the design.”

Instead of making an incremental change to account for a new spec, AI may come up with something completely different, with no correlation between versions, Kamdar explained. “There’s a cost of letting AI do all of these things.”

Reusing designs across multiple generations of chips has long been the go-to strategy as a way of amortizing non-recurring engineering (NRE) costs and reducing development time. Using AI agents to come up with derivatives adds a whole different way of looking at the problem. AI agents can assess existing architectures and RTL to identify potential bottlenecks, explore design modifications, optimize EDA tool settings, and automate portions of verification and debugging. And they can orchestrate workflows across multiple tools, reducing the manual effort required to adapt existing IP to new specifications.

But the resulting AI-generated design is not necessarily ready to be implemented in a follow-on chip. Engineers must determine whether proposed changes are physically feasible, manufacturable, cost-effective, and compatible with the new design’s requirements. That, in turn, will determine where AI can and cannot be used, and where EDA tools need to evolve in order to close that gap.

**Software reuse easier than hardware reuse**
Despite AI’s promise, a lot of human effort is still needed in today’s designs. Working with natural language interfaces is a big plus, but minor differences in queries can result in very different answers.

“We were rapidly adapting the automotive solution to robotics because there’s a lot of commonality,” said Baaziz Achour, CTO of Qualcomm. [1] “Many of the key functions are similar, such as perception, path planning, and foundational technologies like sensor fusion, object recognition, location, and control. We were able to take the full automotive solution and apply it to robotics. We have very effective solutions for scaling the software. However, hardware IP scaling and SoC integration still require significant human effort.”

Those differences can also be significant across domains. for example, developers may increase the number of cores in an NPU and use tools to analyze bottlenecks as application workloads shift. But this type of scaling is very different with mobile multimedia, such as a camera, Achour explained. “Across a lot of this AI spectrum of products, the basic camera and display blocks are similar, but the requirements are very different in camera count, speed, and power.”

**Fig. 1: Designers can use tools to adapt common IP, but there is still a non-recurring engineering cost for SoC implementation. Source: Qualcomm/DAC**

While designers can leverage core IP blocks, such as an image signal processor, every processing core, camera, and display across these devices must meet diverse requirements and cost targets. “Currently, we often create separate architectures and hardware design variants for each case,” said Achour. “Can EDA help us build one flexible architecture that adapts to these diverse requirements instead of manually customizing for each time?”

The answer? Maybe. Ensuring that a chip design will function flawlessly requires an ecosystem. Automating some steps in the design flow can help, but how much automation and which steps are still being explored. Nevertheless, there are plenty of places where engineers would welcome more flexibility and automation, such as iteratively tuning EDA tools to meet design targets.

“Three months were spent in recipe tuning of EDA tools,” said Achour. “Neither the RTL nor the floorplan were changed in these iterations, so this is a huge source of inefficiency. EDA tool companies have AI-aided fine-tuning, but that consumes a lot of compute. Further innovation is needed for this.”

**Fig. 2: EDA tools to help designers reuse IP need to account for area, thermal, PDN, and much more. Source: Qualcomm/DAC**

The overall goal for engineers is to reduce runtime and compute, shortening time to market, increasing coverage and improving confidence at sign-off, and enabling engineers to be more productive. “We need innovation in GenAI, including GenAI that can create design input for the EDA tools, like a human designer, to drive fast convergence, and agents that can orchestrate design flows to reduce human effort for iteratively running tools to refine and optimize the design,” said Achour. “These are critical technologies to rapidly adapt common hardware to evolving AI product demand. We need innovation in AI for SoC design.”

**Capturing IP data and design knowledge**
Before AI can effectively help engineers adapt existing designs to new requirements, it needs access to accurate, organized information about the IP already available, including its configurations, constraints, dependencies, and previous implementations. Capturing and managing that information, along with the engineering knowledge and methodologies used to develop it, is essential to making AI-assisted derivative design scalable.

To help solve these challenges, established EDA vendors and startups are releasing physics-based, assistive AI co-pilot technology to speed up design exploration, PPA optimization, RTL generation, and verification.

However, before deploying an AI tool to create a brand-new design or a derivative design from existing IP, engineering teams must first collect the knowledge already inside the organization. After that, IP lifecycle management software is needed to connect engineering data, automate workflows, improve traceability, and make valuable IP easier to find and reuse.

“How do you pull different IPs, and where is information about that IP?” said Keysight’s Kamdar. “You could have information that says this IP works great for certain power levels. If you are developing an earbud, the available power may be much lower, so you know which IP will not be suitable. You have to look for a different source of IP from the finished product. You can create a software bill of materials (SBOM) or hardware bill of materials (HBOM) that lists all the IP you used, and you can confirm whether that was the latest and greatest version of the IP. Were there other variants of the IP? There are all kinds of different ways to do IP management.”

Teams also need a way to share the AI prompts, skills, and workflows they develop so that everyone can benefit from communal wisdom. “We invested in a platform and innovation store that allows our people to share prompts, plugins, check-ins, and solutions across teams,” said Ram Narayan, senior director of engineering at [Arm](https://semiengineering.com/entities/arm/). [2] “That was done primarily with the vision that teams can share skills and upskill themselves through that exchange. They can use the platform to upskill teams across the company, as well. This is an opportunity to bring people together around common ways of working and common learnings, which may have been lost over the years because we have acquisitions of groups, and groups going off and doing things differently. This is a real opportunity to enable these practices.”

An organization’s specific workflows need to be captured to get the best results from agentic AI-based design exploration tools.

“A company’s methodology is as important as the design, and the methodology they have used for the last 20 years to be able to tape out their chip has brought a lot of learning,” said Solaiman Rahim, chief product officer at [ChipAgents](https://semiengineering.com/entities/alpha-design-ai-chipagents/). “For example, ‘Use this cell/ don’t use this cell. Optimize for PPA that way. Don’t do this. Don’t do that. Or, do this.’ When you are in the ECO stage, and you have crosstalk, you can talk to the customer, and they say, ‘Oh, for crosstalk at this modem company, I have a very specific way of solving it. I have done the same thing for the last 10 years, and I am able to solve the crosstalk.’ That’s what we call the ontology.”

This is a very promising use case for agentic AI. A common approach from EDA tool providers today is to have an agentic collaboration platform sit with the customer, allowing sharing between users while also feeding data, methodology information, and design information back into agentic workflows so they can do the best possible job and deliver the best possible outcome. In ChipAgent’s approach, all proprietary customer data stays on-prem. “This belongs to the customer,” Rahim noted. “It is not something that comes back to us.”

**Automating interconnect design**
While organizations wrestle with how to apply AI, they also are leveraging improvements in algorithmic optimization, software-driven simulation, and deterministic EDA. This is especially important when it comes to data movement, which is one of the key performance bottlenecks, along with moving data in and out of memories and processors. A tiled, algorithmic fabric is easier to scale up or down for derivatives than crossbars.

“For our switch customers who have been working with crossbars in the past, and have had deep, lived experience over decades, it is still a very hands-on experience with hand-coding RTL to build huge custom networks, and almost hand-wiring things,” said Saurabh Gayen, chief solutions architect at [Baya Systems](https://semiengineering.com/entities/baya-systems/). “They say, ‘When this wire comes in, it’s going to come in here, then this other data is going to come from there, and we’re going to make it like an arbiter. This is a painstaking process where the whole design just gets bigger and more difficult by an n-squared factor. This is super painful for engineers, companies, and project managers, as well. It’s an incredible source of risk for them, because it’s iterative. It’s manual. They don’t know if they’re going to find surprises later.”

Massive parallelism and other techniques have transformed what previously looked like a complex engineering project into a very manageable math problem. “Suddenly, this becomes an algorithmic construct that says mathematically we will give you the exact performance properties you need,” Gayen explained. “This will create, literally, a grid of identical tiles. Top-down, you get that guarantee that it meets the performance needs ahead of time. Then in terms of implementation, when it’s the physical design, you actually build it and harden those designs, then figure out how to put it within a chip.”

In today’s landscape, a software-first approach is needed to build hardware, adapt it to new use cases and better products, and reduce customer cost, pain, engineering effort, and time to tape out. “It’s all built step by step,” Gayen observed. “For example, when I came in, we already had a really good software-defined flow, which is new for hardware. People don’t like writing software. They like getting their hands dirty and writing RTL. Having that software perspective of coming in and generating RTL is something that unlocks a different type of thinking and allows breakthroughs like this to happen. Companies are happy, and the engineers are happy because they don’t have to do the painstaking manual work anymore.”

**Multi-physics optimization limits**
However, for design exploration or reusing IP, no tool yet optimizes timing, IR, and thermal together at the RTL or architecture level.

“Today, we don’t have anything that helps the RTL designer all the way,” said Vinay Patwardhan, senior director, product management at [Cadence](https://semiengineering.com/entities/cadence-design-systems/). [3] “We have something that can help customers from the netlist stage. We have a vision for going all the way to architectural, but right now it’s either timing-based improvement, IR-based improvement, or thermal-based improvement — not all three together as a multi-physics problem. If you want improvement at the RTL stage, you have to incorporate all of them into the source code, which isn’t available because thermal analysis works on layout layers. IR needs the locations of the power sources. At the RTL stage, there is no physical awareness of any of this, so it is a difficult problem. However, if we can find correct ways to model and abstract all those effects at that early stage, then it will be possible. There is some work going on in that phase, but to answer clearly, we don’t have anything in the RTL today. We can optimize the netlist continuously with feedback.”

Tool providers are addressing the challenge from many angles. For example, ChipAgents developed Build-A-Chip-Bench to evaluate AI agents from workload spec and RTL generation through synthesis, physical implementation, and layout verification.

**Fig. 3: Key steps from workload specification to GDS. Dashed arrows show problems found downstream that send the agent back to revise an earlier step.** [**Source**](https://chipagents.ai/research/build-a-chip-bench)**: ChipAgents**

While these advances show AI’s potential to automate increasingly complex design workflows, generating a design is only part of the challenge. Each stage of implementation introduces physical constraints and interdependencies that can affect decisions made earlier in the process. Changes intended to improve one aspect of a design may create problems elsewhere, requiring tools to account for the interactions among electrical, thermal, mechanical, and other physical effects.

The need for agentic tools to be grounded in fundamental physics is one reason why end-to-end solutions are still under development.

“The limiting problems are no longer inside the chip,” said Hardik Kabaria, CEO of [Vinci](https://semiengineering.com/entities/vinci/). “They’re physical problems that live at the boundaries — heat moving from die to package to board to enclosure, thermo-mechanical stress across heterogeneous material stacks, power density interacting with cooling strategy at the system level. The physical world doesn’t respect the organizational boundaries the industry has drawn around it, and neither do the failures.”

Others agree. “EDA tools must expand beyond single-die optimization to system-level design, including multi-die integration, packaging, and software-hardware co-design, evolving toward intent-centric platforms rather than collections of disconnected point tools,” said Insaf Meliane, director of product management and marketing at [Arteris](https://semiengineering.com/entities/arterisip/). “One major gap is verification, where rising design complexity continues to outpace engineering productivity despite significant AI advances.”

These challenges become even more complex as designs move beyond the chip and package to the board level, where reused IP and previously verified components must operate within new electrical and physical environments. While reusing proven designs can reduce engineering effort, changes in placement, connectivity, and surrounding circuitry can introduce interactions that were not present in the original implementation. This makes verification a critical part of derivative design, even when the underlying components have already been validated.

**Verification at the board level**
As with SoC IP data management, a robust data management foundation enables teams to reuse known good blocks on the board.

“They verified them in the past, and they could say, ‘This block doesn’t need to be verified,'” said David Wiens, product marketing manager at [Siemens EDA](https://semiengineering.com/entities/mentor-a-siemens-business/). “If they use that block more than once, they only need to verify it once. But in reality, blocks of data and blocks of designs can and will behave differently depending on what’s around them. It’s a step toward simpler verification, but you still have to be careful. You have this one circuit, and you place it on the top layer of the design, but whatever’s running underneath it that’s native to that, that’s custom to that design and may in fact interact with it. You could put a shield around it if you wanted to really trust it and really make sure that it’s not impacted. But particularly with signal integrity, that’s a bit of a scary proposition to say, ‘I’m just going to trust that it’s more than likely to pass by itself.’ It’s a question of what it interacts with on the board.”

**Fig. 4: Data management is a key component of using AI tools to speed up any part of the design flow. Source: Siemens EDA**

Agentic AI tools can now shrink verification time. Siemens reported that its HyperLynx Agentic Toolkit reduced the design analysis for 112 high-speed channels from several weeks to a couple hours. “In a manual process, engineers would first need to figure out the signaling protocol,” Wiens explained. “What SerDes protocol is it using? I’ve got to dig up the manual, which can be hundreds of pages long. I’ve got to find the rules within that, and the conditions to set up my simulator. Then I’ve got to push the button and wait for it, and then when I get it back, I’ve got to visualize. I’ve got to look at the results one waveform at a time. Did it pass? Did it fail? And if not, I’ve got to figure out why, and I’ve got to iterate.”

With new agentic solutions, the AI can inspect the database itself. “It can identify potential issues off the bat before it even simulates,” he said. “Then it automates the workflow. That’s a big thing because it’s part of what democratizes the tool. Specialists understand both the workflow and the results. Democratizing that automation, simplifying it, means anybody can push the button. With visualization, when you’ve got a ton of data, you don’t want to look at it one at a time. We can use AI to take that data and visualize it to produce different types of results that aren’t just simple waveforms. The AI can diagnose where the problem is. ‘This eye [diagram] is failing. Here’s where I think the problem is, and here’s what we recommend you do next.’ It takes the engineers through that entire path.”

The speedup doesn’t come only from AI and software capabilities. “It’s about leveraging hardware horsepower, GPU horsepower, CPU cluster horsepower,” said Wiens. “That’s what gets us the speed. But there are also areas of AI that help us explore the design space faster without brute-force simulation. Agentic AI accelerates the steps, mostly through smarter execution, and then delivers trusted outcomes because it’s physics-based. It’s leveraging known good simulation engines, and IP can be managed in a safe way on-prem.”

Leveraging GPUs and CPUs comes with computational costs, a concern raised by Qualcomm’s Achour. Moreover, engineers still must manually implement many of the changes recommended by agentic AI tools.

“What engineers do next is go back to the design, the actual layout or schematic, and make the changes that were recommended,” said Wiens. “Today, that’s still largely a manual process. Watch this space. Automating the actual place and route and things like that is a lot harder than automating workflow.”

**What AI still can’t automate**
AI-based design tools are advancing rapidly, with vendors introducing new capabilities for RTL generation, design exploration, physical optimization, and verification. These advances are reducing engineering effort in individual stages of the design process, but efficiently adapting existing hardware IP to new applications remains a much broader challenge.

Making derivative chip design more scalable will require more than increasingly capable AI models. Design teams need organized, accessible IP data; reusable engineering methodologies; tools that can evaluate architectural and physical trade-offs; and verification workflows that account for changes in configuration, implementation, and operating environment. Agentic AI may help connect and automate these processes, but the underlying tools must still produce results grounded in physical reality.

At the most fundamental level, many AI tools are text-based LLMs. “They are really, really good at predicting the next word, the next phrase, the next line, then the next paragraph, and that means AI can be used to write text-based chip design specs or chip design documents like RTL design,” said Keysight’s Kamdar. “AI can be used to write verification scripts that will test RTL and prove it’s good RTL or not, or find flaws in it. AI can read a long series of debug logs that could be gigabytes long, and humans will take forever to go through that. AI can quickly say, ‘Hey, did you go to line 79? That’s where I see a major issue.’ Largely, that’s what AI is helping with. There are so many other aspects of chip design that are not text-based, not suitable for words, and they still need humans actively.”

For chip architects and design teams, the opportunity is not simply to generate new designs faster, but to reduce the engineering effort required to turn proven IP into new products. Achieving that goal will depend on how effectively AI-driven automation can work with established EDA tools, engineering knowledge, and physics-based verification to identify what can be reused, determine what must change, and validate the resulting design. The real measure of AI’s success in derivative chip design will not be how quickly it generates new RTL, but how reliably it can help engineers transform existing IP into verified, physically viable designs with less manual effort.

**References to DAC presentations**

1. “[Design Automation for Emerging AI](https://63dac.conference-program.com/presentation/?id=K102&sess=sess179): From AI Pins to Datacenter” (Qualcomm)
2. “Is [EDA AI Delivering](https://63dac.conference-program.com/presentation/?id=PAV104&sess=sess220) On Its ROI Promise?” (Arm)
3. “Is the EDA Industry Fundamentally Ill-Prepared for [True 3D Heterogeneous Integration](https://63dac.conference-program.com/presentation/?id=PANEL105&sess=sess203)?” (Cadence)

---

**Related Articles**
[From Spec To Formal Properties](https://semiengineering.com/from-spec-to-formal-properties/)
Can LLMs turn a specification into a set of formal properties that can be used to verify an implementation? The answer is getting closer to being yes, but with caveats.

[Auto-Generation Of Properties: Methodology Insertion](https://semiengineering.com/auto-generation-of-properties-methodology-insertion/)
Technology is only useful if it improves an existing methodology. Property generation is still refining that goal, but in the long term it could be very useful.

[EDA’s Future Is Evidence-Driven Automation](https://semiengineering.com/edas-future-is-evidence-driven-automation/)
AI may accelerate semiconductor design, but users still need formal proof, semantic continuity, and auditable workflows to trust automation.
