items.title: AI Vs. High-Level Synthesis
items.content:
**Key Takeaways:**

- The main advantage provided by HLS is productivity, but those gains diminish if not accompanied by a robust verification methodology.
- AI agents around current HLS tools will allow more exploration and build on existing trust but full AI potential may want to work outside those bounds.
- Producing RTL is the easy part. HLS has to generate RTL that is implementable, that meets power, performance and area constraints, within a defined context. AI struggles with this today.

---

High-level synthesis (HLS) initially struggled to find a market, but eventually it became a valuable tool for certain kinds of design. It is now threatened by the promise of AI, which some predict will allow engineers to go from specification to finished silicon while avoiding many EDA tools, including HLS.

Most developers of HLS solutions are not troubled by this today, though they do see many changes on the horizon.

HLS has been most valuable for algorithmic accelerators, although that could change. “When I have something that is too slow or power hungry to run on a CPU, I may want to look at custom silicon,” says Stuart Clubb, technical product management director at [Siemens EDA](https://semiengineering.com/entities/mentor-a-siemens-business/). “I might choose to go the path of IP reuse, and that is the most likely answer for a bus interface or peripheral. HLS got shoved off to the new blocks — things that hadn’t been done before and needed some smart architectural hardware design, and solving problems that hadn’t been tackled before.”

The main advantage of HLS is productivity. “HLS handles complex control logic and data path equally well, with 10 to 20 times less code than RTL,” says Badru Agarwala, CEO and co-founder at Rise Design Automation. “Less code is easier to review, so you can trust what you’re shipping, and easier to edit when the specification changes. That is what lets a design scale from a single block to a large subsystem, whether an engineer or an AI writes it.”

Those productivity gains can be significant (see figure 1, below.) “When we talk about HLS, the goal is not to do everything using HLS, or when we attempt LLM to RTL, the goal is not to do everything on LLM to RTL,” said Diptesh Nandi, senior product marketing manager at Microchip. “There will be a certain portion that requires time to market, or faster processing that will not be optimized. If you use HLS, it’s probably going to consume more power because it’s not going to be optimized (compared to hand-crafted RTL). If you take the LLM-to-RTL route — where you focus on time to market and then apply it on the development time, the training time that you require where you’re creating the whole tools flow, or creating the whole design — then you will spend less time developing the whole solution, less time training the whole solution, thereby saving power.”

**Fig. 1: An HLS flow for FPGA designs. Source: Microchip**

The real challenge is that chip complexity is growing faster than engineering productivity. “Writing RTL was never the biggest bottleneck,” says Rise DA’s Agarwala. “Amdahl’s law applies here. Making one relatively small part of the development process dramatically faster doesn’t help much if the rest of the process remains unchanged. Most of the schedule is spent on verification and the iterations needed to meet performance, power, and area targets.”

This does play into one aspect of HLS, which is that verification time of C code is orders of magnitude faster than RTL. Given that HLS can synthesize designs quickly, and those can be verified at the abstract level, it enables an AI agent to evaluate a lot of alternatives in a small amount of time. This coupling may be the big winner, but we are not there yet.

“Software is leading the pack,” says Tom De Muer, fellow at [Keysight EDA](https://semiengineering.com/entities/keysight-technologies/). “Digital design is coming next, followed by mixed analog, and then the full physics. High-level synthesis sits at that digital part. It’s lagging software. In addition, we have the problem in the semiconductor world that you cannot prompt something very vague and expect something to come out that’s production-ready.”

To see widespread adoption, it has to solve a real problem. “For 50 years, EDA progress meant climbing abstraction,” says Mehir Arora, head of engineering at [ChipAgents](https://semiengineering.com/entities/alpha-design-ai-chipagents/). “We built RTL, then HLS, because the human mind cannot hold the full design space. Abstraction narrows the potential design space for an engineer, making it possible for them to reason about it. But it is a loss of potential QoR. HLS was never about better hardware, but a price of designing for human capacity.”

Still, trust must be gained for any new tool or abstraction. “When we talk about AI doing this, there is some resistance from people like us because we have been burnt by things that we didn’t understand,” says Keysight’s De Muer. “For instance, if you have a design that works, that’s great, but it works under the test conditions that you know that you tested it with. But we all had our tape outs that went into production. We had full 100% regression test, but in the field something failed, and then you need to understand how it works to fix it.”

It took a long time before HLS was trusted. “HLS is now providing significant value for a specific segment of designs,” says Dave Kelf, CEO at Breker Verification Systems. “One of the most significant barriers to entry for the technology, and indeed logic synthesis originally, was the disconnect between the abstract model, especially regarding circuit timing, and the final design output. Engineers had trouble making that connection, making them nervous about trusting the results.”

What is stopping AI from doing the synthesis itself? “The rules for the synthesizable subset of C++, and by extension SystemC, have remained relatively constant for probably the last 10 to 15 years,” says Siemens’ Clubb. “In the C+ world, modeling streaming interfaces needed some level of IP to be able to represent that in an untimed sequential language, versus trying to model the explicit concurrency. We created AC channel and bit-accurate data types. A designer, or AI, needs to write out code that understands these. There’s just not a lot of training material.”

**Verification**No new abstraction is going to be successful if you don’t have both a development and a verification methodology that work together. The widespread adoption of RTL required both RTL simulation and static timing verification. ESL required C and SystemC simulation and equivalence checking.

“On the verification side for HLS, people have clamored for sequential equivalent checking,” says Clubb. “It is slowly improving, but as with any formal verification challenge, there are limitations, capacity issues, things associated with latency and throughput. There’s still a lot of RTL verification required.”

Building trust takes time. “We already trust synthesis tools to perform complicated transformations without inspecting every gate,” says Agarwala. “That trust comes from verification, not from how the implementation was generated. Coverage-driven verification is equally important. Requirements can be mapped to assertions and functional coverage points, showing which parts of the specification have been exercised and which still need attention. Formal verification adds another level of confidence by checking RTL properties exhaustively within the assumptions of the formal model. The goal is to make verification faster and more complete, not simply generate RTL faster.”

The need to perform simulation on the output slows down performance and adoption. “The issue that arises, especially with analog and RF, is that you need to verify them against a physical oracle, a high-frequency simulator,” says De Muer. “Those take a long time to simulate. An agent typically needs multiple runs, and if that run takes you two or three hours, it naturally limits how much exploration can be done. Comparing it to software, you can produce a program, compile it, test it, and it stands up. In a fraction of a second, you have a data point to learn from. That’s not the case when you’re doing a 200 or 300 gigahertz design. Many runs are required so that models can improve.”

**AI’s potential**In a similar manner, the primary advantage that AI can provide is productivity. By finding better architectures through a process of trial and error, it may eventually get to better designs, but that is not the case today. “The next leap in engineering productivity won’t come from doing the same work faster,” says Agarwala. “It will come from fundamentally changing how work gets done. The biggest productivity gains will come from shortening the time between an idea, an implementation, and a verified result. The teams that succeed will be the ones that can explore, measure, and verify the best architectures fastest.”

But that is not going to happen with agents. “Somebody once said that AI is a really good cover band,” says Clubb. “It’s seen the sheet music. It knows all the lyrics, and it will give you a variation on a theme. But for something completely new, maybe not so much. AI is still a way off, and it’s still very reliant on skill files that somebody else has to put together to guide how to do it. There’s not enough volume of training material. Even with these trillions of parameters and all of this input to these frontier models, they’re still not there yet.”

In addition, agents are built around existing tools, which may not be the best idea. “An LLM is much more acceptive for lower-level abstractions,” says ChipAgents’ Arora. “Give it verification and fast feedback and it can skip abstraction layers. Taking CUDA kernel generation as an example, we’ve seen LLMs write CUDA or even lower-level PTX without traditional compiler optimizations, but generate better output. Similar trends are happening in EDA and the IC flow. While humans are well suited to microarchitecture => HLS => RTL => netlist, we already see that LLMs are better at producing RTL directly when equipped with physics surrogates to predict PPA. Indeed, in the future, we may see LLMs directly generate netlists, eliminating another layer of indirection.”

Many people point to a context issue today. “If I say, ‘Design me an inductor for some IC design,’ my agent will do this, but it probably didn’t care about how well it will perform in situ in a bigger context,” says De Muer. “Does it even select the process I’m allowed to use? All of those things are missing. AI is helping to translate those intents. But you still need to be very specific because where the engineering matters, for the semiconductor pieces, all of these things need to be specified. They are not coming out of thin air.”

This is an opportunity to bring more of the context together for some problem domains. “Engineers can develop and verify the design within a TLM-based system simulation environment, alongside processors, memories, and other components, and then synthesize that same description into RTL,” says Agarwala. “This avoids maintaining separate functional models that can gradually diverge from the hardware implementation. Software development and system-level verification can also begin before RTL is available.”

That context is the ultimate shift left as well. “HLS historically, and most RTL designers, have striven to produce RTL that closes timing because if it doesn’t close timing, it’s useless,” says Clubb. “In HLS we do a lot of algorithmic, arithmetic stuff that has cascading wavefronts. When you get to a gate-level netlist, and in order to close timing, it’s not just a nice bunch of fast adders and AND gates or multipliers. There is a benefit to making sure that you don’t put too many operators between registers, because then your glitch power starts to get unmanageable. Even though your area goes down, if you over-pipeline, you’ve got too many registers. That puts your switching power up and puts your clock tree power up. You can do design exploration to hone in on the local saddle for power, or the local saddle for area, or — and this sounds like a prompt — find me the lowest power that doesn’t exceed the smallest area by 5%.”

One of the concerns is design stability. “With AI-generated RTL, changing the pipeline, resource allocation, or memory architecture often means generating a new implementation and verifying it again,” says Agarwala. “Every rewrite creates another opportunity for subtle bugs. HLS takes a different approach. We can keep the functional description unchanged while using synthesis constraints to control pipelining, parallelism, resource sharing, and memory organization. This allows AI to explore hundreds of implementations without regenerating thousands of lines of RTL. Some architectural changes still require modification of the source, but those changes are generally easier to make and verify at a higher level.”

**Reality**The big question is exactly how well can AI do this today? “It does really badly, mainly because the type of code that we are handling in HLS does not usually have an easy one-to-one mapping for RTL,” says Clubb. “Once you start the process of scheduling and laying out a data path, you need to understand the process technology and the frequency that you are aiming for. What interfacing do you want? Is this a single-ported memory as an array? Is it a dual-ported memory that has memory bandwidth limitations? Can I split that up? Can I re-architect that? There are things you can do as microarchitectural constraints in HLS because they’re programmatic, but for the interfacing things like stalling, flushing, bubble compression, AI is not good.”

Still, if you have productivity gains, is it good enough? “If you need a small widget and you don’t care too much about performance, you don’t care too much about power consumption, if all of those things are irrelevant to you, AI can produce something reasonable for digital or even analog design,” says De Muer. “But even if we reduce that time to zero, the end-to-end results or gains are pretty modest. We need to look one step further, but that’s a long journey, and it comes from changing the workflows.”

Some of the gains are consumed by additional verification demands. “There was a recent paper out of Harvard talking about how AI-generated code in general is pushing more effort into verification of that code,” says Clubb. “That means the ROI for many companies is becoming questionable.”

For now, AI appears more likely to augment HLS than replace it. While AI can accelerate RTL generation and architectural exploration, producing silicon-ready designs still requires verification, implementation awareness, and careful optimization for power, performance, and area. Whether AI ultimately replaces existing abstraction layers may depend less on its ability to generate code than on its ability to produce predictable, verifiable results.

---

**Related Articles**[Hardware From Specifications Using AI](https://semiengineering.com/hardware-from-specifications-using-ai/)
Can AI really generate hardware from specifications? It may not matter, because that’s only a small part of the problem.

[Auto-Generation Of Properties: Methodology Insertion](https://semiengineering.com/auto-generation-of-properties-methodology-insertion/)
Technology is only useful if it improves an existing methodology. Property generation is still refining that goal, but in the long term it could be very useful.

[Shift Left Is Becoming A System-Level Problem](https://semiengineering.com/shift-left-is-becoming-a-system-level-problem/)
Rise in complexity is pushing engineers to validate hardware, software, and physical constraints earlier in the design flow, but fragmented workflows make that difficult.

The post [AI Vs. High-Level Synthesis](https://semiengineering.com/ai-vs-high-level-synthesis/) appeared first on [Semiconductor Engineering](https://semiengineering.com).

items.title: AI Can Read The Code, But Can It Understand The Chip?
items.content:
**Key Takeaways:**

- Agentic AI could dramatically increase chip design productivity, but multiplying autonomous workloads will place unprecedented demands on EDA data management systems, compute resources, and network infrastructure.
- Fragmented design data, inconsistent data quality, and strict IP security requirements are major obstacles to deploying AI at scale, making data governance, accessibility, and traceability increasingly critical.
- Frontier AI models are becoming more capable of automating traditional EDA workflows, but achieving deeper optimization of chip layouts, waveforms, and other domain-specific data may require specialized models and hybrid AI architectures.

---

**Experts at the Table**: Agentic AI promises to close the chip design productivity gap, but the explosion of autonomous workloads is exposing fundamental limitations in how EDA data is stored, accessed, secured, and managed. Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss this at the 2026 Design Automation Conference with Chuck Alpert, AI fellow at [Cadence](https://semiengineering.com/entities/cadence-design-systems/); Simon Rance, general manager, IP and Data Management Business at [Keysight EDA](https://semiengineering.com/entities/keysight-technologies/); Sathish Balasubramanian, head of product for EDA AI and Solido at [Siemens EDA](https://semiengineering.com/entities/mentor-a-siemens-business/); Ramesh Narayanaswamy, scientist at [Synopsys](https://semiengineering.com/entities/synopsys-inc/); and Dean Drako, CEO of [IC Manage](https://semiengineering.com/entities/ic-manage/). What follows are excerpts of that discussion.

**L-R: Cadence’s Alpert; Keysight EDA’s Rance; Siemens EDA’s Balasubramanian; Synopsys’ Narayanaswamy; IC Manage’s Drako.**

**SE: What are the biggest challenges your customers are dealing with for implementing AI in EDA data management?**

**Drako**: The biggest problem facing large customers with globally distributed design systems is continuing to scale to larger, more complicated designs and to reuse IP. Right now, designs are a giant assembly of IP components that need to be assembled, verified, and put together. With AI coming into the equation, those customers want clean databases that the AI can use. They want easy access for the AI to get to that IP, leverage it, and manage the complexity the AI introduces in running more jobs faster. That puts a bigger load on the design management system and the distribution of that data.

**Alpert**: There’s a huge productivity gap, so they need AI. It’s not like, ‘Oh, it would be nice, so we’re more productive.’ They’re desperate because the gap between designs and our ability to improve keeps growing,  even though EDA always improves year over year. Hopefully agentic AI will narrow the gap. In terms of deploying it, part of the biggest challenge is that there’s so much noise. There are so many options — internal/ external models, startups. How do they figure out what to do to make a production-worthy AI flow? That’s probably a real challenge for them.

**Balasubramanian**: What we are seeing right now is there’s so much AI stuff, both in terms of terms and nomenclature and what people think they can do and cannot do with AI. In the last couple of years, top customers have at least figured out what to do and what not to do at a high level, but the key challenge I see is that many new factors are coming into play. What they’re worried about right now is the quality they’re seeing. They want to have a deterministic flow. They also want to make sure that they are not overkilling in terms of their token budgets and compute infrastructure to get those same answers fast — correct answers. So there’s quite a bit of nuance in how they’re deploying, and it’s really based on where they are focusing and what problem they’re solving. And they are getting to a point where they know what to solve. It’s not like this push-button flow for the entire problem, where you push a button and say I want a chip for this case. They are becoming more realistic. And another point is there are so many variables. Every customer wants to do everything, but then they get stuck in this loophole about what is the right thing to do.

**Narayanaswamy**: In dealing with customers, we see they’re looking to close the productivity gap. There are all these magic numbers, like we are 2× short of the number of designers people want for all these new design starts people want. On the data management side, we see a couple of flavors of issues. One is, ‘Where the heck is my data going?’ Because you license IP, can you train with that licensed IP? Probably not. But somebody needs to govern that. Or even, ‘Under what contract are you handing that to an LLM?’

**Drako**: An LLM might go and use something that you didn’t know it used.

**Narayanaswamy**: If you don’t have an enterprise account with Anthropic and you don’t click the right button, everything you’re doing is there, and Anthropic will train with what they want. So the governance is one. The second is the internal things we build out of this. So you have agentic memory. That sounds good. It helps the flow, but what did you stick in it? And when I am transitioning from, say, when this chip is done, or this block is done, to the next design, what do I carry forward? Historically, we haven’t saved reproducible stuff. But now, there’s a whole new set of things. And the third thing is that models are, in some ways, horrible at dealing with the volume of data. You say I have a waveform database. The model is smart enough to take that waveform database and turn it into text. But that waveform database was like a terabyte of stuff, and you just spent how many tokens going there? You need to provide something where the model can query what it needs or the abstraction it needs. I’ve even seen where, if you give a model enough time, it starts writing a little MCP server. It goes and finds the API from somewhere. So it’s doing all these sub-optimal things, and I don’t think our customers can afford this stuff anymore at scale. Those are things we are looking to solve.

**Rance**: Our customers have been using our solutions for almost 30 years now, and they’re realizing they’re sitting on a treasure trove of data to leverage for AI. But the challenges that they’re finding are that data is all over the place. What’s the quality of that data? How can we trust that data? And then, how can we govern and secure that data so it doesn’t get released to an LLM, flawed, or to the wrong people? Data management has been seen as a necessity, but it’s just about managing the data. Now it’s, ‘How do you help us find that data, organize it, secure it, and control it so our AI isn’t leaking any of our IP?’ And, ‘How can AI can leverage that and help with better reuse of IP?’ That’s been a challenge for 20 years or so. Solutions like IC Manage, ours, Perforce, and others help with IP reuse, but how it’s packaged and how reusable it is are always a challenge. In the AI era, there’s a lot more automation that can be wrapped around that to help with real IP reuse, but it comes back to those foundational pillars that our customers are seeing in that challenge — quality, trust, and how we cover and trace it.

**SE: Scaling was mentioned right off the bat. What does this mean for EDA data management today?**

**Drako**: An engineering project to design a chip may be 10 engineers, 100 engineers, or 1,000 engineers. But what we want, to overcome the productivity issues that everyone’s bringing up, is to use agents to augment those engineers. So maybe have those engineers, instead of operating in 10 workspaces in one workspace each, have 10 or 20 agents that each of them is directing. They get parallelism with all these agents doing work, and they’re more like the director of the orchestra, and so their productivity goes up. To do that, those agents need workspaces. They’re checking stuff out of the version control system or out of the design management system, they’re doing work on it, and then they’re checking it back in, and so you’ve just 10× or 20×’d the load on your design management system, your network file system (NFS), and you’ve 10× or 20×’d the number of licenses you need to buy from Cadence or Siemens or Synopsys or Keysight, or whoever, because you know that that much more is going on. So there’s a scaling issue. We focused on scaling the design management piece, which we’ve always been very strong at. But if you go and say, I’ve got 1,000 engineers, which used to have 1,000 workspaces that you’re managing and updating on an hourly basis, now I’ve got 25,000. The scaling problem is quite large, so that’s one aspect. Then we’ve done a lot of work on the NFS component. NFS is a great solution, but everything has to go over the network. It’s very inefficient. It’s a very chatty protocol, so it’s slow. That means all our customers are constantly fighting speed issues with the file system and the servers. When you want to launch a regression run, and it’s going to launch at 10 p.m. when everybody’s out, but it’s going to launch on 5,000 servers, you’ve got to get all 5,000 servers to have the same data so that you can run all those regression tests. That’s a huge load on the file systems. We had one customer who would launch the regressions every night, and the elevator would stop running because they’d somehow hooked the elevator into the local network, so nobody could leave. So we introduced what is essentially an NFS booster to help with that problem. And then you’ve also got scaling of CAD. If you think about it, there’s a small organization of CAD and IT guys supporting 100 or 1000 engineers. Now they’ve got to support 100,000 engineers plus 10,000 agents, who are also trying to use that same infrastructure to get work done.

**Narayanaswamy**: An interesting side of scaling the business is also velocity. We were running some experiments, and somebody said, “Look, we run these 20 epochs, but it’s actually over 20 nightly runs. Suddenly, those 20 epochs are happening in 8 hours. So you grab the LSF queue, and your agent is hanging on to it. So the bursty workload is one thing. Predictability is another.

**Drako**: One of the things customers are very concerned about, and is a big focus, is security. Inside of [our technology], there are a lot of security components to limit access, often for government contracts, often for locations in other countries where they don’t want them to have full access to everything in the design. There are lots of very practical reasons that aren’t really obvious when you just think about it, and so all of those security components, security restrictions, or security controls are going to be critical in the AI execution as well because the AI can get a little rambunctious and actually kind of start creating things like you mentioned and try to get to things. We’ve seen a bunch of stories in the press about AI going rogue and digging into places it shouldn’t. With those security issues, oftentimes there’s security by obscurity, or mediocre security constraints, or people haven’t thought through the security a whole lot. There’s going to be a lot more in the data management world around security with AI in the game, because AI doesn’t necessarily have the same conscience that an employee might, and it isn’t bound by the same laws.

**Narayanaswamy**: That’s why we’re going around doing secure sandboxes. The more conscious customer is really saying, ‘There’s an LLM call. I need to know what access that sub-agent is going to have.’ It needs to be bounded. Most customers have gotten smarter. They used to do the air gap themselves.

**Balasubramanian**: One customer said, ‘Every prompt is an IP that I’m giving away. If I’m trying to say, ‘Do this in a way that does this,’ that’s the way I’m actually designing or doing something. I’m actually giving advice, so we really are planning to go for air-gapped on-prem.’ I would say everyone is thinking about it right now.

**Alpert**: That trend’s reversing now. A year and a half ago, all customers were saying, ‘Oh yeah, only air-gapped on-prem. We need to use open-source models.’ But frontier models like Claude, OpenAI, and Gemini have gotten so good that people don’t want to sacrifice quality. They’re figuring out how they can use these and connect with them. I’d say more customers are on that side of the fence now, but maybe they’re also making special deals where they can host it themselves.

**Drako**: Customers are figuring it out. Because it’s all new, there’s a big strategy question: ‘Do I go and invest in my own AI models and train them on my designs?’ These are all LLMs, and they do very well when it’s language. If I’m looking at Verilog, they’ll do well. If I’m looking at a waveform file, they don’t understand it, so they convert it to text. If I’m looking at layout, they don’t understand it. They’ve never been trained on it. They’ve never seen it, and it’s not words. There’s a big question of who’s going to create AI models that are trained on it and understand it. Is that going to be the EDA companies, or the Nvidias and AMDs who are going to go do that? They don’t know right now. Everybody’s trying to figure it out.

**Rance**: We’re seeing a bit of a hybrid of that, where we’re training our own models, but then we’re creating the infrastructure to provide to them. So they can add and create their own models in conjunction with that, and get a lot more value when they combine our EDA tools with the models and the data. Then they’re using the environment to train and create their surrogate models, put that into the workflow, and build trust between the two. ‘This is what it’s doing. It’s contained to that, secured. We don’t have to worry about it going rogue.’ They’re doing it in small phases and rolling it out, but they’re creating agentic workflows that are very tightly constrained right now to prevent leakage.

**Narayanaswamy**: In terms of the modeling, Chuck makes an important point. When you need reasoning, if you don’t use a frontier model, you may be applying the wrong tool. But for the more domain-specific stuff, there’s this hybrid where you could have sub-domain models, even some very specialized things. Models seem terrible at things like assertions, which are very specialized temporal assertions that reason over time. And you could say, ‘Let’s have a model that is quite good at assertions — but for reasoning.’ That is the tension. Maybe folks like Anthropic need to come to the table and provide a level of trust. It’s a ‘trust me’ business with all of them. Something has to change there.

**Alpert**: When it comes to training models, the problem with that is like, ‘Okay, let me pick a model to train. It’s probably open-source, which means it’s probably already behind the frontier models. Now I’m going to work on that for three to four months and deploy it to the customer. But now it’s probably a year behind because some new model will come out. That means the training we’ve done has to be good enough to pass. That’s a tough, tough game, and it’s a cat-and-mouse game. It’s like, ‘I train on this model, but now I have to retrain on some new model.’ The danger is that the frontier models will just obliterate what we’ve trained. That’s happened before. Will it continue to happen? I don’t know. Maybe they’re stuck in a place. Then three months from now, it’s like, ‘Oh, there’s a model that’s pretty good at that and understands it.’

**Balasubramanian**: The frontier models are getting better, but one thing they still lack is enterprise data. They just don’t have access to it. On the front-end side, they can probably get away with it, but not on the RTL generation side.

**Drako**: They don’t need it. There’s enough RTL code out there publicly that they can get. They can do it, but there are not a whole lot of layouts in the public world.

**Alpert**: Here’s where I’ll disagree. We can now do skills. We can now give expertise to LLMs, so you could say a lot of people who do place-and-route actually never look at it. They’re just command-line junkies, and they get reports and the like.

**Drako**: That’s if you’re using the tool. But that’s the command-line interface, the log files, the human interface. The LLM can plug in and do what the human did on the tool. But if you actually want to get AI in the tool, and the results aren’t a log file, you want to look at the layout and say, ‘Oh, that’s not the layout I want.’

**Alpert**: It’s one thing to say we’re trying to make humans more productive, so we can now automate the job they did with the stuff with the command line. What you’re saying is that you think we could reach a higher level of PPA.

**Drako**: You’ve just got to differentiate those two piles.

**Alpert**: So as we’ve been saying about closing the design productivity gap, that’s not needed. You don’t need trained models. But if you want to reach that next level, then now it’s time for some real creativity. What’s going to be really interesting is how we as an industry, for example, write a new place-and-route tool that’s truly agentic, image-based, and all that.

**Drako**: It will eventually happen. It’s inevitable.

**Alpert**: But quantum computing is a matter of time, and I’ve been hearing about it for 30 years. I’ll be retired by the time it comes out.

**SE: Quantum is 5 to 10 years out.**

**Alpert**: Quantum might be available today, but when is more than 1% of semiconductor revenue going to go to quantum? That’s my bar. Like, is that 5 years, 10 years, 20 years? I don’t know.

items.title: Many languages, one common neural code
items.content:
Languages take on thousands of forms. Some are tonal, like Vietnamese, where shifts in pitch convey distinct meanings. English relies on precise word orders, but this matters less for Russian, where words can be swapped without changing the intended message.

Despite so much variety in the linguistic kingdom, an MIT study has found that the human brain may process all sorts of languages in a universal way.

Artificial intelligence made this finding possible. In the study [published today in *Nature Neuroscience*](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41593-026-02523-6)*,* the researchers used multilingual models to predict how the human brain responds to various languages. Those models also helped the researchers detect a shared brain process across people who collectively spoke 21 different languages.

“Of course, there are many differences in the ways humans converse with each other. But our team found that there is something fundamentally similar in how the brain communicates,” says [Evelina Fedorenko](https://mcgovern.mit.edu/profile/ev-fedorenko/), who is an investigator at MIT’s McGovern Institute for Brain Research, an associate professor of brain and cognitive sciences, and the senior author of the paper.

The study is the first to use multilingual models to predict brain responses across many languages. As researchers develop AI language tools to diagnose brain disorders, this work can extend their benefit to speakers of more languages, and may one day even keep endangered ones from vanishing.

**Parsing the linguistic mind**

Language allows us to share our thoughts about the outside world and the ones we create in our minds. That power lives within a network of brain regions located in the left hemisphere.

“Every language is managed by these same parts of the brain,” explains Andrea Gregor de Varda, the lead author of the new study, a postdoc in the Fedorenko lab, and fellow in the [K. Lisa Yang Integrative Computational Neuroscience (ICoN) Center](https://yangtan.mit.edu/our-research/k-lisa-yang-icon-center/).

While scientists know that all languages activate the same parts of the brain, de Varda and Fedorenko wanted to know if that meant the brain processes them in the same way.

For example, they wondered, does the brain of someone who speaks Korean operate comparably to the brains of a Hindi or Spanish speaker?

It’s extremely hard to answer that question if you lack the right tools, de Varda says. And they needed one capable of creating a common code for comparing all sorts of languages — a task that is well-suited to artificial intelligence.

**Where AI meets the brain**

Large language models (LLMs) — such as those powering ChatGPT and Claude — interpret language much like the human brain, although they weren’t designed to do so. That surprising similarity is allowing de Varda and others in the field to wield these tools as a piercing [lens into the human mind](https://mcgovern.mit.edu/2025/11/19/the-cost-of-thinking/). Such studies often explore LLMs’ ability to learn or make sense of linguistic elements, such as grammar and meaning, to glean insights into how the brain might handle communication. But early LLMs used to work within a single language. The MIT researchers thought another class of models might help expand that scope.

“Multilingual language models are LLMs that can process hundreds of languages at once,” explains Fedorenko. Like other AIs of their kind, multilingual models ingest words or phrases and output numbers that scientists can extract. “Those numbers show how the model represents that bit of language,” she says. Now the team could study many languages at once using a single numerical code from the models. But the extent to which the models aligned with the human mind still lurked in the unknowns. De Varda believed he could coax an answer into light through a computational approach.

Using machine learning, he merged two data sources: the multilingual models’ code and scans of people’s brains as they performed linguistic tasks. The product was an AI tool known as an encoding model. It takes a multilingual model’s code, say, for a sentence, and predicts how the human brain might light up in response to the same input.

Encoding models at the time only existed for a handful of languages including English, French, and Chinese. But de Varda sought to test whether those models could be extended to more — and importantly, understudied ones. Doing so could reveal new aspects in which AI mirrors the human brain, and even detect a shared neural component across speakers of various languages.

**A mental bridge between languages**

The Fedorenko lab already had preexisting brain imaging data from speakers of 12 languages: Afrikaans, Dutch, Farsi, French, Lithuanian, Marathi, Norwegian, Romanian, Spanish, Tamil, Turkish, and Vietnamese. They recruited speakers of nine additional ones for their new study — Italian, Portuguese, German, Russian, Polish, Hindi, Arabic, Mandarin, and Korean — and recorded their brain activity while they listened to stories from “Alice in Wonderland” in their native language. By coupling that brain imaging data with outputs from multilingual models, the team created encoding models for those 21 languages.

“We found that the encoding models accurately predicted brain responses in all of the languages we studied — even in Marathi and Lithuanian, that, in contrast to English, we only have a limited amount of data on,” says Fedorenko. “The fact that there’s this emergent similarity between models and humans across so many languages is really quite exciting.”

Another finding was more interesting still. Even though the researchers trained an encoding model in a single language, it could predict brain activity for a language it had never seen before. For example, an encoding model trained to predict brain responses in French could also predict responses in Vietnamese, without ever being trained in Vietnamese. It was a truly fascinating discovery, de Varda says, because this was only possible if all the speakers’ brains were representing language in a shared way: a neural thread binding human communication.

What was that shared component? Dissecting different linguistic features across all the languages suggested that it has something to do with meaning. “That’s the intended power of communication, right? To share meaning; new information or our feelings about the world. So it’s fascinating we see that reflected in this work,” says Fedorenko.

In science, this new study gives brain researchers some explanations for long-held curiosities among them. In society, it could steer emerging technologies into a more inclusive direction. Scientists are starting to explore clinical uses of AI language tools, such as those that can detect cognitive decline based on brain activity patterns during language.But most of those studies, and the methods clinicians use today, are in common and well-studied languages like English. By showing how AI and the human brain overlap across many diverse languages, this new research may be a step toward clinical tools that do not leave most speakers out.

In another vein, reversing the Fedorenko lab’s approach might help preserve languages on the brink of extinction. “Say you had one single speaker of a language that is dying out. You might imagine a case in which we can train a model in the opposite direction: give it images of that speaker’s brain, and it could translate those into language,” notes Fedorenko.

De Varda adds that there are features that clearly differ between languages, too, and that those must be somehow represented in the brain and even LLMs. Defining those differences in future research, he says, might unearth new fragments of knowledge to complete the puzzle of the linguistic mind.

items.title: 科研成果 | 智能计算实验室方承煜同学成果被NeurIPS2026接收｜NeurIPS 2026
items.content:
*来源：THUSIGSICLAB*

*文章链接：https://mp.weixin.qq.com/s/AadX6xpxE2gywQDMF4dyQQ*

论文题目：PRISM: Rethinking Atmospheric Scattering Reconstruction as a Unified Understanding and Restoration Model for Real-world Dehazing

论文链接：https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.07048

**论文简介**

01

研究概述

真实世界图像去雾面临非均匀雾分布、空间变化的颜色偏移，以及真实配对数据稀缺等挑战。本文提出 PRISM，将单幅图像去雾视为场景内容与大气散射过程的联合重建问题，在统一的物理模型下，同时恢复清晰图像并估计雾造成的退化。

PRISM 的核心是近端散射大气重建框架 PSAR。它借助优化展开，交替更新场景辐亮度、透射率和空间变化的大气光，使图像复原与散射估计相互约束。为缩小合成雾与真实雾之间的差异，本文进一步设计在线非均匀雾合成流程，以及面向未配对真实雾图的选择性自蒸馏自适应方法 SSDA。后者通过感知质量筛选可靠伪标签，并利用散射变量检查复原图像中的残余雾，从感知与物理两个角度提升真实场景表现。

PRISM 与已有方法的结果对比，展示颜色自然度、残余雾及伪影方面的差异

02

主要贡献

第一，提出具有物理结构的 PSAR 框架，显式估计大气散射变量，并通过近端优化步骤联合重建场景辐亮度与散射过程。

第二，提出在线非均匀雾合成流程和 SSDA，将质量门控蒸馏与物理散射先验结合，实现未配对真实雾图上的自适应学习。

第三，在真实世界去雾基准上进行系统评估。实验表明，在论文采用的评估协议下，PRISM 能够兼顾去雾效果、颜色自然度与细节保持，并在多项指标上取得有竞争力的结果。

**研究背景与问题建模**

真实场景中的雾往往分布不均，还会与局部彩色雾、车灯、建筑窗户等引起的颜色偏移，以及相机噪声和压缩伪影共同作用。仅凭一张有雾图像，同时推断原本的清晰场景与雾的物理属性，本身就是一个高度不确定的问题。直接学习从有雾到清晰的映射，通常缺少显式物理约束；传统散射模型方法则往往先估计透射率和大气光，再反演清晰图像，未充分利用三者之间的相互制约。

将物理模型与优化展开结合，为联合复原提供了更有结构的路径。已有方法中，PDN 将先验优化引入展开框架，但最终重组方式难以适应真实复合退化；CORUN 联合更新透射率和场景辐亮度，却采用全局恒定大气光，限制了对局部照明及空间非均匀散射的表达。与此同时，规则化的合成雾与真实退化仍存在域差，若不加筛选地使用伪标签进行自蒸馏，还可能不断累积错误。

**大气散射模型与联合重建**

大气散射模型可以从两个部分理解有雾图像的形成：一部分是原始场景光线在传播过程中受到雾的衰减，另一部分是大气散射引入的环境光。透射率描述原始场景信息保留了多少，大气光影响雾幕的亮度和颜色，场景辐亮度则对应希望恢复的清晰图像内容。

与将大气光视为整幅图像中的固定常量不同，PSAR 允许大气光和透射率随空间位置变化。这样既能描述不同区域雾的浓淡，也能刻画局部颜色偏移。更重要的是，三者不再独立估计，而是在同一个散射模型约束下联合更新，让清晰图像的恢复与雾的解释保持一致。

PSAR 的变量估计，依次为初始 A、初始 T、输入雾图、输出 A、输出 T 和输出 J

图 2 中，场景辐亮度以输入雾图初始化，大气光与透射率分别以 0.9 和 0.5 初始化。经过重建，透射率图呈现出与雾分布对应的空间差异，大气光图则反映场景相关的亮度与颜色变化。这些显式估计不仅参与图像复原，也为后续真实域自适应提供了物理依据。

**PSAR 近端散射大气重建**

PSAR 将一次复杂的联合重建过程拆解为多个连续阶段。每个阶段沿用同一大气散射目标，依次更新大气光、透射率与场景辐亮度。更新时既考虑当前图像是否符合散射模型，也限制新估计与上一阶段结果之间的变化幅度，避免各变量在迭代中出现过大的波动。这种方式对应于近端优化，而将多个阶段串联起来，就是优化展开。

PSAR 的阶段结构与整体架构。大气光保持近端闭式更新，透射率和场景辐亮度估计经轻量学习修正

具体而言，每个阶段首先根据当前的清晰图像与透射率估计，计算新的大气光；随后更新透射率，并通过轻量网络修正其结构性误差；最后利用更新后的散射变量重建场景辐亮度，再由另一轻量网络补偿图像中的纹理和辐射残差。下一阶段接收这些更新结果，继续细化重建。

这种设计兼顾了物理可解释性与学习模型的灵活性：大气光分支保留解析更新，透射率和场景重建分支加入学习修正。前者减少对弱约束变量的额外拟合，后者用于补偿理想散射模型难以覆盖的复杂退化。论文最终采用四个展开阶段，在效果与模型复杂度之间取得较好的平衡。

**在线非均匀雾合成与预训练**

真实雾既缺少大量成对的清晰图像，也难以通过简单的均匀散射过程充分模拟。为增加预训练样本的退化多样性，本文在 RIDCP 数据基础上采用深度引导的在线雾合成流程，并扩展了空间非均匀雾密度和近景雾强控制。合成在训练过程中动态完成，无须事先生成固定的雾图数据集。

01

非均匀密度场与近景雾控制

合成时，方法首先对清晰图像进行随机亮度调整并加入噪声，再结合深度信息采样基础雾密度。对于非均匀雾分支，系统会生成低分辨率随机噪声，并经过平滑、上采样和数值调整，将其转换为缓慢变化的空间雾密度场；同时保留一定比例的均匀雾样本。这样，模型在训练中既能看到整体均匀的雾幕，也能接触局部浓淡不同的雾分布。

此外，方法引入近景雾参数，通过调整深度相关的散射衰减，控制靠近相机区域的雾强。渲染时还会随机改变大气光的亮度与 RGB 颜色，并施加压缩退化。空间密度变化、深度衰减、局部颜色偏移和近景遮蔽共同扩大了合成样本的覆盖范围，使预训练更接近复杂真实场景。

02

预训练目标

预训练不仅要求模型恢复清晰图像，还监督其透射率估计，并通过多种约束协调视觉效果与物理解释。其中，像素级损失保证复原图像和透射率接近合成数据中的真值；大气光的全变分正则鼓励其保持平滑的空间变化；对比感知损失拉近复原结果与清晰图像的视觉特征，并使其与有雾输入拉开距离；对抗目标则帮助结果符合自然图像的统计特征，减少不自然的高频伪影。

值得注意的是，渲染时设置的大气光主要承担图像整体颜色和亮度的锚定作用，并不等于真实场景逐像素的大气光分布。因此，作者没有直接要求网络预测的大气光与渲染值逐像素一致，而是通过图像重建、透射率监督以及平滑正则间接约束这一变量，避免大气光分支错误吸收图像纹理。

**SSDA选择性自蒸馏自适应**

仅靠合成数据预训练，模型仍可能在真实浓雾、复杂光照和颜色偏移场景中表现不稳定。为此，SSDA 采用均值教师架构：EMA 教师处理真实雾图的弱增强版本，生成候选清晰图像；学生处理对应的强增强版本，并从可靠的教师结果中学习。整个适配过程包含两个互补模块：质量门控自蒸馏 QGSD 和基于物理的散射正则 PGSR。

SSDA 总体流程。QGSD 筛选教师伪标签，PGSR 通过教师估计的散射变量检查学生复原结果。

01

质量门控自蒸馏 QGSD

自蒸馏的主要风险在于，教师输出不一定始终优于学生，直接将所有结果作为伪标签可能强化错误。QGSD 因此增加了一道质量筛选：使用 MUSIQ 和 NIMA 两种无参考图像质量指标，分别从多尺度视觉质量和美学表现评价复原结果。只有当教师结果在所有选定指标上均严格优于学生时，当前样本才参与蒸馏。

对于通过筛选的样本，学生同时接受像素级监督与对比感知约束，以学习教师的清晰图像输出。由于 QGSD 只依据最终复原图像决定是否蒸馏，它并不依赖显式的透射率或大气光估计，也可以迁移到其他图像恢复网络中。

02

基于物理的散射正则 PGSR

感知质量评分并不能完全反映去雾是否充分：一张图像可能看起来细节丰富，却仍留有雾幕。PGSR 为此加入物理层面的检查。它将学生复原后的图像再次送入 EMA 教师，观察教师估计的透射率。如果某些区域仍被判断为低透射率，就说明那里可能存在残余雾，需要进一步约束。

不过，低透射率估计并非在所有区域都可靠。平滑区域、强光源和接近饱和的高亮像素容易引入误判。PGSR 因此结合像素与估计大气光的差异、局部纹理强度以及高亮抑制，确定哪些位置更适合施加约束。对于这些相对可靠的区域，方法只惩罚低于目标水平的透射率，目标值设置为 0.9；对于已达到目标的区域，不再继续推动去雾，以减少过度增强和不自然伪影。

最终，SSDA 将质量筛选后的蒸馏监督、残余雾的物理约束与大气光平滑正则联合使用。学生持续更新，教师则通过 EMA 平滑跟随学生，为后续迭代提供新的候选伪标签和散射估计。

**实验结果与分析**

01

定量比较

论文主要采用 FADE 衡量残余雾，并使用 PAQ2PIQ 和 CLIPIQA 评价感知质量。在 RTTS 与 Fattal 两个真实场景数据集上，完整 PRISM 均取得所比较方法中最低的 FADE，以及最高的两项感知质量分数。

RTTS 与 Fattal 定量结果。原论文表 1 截图，红色为最佳、蓝色为次佳。

在配对真实数据集 NH-HAZE 上，PSAR 取得 20.10 dB 的 PSNR 和 0.688 的 SSIM，均高于表中比较方法。这一实验主要评估 PSAR 的像素保真度与结构相似性，与完整 PRISM 在无参考真实场景上的评价形成补充。

NH-HAZE 上的 PSAR 评估

补充评估中，PRISM 在 RTTS 上的 NIMA、MUSIQ、ManIQA 和 LIQE 分数分别为 5.347、70.02、0.362 和 3.569，均为所比较方法中的最佳值，与主要指标的整体趋势一致。

02

定性比较

从可视化结果看，D4、RIDCP 等方法在浓雾或非均匀雾区域可能留下明显雾幕；CORUN、CoA 的部分结果存在色偏或暗部伪影；HazeFlow 的若干示例则出现不自然的紫色色调。相比之下，PRISM 在论文展示的场景中能够更充分地去除残余雾，同时保持相对自然的颜色、纹理与光照。

RTTS 与 Fattal 的定性比较。列依次为输入、D4、RIDCP、CORUN、CoA、HazeFlow 和 PRISM。

03

重建结构与合成流程消融

消融实验验证了 PSAR 各设计的作用。去掉场景重建分支的学习修正后，三项主要指标均下降；去掉透射率修正时，虽然 PAQ2PIQ 略有提升，但 FADE 和 CLIPIQA 变差。额外增加大气光学习修正没有带来收益，反而使 FADE 与 CLIPIQA 恶化；将空间变化的大气光改为全局常量，也会使三项指标整体下降。

在线非均匀雾合成同样发挥了作用：替换为均匀雾合成后，FADE 从 0.869 升至 0.955。阶段数实验则表明，四阶段已能取得较好的综合效果，继续增加至六阶段并未带来一致改善。

04

SSDA 的组成与泛化

PSAR 阶段数与 SSDA 组成模块消融。

去掉 QGSD 后，三项主要指标均变差；去掉 PGSR 后，CLIPIQA 虽略有提升，但 FADE 明显恶化，反映出感知纹理质量与残余雾抑制之间的权衡。迁移实验还表明，QGSD 和 SSDA 不仅适用于 PSAR：DGUNet 加入 QGSD、CORUN 预训练版本加入完整 SSDA 后，三项指标均得到改善，FADE 分别从 1.111 降至 0.940、从 1.044 降至 0.745。

教师更新策略也影响适配效果。固定教师与移除 EMA 时，FADE 分别为 0.583 和 0.526，均高于完整 PRISM 的 0.470。此外，直接监督渲染大气光，或者引入更复杂的像素级大气光随机变换，都没有带来额外收益。这些结果支持论文采用的 EMA 教师更新方式与大气光约束设计。

05

训练阶段可视化

训练阶段的结果进一步呈现了两部分方法的互补性：预训练后的 PSAR 已能去除大量雾，但在重度退化区域仍可能出现残余雾和颜色失真；经过 SSDA 适配后，PRISM 在浓雾与强色偏区域进一步减少伪影，并改善颜色自然度与细节保持。

训练阶段比较。三行依次为输入、预训练 PSAR 与自适应后的 PRISM。

**总结**

PRISM 的核心思路，是让去雾结果与雾的物理解释共同优化。PSAR 通过近端优化展开，将场景辐亮度、透射率和空间大气光纳入统一重建过程；在线非均匀雾合成则提高预训练对复杂退化的覆盖能力；SSDA 进一步利用可靠伪标签和散射先验，缓解从合成数据迁移到真实场景时的性能下降。

整体来看，本文的价值不仅在于提升去雾指标，也在于提供了一种结合物理模型、学习型重建与真实域自适应的思路。实验和消融结果表明，这些模块能够相互补充，在去除残余雾的同时，更好地保持颜色与图像细节。

图文 | 方承煜

编辑 | 吴鑫

审核 | 李老师

items.title: 科研成果 | NeurIPS 2026发表CCCI西南财经大学计算机与人工智能学院博士生蒋翔宇工作｜NeurIPS 2026
items.content:
*来源：认知计算与群智协同创新实验室*

*文章链接：https://mp.weixin.qq.com/s/hgf9ipDLqSuuepr2gDyJGQ*

近日，国际人工智能顶级学术会议神经信息处理系统大会（Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems，NeurIPS 2026）公布录用结果，南财经大学计算机与人工智能学院博士生蒋翔宇作为第一作者的论文《Beyond MSE: Differentiable Complexity Priors for Structure-Preserving Neural Denoising》被录用，西南财经大学为论文第一署名单位。

NeurIPS 是中国计算机学会（CCF）推荐的 A 类国际学术会议，也是机器学习与人工智能领域具有重要影响力的学术会议之一。会议创办于1987年，聚焦机器学习、深度学习及相关交叉领域的前沿研究，为全球学者提供高水平学术交流平台。

论文：Beyond MSE: Differentiable Complexity Priors for Structure-Preserving Neural Denoising

第一作者：蒋翔宇（博士生）

导师: 杨新教授

第一署名单位：西南财经大学

论文概述：

可微复杂度先验引导的结构保持神经去噪框架

在无线通信、生理信号监测和动态系统控制等应用中，噪声会干扰信号中承载有效信息的时间结构。现有神经网络去噪方法通常以均方误差（MSE）作为主要训练目标，关注重建信号与真实信号在各采样点上的数值差异。然而，数值误差的减小并不一定意味着信号结构得到保留，模型在去除噪声的同时，也可能平滑掉局部变化、重复规律及跨尺度特征。在脉冲噪声、非高斯噪声和非平稳干扰下，这一问题尤为突出。如何在抑制噪声的同时保留对下游任务有用的时间结构，是该研究关注的核心问题。

针对上述问题，论文提出一种以可微复杂度先验为核心的结构保持神经去噪框架，将排列熵、样本熵、Lempel–Ziv 复杂度和 Higuchi 分形维数四类经典时间序列描述指标引入神经网络训练。这些指标能够从局部排序、重复模式、符号序列及多尺度变化等角度刻画信号结构，但其中的排序、计数与离散解析等操作难以直接参与梯度计算。研究通过构建软近似、引入直通梯度估计及校准机制，使经典复杂度指标能够为端到端训练提供优化信号。

在此基础上，论文设计了三种相互配合的训练机制。首先，将多尺度复杂度特征与含噪信号共同输入网络，帮助模型识别局部结构；其次，以复杂度一致性约束对齐去噪结果与干净参考信号的结构特征，减少单纯优化采样点误差造成的结构损失；同时，根据噪声引起的复杂度变化安排训练样本，使模型在训练早期更多关注结构扰动较大的样本，再逐步恢复均匀采样。该框架可与卷积神经网络、Transformer、图神经网络等不同骨干结构结合。论文还在明确假设下，对软排序熵的噪声单调性及复杂度误差与判决间隔之间的关系给出了理论分析。

实验围绕通信信号去噪展开，并进一步考察了心电信号、模拟地震信号及间歇观测下的控制任务。在论文设定的通信实验中，相较于不使用复杂度一致性约束的匹配模型，加入该约束后，五个随机种子下的排列熵与 Higuchi 分形维数误差分别降低79.6%和63.0%；在六类去噪骨干网络的24项结构指标比较中，有21项得到改善。在每1.6秒获取一次观测的 Pendulum 动力学模型实验中，复杂度一致性约束使平均控制代价降低10.2%。这些结果表明，显式约束时间结构能够改善神经去噪的结构保真度，并在特定观测条件下为下游控制任务提供帮助。

蒋翔宇，西南财经大学计算机与人工智能学院博士生，研究方向为人工智能理论与应用。围绕神经网络去噪与时间序列结构建模开展研究，探索可微复杂度先验在信号恢复和动态系统建模中的应用。本次以第一作者身份完成的结构保持神经去噪研究被 NeurIPS 2026 录用。

认知计算与群智协同创新团队（CCCI）是西南财经大学依托互联网金融创新及监管四川省协同创新中心成立的一个跨学科研究团队。团队长期致力于探索机器学习、数据挖掘和金融科技等前沿领域，聚焦新型机器学习范式，围绕学习可持续、知识可传输、性能可使用、效率可控、隐私可保护、安全可证明等核心问题，深入研究具备人脑认知稳定性-可塑性能力的新一代人工智能理论和方法，努力推动人工智能新质生产力与数字经济的交叉融合发展和应用成果转化。

联系方式：杨新老师 yangxin@swufe.edu.cn

items.title: AI-driven technique could help engineers design analog chips faster and with less expense
items.content:
A new technique developed by MIT researchers could help engineers use artificial intelligence to streamline the design and innovation of analog integrated circuits, semiconductor chips that perform vital functions like communication and power management in electronic devices.

In the future, this method could allow engineers to prototype faster, explore a wider range of chip designs, and discover new design schemes that might improve the performance and energy efficiency of robots, medical monitors, or industrial sensors.

Designing analog integrated circuits that meet specific requirements is usually a cumbersome manual process due to the enormous number of possibilities. Frontier generative AI models have shown success in automating the process, but using these resource-intensive, cloud-hosted models could expose proprietary circuit design and semiconductor foundry data to malicious users.

The MIT method, called Small LM Iterating on Circuits, or SLIC (pronounced “slick”), enables engineers to train a small language model to perform analog circuit design as well as or better than a frontier large language model (LLM).

This small model is inexpensive and efficient enough to run on a laptop. Because it’s trained and deployed locally, it can use a company’s circuit design data without raising privacy risks.

When compared to complementary baselines and open-weight frontier LLMs, a small model trained by SLIC more effectively generated designs that achieved the circuit objectives.

“We’ve provided an alternative option to automate analog circuit design. With our technique, engineers can train a small, locally deployable model, using their own confidential data, and then deploy it in their own environment to ensure their assets remain protected,” says Yan Xu, an electrical engineering and computer science (EECS) graduate student and lead author of a [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13452v1) on this technique.

She is joined on the paper by senior author Ruonan Han, a professor of EECS and a member of the MIT Research Laboratory of Electronics; Zhengqi Gao PhD ’26; Wenjie Lu PhD ’18, a former MIT postdoc who is now a principal research scientist at Analog Devices, Inc.; Xin Zhang, a research manager at IBM Research; Duane S. Boning, the Clarence J. LeBel Professor in EECS and MIT vice provost for international activities; and others at IBM Research and Analog Devices. The research will be presented at the 2026 Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems.

“Through some specialized training and area-specific research, we can use much smaller models that consume far fewer resources to achieve almost the same results as flagship models in analog circuit design,” says Han. “This opens many more possibilities in the design of complex chips, especially if we care about costs, data privacy, and customization.”

**Mimicking human learning**

Analog integrated circuits enable a device to interact with the physical world. For instance, these circuits boost incoming wireless signals in smartphones and process outputs from sensors that track a car’s engine temperature.

Real-world signals tend to be unpredictable, so engineers must balance a wide and complex array of targets and tradeoffs to maximize analog circuit performance. This has made the design problem especially challenging for AI models.

“To design a circuit, engineers find a good starting point based on their intuition and then, drawing on their knowledge of circuit design, tune a few knobs toward the performance they want,” says Xu. “There is no universal way to solve every circuit design problem.”

Even if a powerful, cloud-based model could design a circuit as well as a human, most companies would be reluctant to send their foundry-specific data to external AI service providers.

With SLIC, the MIT researchers created a training method that teaches a smaller, less expensive, faster language model to design analog integrated circuits that meet user specifications.

The SLIC model uses a few billion parameters, making it several thousand times smaller than frontier models that use trillions of parameters and require enormous amounts of computational resources.

“We tried to mimic the behavior of how a human learns to design a circuit,” Xu says.

They used a technique called multi-turn reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where a model works through a multi-step task while adapting to environmental feedback.

When given an analog circuit optimization task, SLIC uses a large LLM to generate several demonstrations of the open source design process. Then SLIC then uses these demonstrations to guide the small model in mimicking this design process.

After the small model gains some initial knowledge about circuit design, SLIC lets it practice by tackling a new design problem on its own.

The model makes an initial guess of the design parameters, performs simulations, evaluates the results, and iteratively refines the design using knowledge it gained about analog circuits.

Once a design achieves the user’s goals, SLIC prioritizes additional marginal gains. This means the model keeps learning to make improvements that boost performance even when several designs meet the user-defined targets.

**An interpretable process**

Importantly, because SLIC employs models that describe their reasoning using natural language, the user can understand the decisions it makes along the way.

“Although the whole process is automated, the user can see what is going on inside the model. This could help the user gain some new ideas about circuit design, and it also adds a lot of confidence about the decision-making process,” Han says.

An engineer could utilize SLIC by adapting the researchers’ trained model to their data using a fine-tuning process. Or they could employ the SLIC training process to build their own model with company data, allowing for more customization.

“We are seeing an increasing demand for analog chips, but the speed of design has not kept up. This research is trying to bring new capabilities to AI to solve a problem that industry has been stuck on for decades,” Lu says.

When the researchers tested SLIC’s ability to design a circuit that met desired performance metrics, their small model came close to matching the performance of the latest GPT model (GPT-6-Astra). It did this while using a fraction of the computational resources.

The researchers also found that the SLIC model maintained its performance when tackling previously unseen circuit structures and adapting to more advanced technology nodes (design and manufacturing rules) and real commercial processes.

Because SLIC teaches a model the general chip design process, the system is not tied to any company. This makes it a more scalable approach that could be used by many organizations for a range of circuit applications.

“The knowledge the model has gained about circuit design is universal in nature. That is the powerful aspect of this tool,” Han says.

In the future, the researchers want to explore self-improving models that can independently learn to handle more diverse topologies and design targets. They also want to use SLIC to build a multi-agent framework, in which many small language models work on different parts of a complex circuit design task.

“Yan’s work shows that a locally deployable model can learn transferable design behavior and iterate with a circuit simulator to improve a design, which could reduce repetitive manual tuning for engineers. This is the kind of work the MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab makes possible. We see it as opening the door to more sophisticated custom design, including RF and microwave circuits, in the settings where industry actually works,” says Zhang.

This research is funded, in part, by Analog Device, Inc., IBM, and the John L. Ocampo Endowment Fund of MACOM Technology Solutions.

items.title: Z2RAM Claims SRAM Memory Speeds at Much Greater Density
items.content:
[Pat Gelsinger](https://www.linkedin.com/in/patgelsinger/) is familiar with the graveyard of failed memory technologies. “We haven’t had a new memory for three decades,” says the former Intel CEO. SRAM, DRAM, and flash memory still dominate. Gelsinger has witnessed the rise and fall of several potential alternatives—most recently [Optane](https://spectrum.ieee.org/has-intel-invented-a-universal-memory-tech), Intel’s failed attempt to create “universal memory.”

But Gelsinger, who is now a general partner at venture capital firm [Playground](https://www.playground.vc), believes that AI is forcing a rethink of the entire computing stack—and that memory is a key part of that shift.

Playground has backed [Nagare Labs](https://www.nagarelabs.ai/), a company spun out of Georgia Tech working on a prototype memory technology called Z2RAM. Instead of replacing existing memory, Z2RAM will attempt to offer a new layer in the existing memory stack that could prove useful for AI workloads and for other tasks that benefit from low latencies.

“This is an SRAM addition, rather than a DRAM replacement,” says [Suman Datta](https://www.linkedin.com/in/suman-datta-professor/), a Georgia Tech professor and former Intel transistor researcher. Datta cofounded Nagare Labs with colleague [Shimeng Yu](https://www.linkedin.com/in/shimeng-yu-60843648/). The company emerged from stealth on 26 October with US $5 million in funding led by [Playground](https://www.playground.vc/people).

## Z2RAM for Faster Memory

Datta says Z2RAM’s name also describes its design. “Z2” refers to two Zs: The first stands for stacking in the z (vertical) axis; the second stands for zero capacitor.

A conventional DRAM cell stores a bit as charge on a capacitor. Reading the bit drains it, so the data must be written back each time. That stretches DRAM access to 40 to 50 nanoseconds, Datta says.

Z2RAM ditches the capacitor and uses two transistors per cell instead. The first writes the bit and the second reads it without disturbing it, so the two operations no longer share a port as they do in DRAM, where every read drains the capacitor and causes a write-back. Putting the charge on the read transistor’s gate also amplifies the signal, so a smaller stored charge can still be sensed quickly.

Datta says this new design yields best-case estimated read speeds of one to two nanoseconds, making Z2RAM significantly faster than DRAM. And although it’s still not quite as fast as SRAM, it has the potential for much greater density. An SRAM cell is built in the same front-end design process as the processor it’s a part of, so every additional bit competes for area on an expensive logic die. In addition, [the size of an SRAM cell has proven increasingly difficult to shrink](https://spectrum.ieee.org/sram-intel-tsmc).

Nagare’s solution is to stack the bits. The company’s first generation of Z2RAM will target six layers, for a target density of 185 megabits per square millimeter. Datta says that’s about five times [what SRAM achieves](https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/tsmcs-n2-process-has-a-major-advantage-over-intels-18a-sram-density). Eventually he projects that the company could stack up to 106 layers, which, if it proves possible, would give Z2RAM a density 90 times as great as SRAM.

Datta says stacking is possible because Z2RAM’s transistors can be built with plasma-enhanced atomic layer deposition at less than 450 degrees Celsius. Although hot, it’s still relatively cool enough to add memory layers on top of a finished CMOS wafer without degrading it. Nagare’s plan is to tape out the memory’s control circuits first on a mature logic process, then build the memory array above, with multiple layers per lithography step. The finished chip can then be bonded on top of a processor as a chiplet.

## Overcoming Z2RAM Memory Stability Hurdles

Z2RAM’s goals still face notable technological hurdles. Datta says that when a write ends and the write transistor switches off, capacitive coupling from its control line disturbs the stored charge, which narrows the margin for reading the bit and could lead to read errors.

Nagare Labs’ answer is a patented metal shield inside each cell, which separates transistors. Using a shield is not without its downsides, as it makes each cell physically wider, which in turn reduces the memory’s density. Z2RAM expects vertical stacking to mitigate the issue.

Stability is another potential obstacle. “Right now the biggest challenge for oxide semiconductor transistors is the threshold voltage stability under bias and temperature stress,” Datta says. If the voltage at which a transistor turns on drifts, a stored bit can be misread. Fixing that issue requires tuning the channel, the gate stack, and the contacts together. Nagare is still experimenting with various recipes that use oxides of indium and gallium, sometimes with zinc added, as well as with tungsten-doped indium oxide, to find the best solution.

Making the connection between Z2RAM and a processor is the final hurdle, as there’s no standard for how this new kind of memory attaches to an AI chip. Datta sees an opening provided by high-bandwidth memory, where the industry is shifting from standard designs toward custom ones. Memory designs typically conform to standards by [JEDEC](https://www.jedec.org), an industry standards organization, but companies looking for memory to pair with AI accelerators are more amenable to a customized solution.

## Z2RAM for Edge AI and Robotics Latency

For Gelsinger, the next milestones are clear: Get the device out of a university lab, sign a fabrication partner, and demonstrate it on standard 300-millimeter wafers. He says the $5 million provided by Playground is only the start of what Nagare Labs will require to complete its work. “This will be multiple tranches of real funding,” he says. Datta agrees. “This company requires a lot of runway, both in terms of capital and time,” he says.

In addition to AI accelerators in data centers—a market that all memory technologies currently have in their crosshairs—Datta sees an opportunity in edge AI for robotics. He notes that robots may use a vision model that doesn’t require much memory capacity but that requires extremely low latencies to provide a real-time understanding of the environment. Such systems could be a good fit for Z2RAM.

For now, though, Datta is focused on the tricky path from R&D to Z2RAM’s first commercial memory chips, which could still be years away. “I always tell my students that the application will emerge just based on the capability of your technology,” he says.

items.title: Q&A: Enabling more human-like interactions and understanding in multimodal foundation models
items.content:
*Humans experience and interact with the world through sensory information. This could mean learning correspondences between the sound of bird chirps and the word “robin,” or being able to visually identify and follow your friend “Sarah” in a crowd of people. In many cases, people are able to draw on their latent “multimodal” knowledge — information across multiple data types, from audio to video to text or spoken word — to perform these tasks without many, or sometimes even any, examples.*

*Multimodal foundation models of artificial intelligence are increasingly gaining capabilities that mimic this. However, their apparent multimodal fluency often belies their actual understanding. An MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab team, co-led by Jim Glass, senior research scientist in the MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, has been investigating critical failures of state-of-the-art multimodal models and developing benchmarks and data-efficient methods to overcome these performance gaps with limited supervision. He speaks about this work in the following interview.*

**Q:**What were your goals for this project, and why would you opt to address AI models’ weaknesses over scaling to larger models?

**A:** This project has been going on for many years now, with roughly the same MIT-IBM team of speech and vision experts. We've wanted to explore the relationship between perception (things that you see and hear) and language, largely speaking: We have all of this absorbed knowledge and language skills, text-based, in the form of a large language model, so we wanted to know how you can relate them without using a whole bunch of annotated training data. Sometimes the models have seen certain phenomena, a latent representation of something that they have internally, but maybe due to subsequent fine-tuning or something, it disappears, so, developing techniques to try to make this capability re-emerge is a useful thing.

As you study these publicly available models, you can see weaknesses even in big ones, so I think it's important to try to address these limitations. If you had an unlimited budget, you could go out and create the annotations that you need, but it's also good to be able to try to get these models to learn more on their own. We’ve done that by creating novel benchmarks that we can evaluate against, then developing techniques that perform better on these benchmarks, and getting these models to learn on their own. Throughout our research collaboration — and this has very much been a strong collaboration between MIT and IBM — we have continued to release public benchmarks for people to use, and that's a lasting artifact.

I think the overriding themes are multimodalities with language models, trying to address the shortcomings of these models, and trying to develop techniques that do not require a lot of annotated data to complete tasks better.

**Q:**Can you walk us through how the project has evolved?

**A:** When we first started this project, we were trying to build models that could learn correspondences automatically, not telling the machine anything more than, “This audio caption goes with this picture,” sort of like reading a picture book to a child who's learning language. We would just show it these matching examples, and we'd show it mismatching examples. They could learn that the sequence of sounds that says “lighthouse” corresponds to a picture of a lighthouse, without any text being involved.

Moving beyond speech was to include general audio, and then we started looking at video instead of still images. We would train the model, showing it matching video sequences with the corresponding audio stream and then mismatching ones, and make it reconstruct them. We would also mask some of the images or the audio, and have the model reconstruct it. The model would learn strong relationships; then, far beyond speech, it would learn what parrots sound like, or electric guitars versus acoustic guitars, for example.

Then, when these large language models started coming out — and this was in the early days, before it had been done by the big companies — we started to learn correspondences between audio and language. Since that time, these large multimodal models have become available, and we've started looking at what some of the limitations of these models are, and are trying to improve upon them with these more or less supervised techniques.

**Q:**What would you say are some recent highlights of your work?

**A:** Our [IPLoc research](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2411.13317v2) was looking at the fact that these state-of-the-art models, like GPT-40, can't localize specific objects, given just a few-shot examples. We came up with this technique where we would train it with a pseudonym substitution. There's an example there where we replaced “airplane” with “Elizabeth.” It forces the model to not fall back on things that it had previously learned about and pay more attention to the visual context.

Then, we had an audio-based paper, [OmniR1](https://sls.csail.mit.edu/archives/root/publications/2025/ARouditchenko_ASRU-2025.pdf), that was looking at audio-large language models, so these are models that can listen to something and talk about them. One of the disturbing things we found is some of these benchmarks are [multiple-choice answers](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2026/file/d6c01b025cad37d5c8bab4ba18846c02-Paper-Conference.pdf). A lot of times, these models aren't really listening to the sound, but they're almost gaming the question by looking at the answer. What animal is roaring in this audio — like a chipmunk, a lion, an alligator, and a chickadee, or something? It's not even really paying attention to the audio, [but] just going, “Oh, lion.” Part of the reason people do that is that it’s simple to evaluate, whereas if you asked for a text response, you’d somehow have to grade whether it’s accurate. Do you get humans to evaluate it, which can be expensive and time-consuming, or do you use some other language model to be the judge that can have its own set of issues as well? One way to address that is to evaluate these models on a variety of different kinds of benchmarks.

We realized you could feed random noise, and they were still doing quite well, which shows that they're just paying attention to the question. So, we tried to develop some methods to have it pay more attention to the audio and minimize this behavior.

**Q:**Given resource constraints, what is your approach to adapting these large foundation models, and what blend of AI and algorithmic methods do you use that don't require extensive annotated data?

**A:** These days, we can't create one of these very large foundation models ourselves. We don't have the resources to do that, so we're tending to use these available models and trying to adapt them, train them in a weakly supervised way, methods that don't require as much data, like our work on [test-time reinforcement learning](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2026/papers/Singh_TTRV_Test-Time_Reinforcement_Learning_for_Vision_Language_Models_CVPR_2026_paper.pdf).

Our project was not monolithic, in the sense that we're not all working on one thing. It's more like a thousand flowers bloom, so there's no one particular way that we're approaching things.

**Q:**In the near future, how do you see multimodal research evolving in your MIT-IBM research team?

**A:** Over the years, we probably produced two dozen or so significant collaborative papers, and during this work, it was amazing to me that the machines could learn these correspondences without being told anything. No one had ever shown that machines could do it before we did that. Some of our early work combining audio with large language models was fun, too: seeing the model talk about what it heard and then having a conversation with it. Now, we are starting to take this for granted, but at the time, it was fun to see.

Moving forward, for the coming year, with our MIT-IBM collaboration, we're going to switch gears a little bit and focus more on what's known as full-duplex spoken dialogue systems. These are models that are listening while they’re talking, so it’s more like how humans operate, and this is quite different from what we’ve been doing up until now, which is joint audio-visual work, which we will also continue.

Now, we’ll be focusing on the speech side of things. These full-duplex models have suddenly become an interesting thing to look at, because they would move you away from the rigid turn-taking approach that is used right now when you're talking to some of these models. Ultimately, I think they will be more natural to interact with.

These full-duplex models are just starting to emerge, and some of the ones that are publicly available aren't as good as the big, large language models. They can handle some of these low-level communication skills, but they're still missing some things, like the concept of time, or knowledge depth. So, we're working on trying to address some of these issues.

*This research has been conducted in coordination with the MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab teams of* [*Rogerio Feris*](https://research.ibm.com/people/rogerio-feris)*,* [*Brian Kingsbury*](https://research.ibm.com/people/brian-kingsbury)*, and* [*Samuel Thomas*](https://research.ibm.com/people/samuel-thomas) *of IBM Research, and* [*Hilde Kuehne*](https://hildekuehne.github.io/about.html) *of the University of Tuebingen, who is an MIT-IBM affiliated researche*r.

items.title: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.
items.content:
Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.

The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as [OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai) or [Vercel](https://vercel.com/) that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.

**Update, Nov 21:** Posts on both [Hacker News](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50585962) and [X](https://x.com/michael_chomsky/status/2124008002571428224) report that OpenRouter has sent customers an email notifying them that some of their prompts may have been read. OpenRouter cited the research and said that it received a report that the potential exposure involved prompts sent to MiniMax, a China-based model provider. OpenRouter said the researchers' planted URLs were accessed whether the prompts were sent to MiniMax directly or through three other resellers: AtlasCloud, Novita, and StreamLake. OpenRouter has removed a "Zero Data Retention" label from MiniMax-model endpoints. Hat tip: [Sulat.com](https://news.sulat.com/2026/11/21/openrouter-minimax-prompts/).

[Read full article](https://arstechnica.com/security/2026/11/a-leaky-ai-supply-chain-is-exposing-secret-user-data-at-an-alarming-rate/)

items.title: Man hired by Russia spied on Silicon Valley tech and defense company, feds say
items.content:
A Russian national has been indicted on suspicions he was a Russian spy who stalked and surveilled employees of a Silicon Valley company that was assisting Ukraine in its ongoing war with its eastern neighbor.

Igor D’iu, 25, allegedly photographed the employees and their computer screens as they worked at a coffee shop located near the company’s Palo Alto office, federal prosecutors [said Wednesday](https://www.justice.gov/usao-ndca/pr/russian-national-indicted-acting-foreign-agent-russia-target-silicon-valley-technology). He also kept a list of home addresses of employees and a senior executive. At one point, prosecutors said, D’iu trailed an employee as she traveled home from Palo Alto to San Francisco. An [affidavit](https://www.justice.gov/usao-ndca/media/1472991/dl?inline) filed in the case referred to the employee as FEMP1, short for female employee, and said the event left her “in a state of emotional distress.”

## Evasive and irregular turns

“FEMP1 made evasive and irregular turns, took back roads, and turned into a grocery store parking lot where D’IU continued aggressively following her vehicle,” an FBI special agent wrote. “D’IU followed FEMP1 through U-turns, illegal left turns, and ran a red light to stay with FEMP1 for nearly thirty miles. FEMP1 called 911 while driving and was instructed to drive directly to San Francisco Police Department (“SFPD”) Mission Station. Near SFPD Mission Station, FEMP1 flagged an SFPD patrol vehicle and reported the incident. D’IU left once FEMP1 made contact with the patrol vehicle.”

[Read full article](https://arstechnica.com/security/2026/11/man-charged-with-spying-on-silicon-valley-tech-and-defense-company-for-russia/)

items.title: How to tell a cyberattack from a plain old outage
items.content:
Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a *Diehard IV*–style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US.

Across just four consecutive business days, a [mass Microsoft exchange outage](https://www.wired.com/story/major-microsoft-outlook-outage-hits-365-customers-north-america/) broke IT services [for thousands of companies](https://www.wired.com/story/the-microsoft-outage-is-a-warning-for-the-world/), a Federal Aviation Administration [tech screw-up](https://www.wired.com/story/the-faa-nationwide-ground-stop-is-over/) [grounded airplanes](https://www.wired.com/story/faa-grounds-all-us-flights-until-further-notice/) across the country, a [software problem](https://www.wired.com/story/jpmorganchase-bank-outage-oh-come-on/) affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a [United Airlines system glitch](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/united-airlines-system-outage-rcna609712) delayed flights yet again, and an [NSA classified network’s downtime](https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/17/politics/highly-classified-national-security-communications-network-goes-down) left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. In the midst of a [US war with Iran](https://www.wired.com/story/iran-linked-hackers-are-sabotaging-us-energy-and-water-infrastructure/) and rising fears of [AI-enabled hacking](https://www.wired.com/story/openai-sued-over-the-hugging-face-hack/), this still-unfolding comedy of IT errors colliding across American infrastructure felt to plenty of observers like more than a coincidence.

Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack.

[Read full article](https://arstechnica.com/security/2026/11/how-to-tell-a-cyberattack-from-a-plain-old-outage/)
